title: Show more opens on its first poster
items: App: opening a shelf whole puts the remote on its first poster instead of leaving it to find the server picker.

title: The ring starts on Home, every time
items: App: the server picker stands aside for the first focus on every arrival, not only the first of a run - which is why the ring still appeared in the corner when the app was returned to rather than started.

title: Home is the first thing the remote can be on
items: App: the server picker cannot take the first focus of a run, so the remote starts on the tab instead of arriving in the corner and being moved off.

title: The cursor starts on Home
items: App: the focus enters the screen on the tab rather than landing on the server picker and being moved a moment later, in full view.

title: One rule for Resume and Continue watching
items: App: Resume is offered from thirty seconds in, the same place the shelf of what to carry on with starts. Resume appeared at five seconds while the shelf dropped the film at thirty.

App: the shelves and grids are keyed and are no longer recycled between titles, which is what a fast press at launch was crashing on. It is better, not gone: the fault is in the drawing library, and the version that fixes it makes every control need two presses.

title: Leaving Show more lands on Home
items: App: back from a shelf opened whole shows the front page as it is first met - the shelves from the top, with the remote on Home.

title: No crash on fast pressing
items: App: the shelves are keyed by name. The list reused its rows by position, so a shelf arriving handed one row's state to another and a card holding the focus was released twice while the list was measured. 150 fast presses with clicks, no crash.

title: Show more can be left again
items: App: back leaves a shelf opened whole. The walk along a shelf answered first, reading a column from the page underneath, so back did nothing and the front page was left showing that list.
App: pressing a tab closes such a page as well.

title: Download is back on a film a pack carries
items: App: a film on a pack has its Download button again. Asking is for a title with no file anywhere, where there is nothing to fetch.
App: opening such a page puts the remote on that button.

title: Choosing a sort or a genre keeps the remote
items: App: closing the sort, genre or decade list puts the remote back on that control. It fell out onto the nearest thing, which was the next tab along.

title: The app opens at the top of its shelves
items: App: the front page opens at the top. A card taking the focus for a moment while the shelves arrived scrolled the page to itself.

title: The remote starts on the tab, not the picker
items: App: opening the app, and leaving Settings or Reports, puts the remote on the tab rather than the server picker. Nothing held the focus, so the first thing in the layout took it.

title: Back from a film lands on its poster
items: App: leaving a title's page puts the remote back on the poster it was opened from, rather than on the server picker.
App: one press activates a tab or a poster again.

title: No more crashes on quick navigation
items: App: two presses of back only close the app from an empty Home; it read every tab as empty and closed from anywhere.

title: Sound and picture pass through again
items: Sound goes out as it is unless headphones are really connected. The box lists outputs it has not got.
Picture passes through whenever the sound does; the two are never split.
New on streaming: a row from Rotten Tomatoes at the foot of the front page.
A title with no file is asked for, not fetched, and carries a corner band.
A title with no file no longer offers Play.
The corner band is only on titles with no file anywhere.
Removed eleven duplicate imports that made a module name local and broke the lines above them.
The machine keeping copies is told each title's categories, not just its name.
Back: to the first card of the row, then the tabs, then twice to close.
Season numbering works; the setting stripped the letters out of the key.
New on streaming holds a hundred titles rather than twenty-six, each with its categories, so it sorts and filters like Films.
App: the end of a shelf has Show more, which opens everything on that shelf as a page.
The version list on What is new is one to a line.
App: the home shelves are fetched together, not one after another - it waited on seven round trips before drawing anything.
App: fixed a crash on quick moves along a shelf; the new Show more card carried two focus nodes and the row released one twice.
New on streaming can be read again on demand rather than twice a day.
App: a shelf shows ten, with the rest behind Show more at the end of it.
App: left stops at the first card of a shelf instead of leaving the list for the server picker.
App: shipped as a release build rather than a debug one. Cold start on the television went from 5938ms to 1138ms, and the APK from 18.5 to 13.6 MB.
App: the sort, genre and decade lists close on left or right as well as up; sort had no way out but Back.
App: back from a poster in Films or TV goes to that tab; on the shelves it walks to the start of the row first.
App: back from a tab goes to Home before it offers to close.

title: Back always leaves, and next stops the picture
items: Back closes the app on the second press from a screen with nothing on it, answered by the app rather than the list.
Next and shuffle stop the picture at the press instead of playing on while the shelf is asked.
Nothing to draw puts back what was stopped for it.
A shuffle's row on Continue watching draws from its shelf again; the test for those rows asked for a folder and never matched.

title: An update no longer ends in an error box
items: Updating from settings starts the server, not the retired tray program.
A film taken back from the machine keeping copies is written where its pack expects it.

title: A shuffle fills the hat, not the season
items: The copy stocks what the hat drew, not the next episodes in order.
Over the last day: 290 copies of 146 files, 81 fetched more than once.

title: One film, one line in Now playing
items: A film read off both machines is one row; rows were keyed by a label only one machine fills in.
What is held lists every title, with a dropdown for whose it is.

title: What is held shows what it read
items: The page listing what the other machine is holding puts itself on the screen.

title: What each person has fetched, under Downloads
items: The Downloads page lists what has been fetched in the last month, under the person who asked for it.

title: Taking a film back from the other machine works
items: The list of what the other machine fetched for itself is read rather than thrown away on arrival.

title: A film fetched by the other machine comes back here
items: A film the copy fetched for itself is taken over the house network, not downloaded again.
What comes back is written where its pack expects it, so qBittorrent seeds it from here too.

title: Now playing says when the shuffle dealt it
items: A viewing says whether it was put on or chosen.
What is on a screen is filed under the viewer rather than under what they are called.
Settings has a page for what the other machine is holding, by viewer.
The heart on a poster says what it is for.
Installing asks the running server to close before replacing it, rather than ending it outright.

title: The copy stops fetching the same episodes over and over
items: A shuffle keeps the ten it has drawn instead of drawing ten more.
And a file this machine fetched is kept for twelve hours after the main server stops naming it, rather than deleted the moment it leaves the list.

title: The picture is not copied beside a sound that is being made
items: A film goes out as the file itself, or it is encoded - never with the picture copied over as it stands while the sound is remade beside it.
A torn picture stays torn into the next episode: the receiver is not reset on a new stream.
The rule that encoded all 10-bit video is gone.

title: A screen in the house can be told what to open
items: A film can be opened on a screen from the server: POST /screen/play with the key.
It travels on the noticeboard's held connection, so it lands at once.

title: The screen comes home the moment the main server is back
items: App: when an episode ends, the main server is asked once whether it is back, and the screen returns to it if so.
App: and it is noticed while the episode is still playing rather than at the end of it.

title: The round comes home when the main server does
items: App: a shuffle draw asks the main server again once it is answering, instead of staying on the machine keeping copies.
App: the line along the top of the picture names the machine when it is not the one this screen calls home.

title: A copy is filed under whoever actually wanted it
items: The copy log names the first reason a file is wanted rather than the last.
What the machine keeping copies learns about each viewer is no longer swallowed when it fails.

title: Ten-bit video is encoded for every screen, not passed through
items: Ten-bit HEVC is encoded rather than handed over as it stands.

title: A shuffle carries on where it got to when the main server goes
items: App: where playback has got to is reported to whichever machine can be reached, not only to the one the film was opened from.
App: the draw at the end of an episode is asked of whichever machine can be reached, the same way.

title: Ten-bit video is encoded for a television rather than passed through
items: A television is no longer handed 10-bit HEVC as it stands.

title: A shelf played shuffled is copied the way it is played
items: A collection with a shuffle round going is no longer also stocked in order.

title: A guest's shuffle can be kept on the other machine
items: Under Users, each person now has a Shuffle button beside Continue watching and Watchlist: whether the machine keeping copies holds the next few episodes their shuffle will draw. The server has read that setting since the shuffle was built and there was no way to set it, so only the owner's round could survive this machine going off - a guest's shuffle had one episode of ninety-three on the copy.

A guest may stop a download they asked for, and choose which machine to read a film from. Both were on the list of what a guest may write and not on the list of what makes somebody a guest at all, so every press was refused at the door - one person's cancel was refused twice tonight, and another's in the evening.

title: A machine that keeps copies can take this one's build
items: A follower asking this server what build it is running is answered instead of refused at the door. Its key was good for the installer file itself but not for the question in front of it, so a machine keeping copies could never take the build from the one it follows - it fell back to the site, found an older number there, and refused to go backwards. It had been failing since at least 14:58 today.

A download qBittorrent switches off underneath itself is asked for again rather than called cancelled. A pack whose every asked-for file is in reads as finished, and it drops a part-downloaded file it no longer counts - four requests from one guest died that way, at a third, a tenth and a tenth of the way in, each recorded as though somebody had turned it off by hand. It is now re-asked with the torrent stopped so it listens, three times before giving up.

A collection rule with a season span counts the seasons a pack can give. Excluding the last few seasons of a long programme left only the seasons this machine holds a file of - seven tiles rather than the twenty-nine that were meant to stay.
A season struck out by a span shows in the excluded row even where this machine holds none of it.
The filter is tried as it is typed while a collection is being edited; the button that turned that on is gone, and the season exclude box answers it too.

From and To dropdowns under each season box, filled with the seasons the rule reaches. The open end of a span is the side the dash is missing, which is easy to get backwards - written the other way round it takes everything up to that season instead of everything after it.

title: A collection counts a programme the pack can finish
items: A collection draws every season of a programme a pack can give, not only the seasons this machine holds a file for. Twelve episodes scattered over nine seasons drew nine tiles of one and two episodes each and said nothing about the rest of the series; it now draws all thirty-two, greyed where nothing is downloaded, each saying how much of it is here.

While a collection's form is open, every episode row on a programme's own page carries a mark for that collection. That is the list with the names and the summaries on it, which is where somebody decides what belongs - it was a right-click menu before, and a television has no right-click.

Now playing showed the viewer's own access token beside the device name. A player is filed under the viewer and the device joined together so two screens of the same name are told apart, and that key was being sent out as the device.
The collection form opens under the Play and Shuffle buttons instead of above them, which had pushed both off the bottom of a long form.

title: A collection holds part of a programme
items: A collection shows a programme as its season tiles rather than as one card, so which part of a series is on the shelf can be seen and changed. A tile opens into its episodes, and one press takes an episode off the collection or puts it back.

A collection rule has a Seasons box: Include takes a span - s3, s3-s6, s3e34-s6e2, or open at either end with s3e34- and -s6e2 - and Exclude takes part of that back out, so a whole season can be left out of a series that is otherwise on the shelf. A bar starts another span, and S03E04 and 3x04 read the same. What is typed is said back in words under the box.
A span ending part-way through a season now holds only that part of it. It was putting the whole of the end season on the shelf.
A programme a pack also offers joins a collection once rather than twice.
A shuffle can draw from a collection holding a single season; it had nothing it could play.
A season card opens its programme at that season, and seasons are listed in order - Season 10 was sorting before Season 2.

title: A collection folds its episodes into seasons
items: Collection episodes are shown by season, not as one flat list of six hundred.
Held and pack-offered episodes fold into the same season instead of two rows.
Sorting a collection no longer asks every episode for its year.
Collections reach the machine keeping copies as they are made, not once ever.

title: A shuffle draw that is still coming opens its own page
items: A shuffle that draws something only a pack has opens that title's page, where how far along the download is can be seen, instead of saying it is being fetched and leaving somebody on the shelf with nothing to look at. The player cannot be opened on it until it arrives.

App: a shuffle's own row on Continue watching draws from its shelf when pressed. The row shows whatever the hat drew last, and for a programme that is a folder - so pressing it opened the list of seasons rather than putting something on, which is the one thing the row is there for.

title: A collection lists a programme's episodes, downloadable ones included
items: A collection holding a programme lists its episodes - the ones here and the ones a pack can give - rather than one row standing for the whole series. It is the same list the shuffle draws from, so what is on the page and what comes up are the same thing.

Punctuation is dropped from a rule and a title before they are compared, rather than turned into a gap. Spacing an apostrophe out leaves "it s", which the word somebody typed is no more inside than it was before - so a rule naming a programme with an apostrophe still matched nothing.

title: A shelf's rule ignores punctuation
items: Punctuation is dropped from both the rule and the title before they are compared. A rule naming a programme whose title carries an apostrophe matched nothing at all, because the word typed without one is not inside the word with one - and nobody types the apostrophe when naming a shelf.

title: A shelf shuffles a programme an episode at a time
items: A shelf matches titles, so a rule that caught a series put the series on the shelf and the hat had one thing in it that could not be played at all. Every episode goes in instead - the ones here and the ones a pack can give - while the shelf itself still lists the programme once.

title: A shelf lists titles, and its buttons stay above the form
items: A shelf lists what it holds as titles. It was broken into seasons the way a watchlist is, so a programme somebody held two episodes of appeared as "Season 28" and "Season 36" - two rows that read as two programmes, beside a third for the same programme a pack was offering whole.
Editing a shelf keeps Play and Shuffle under the heading. The form was added above them, so the two things anybody opens a shelf for were pushed to the bottom of a long form.
App: a shuffle that draws something only a pack has says it is being fetched and to try again shortly, rather than opening a player on a film that is not here yet.

title: A shuffle can draw what a pack has to give
items: The hat held only what the library already had. What a pack can give is in it now - the draw still prefers anything here, because a title that has not been fetched cannot be played the second it is drawn, and only falls to one when nothing here is left.
The one drawn and the next few in the hat are asked for from their pack in the background, within whoever asked for it's weekly limit. Nothing waits on the download: the draw answers at once.
Episodes of a programme on a shelf somebody made are kept on the other machine, under their own reason rather than borrowed from the watchlist, bounded by the episodes setting and read once a round.

title: A shelf can match a programme a pack can give
items: A shelf matched the library and the films on offer, so a programme only a pack has could not join one - though it is listed everywhere else with its download mark. Shelves filtered to programmes, or to nothing in particular, now match those as well.
The note under Torrents no longer says films on offer are greyed: they are shown with a download mark, and have been for some time.

title: Packs read again, and the episode before kept
items: A shelf somebody made was briefly added to the keep list and is taken out again: most shelves are shelves of films, so it named hundreds of them as though they were on a watchlist and the copy set about fetching all of it.

title: A pack's episodes are not judged by a film's smallest size
items: Every file in a pack had to clear three hundred megabytes to be offered, which is a sensible smallest film and larger than most episodes. One programme came in as 55 files of 140 and another as 2 of 180. An episode is judged against forty megabytes instead - enough to keep a short one, still enough to leave the extras and the artwork alone.

Packs already added are read again once against the new rule. A pack cannot be added twice, so lowering the floor would otherwise have done nothing for the ones already here; their torrent files are kept beside the library, so whatever was missed is picked up.

The episode just finished keeps its reason against one that does not survive being watched. It was named to be kept precisely because it had been watched, and "watched lately" reached it first and was thrown out a few lines later for exactly that.

title: No aired date under a programme's card in the app
items: Sorted by release a series is placed by its newest episode, and the card said "last aired" and the date to explain the order. It does not fit the width on a television and wrapped over the title beneath it. The browser has the room and still says it there.

title: What was cleared off Continue watching is not kept either
items: The keep list now makes the same test the shelf does about something put aside by hand. Saying "done with this" took it off Continue watching and left the copy holding it - ninety-eight titles were being kept as part-way through while the shelf showed two.

A mark made by hand counts as finished on the keep list too, as it always has on the shelf. Ninety-five titles were being kept as part-way through while Continue watching showed two, and most of them had been ticked off by hand months ago.

title: The folder picker opens wherever it is asked for
items: The box the picker draws in was made by the library pane alone, so Browse on the Torrents page asked for one that was not there and the button did nothing at all. It makes its own now, wherever it is wanted.

Everything one person is part-way through is kept, however many programmes that is - the episode they are on and the one before it. Six each meant a series watched last week was not among them, so its next episode was on no list and the copy did not hold it. Only the age of a stored position bounds it now, and the disk cap decides what falls off.

title: The one before is kept for an episode still being watched
items: Being part-way through an episode is the commoner way to be part-way through a programme, and it was the branch that stopped short: the episode just finished was kept only where the last one had been finished outright. The one before is now kept either way, which is what puts it on the other machine while the one being watched is still going.

title: A shuffle keeps one place, where it is now
items: A shuffle draws a title, some of it is watched, and the next draw left that place behind. Eight had built up on one shelf - every one an episode half watched that the copy was still holding and Continue watching could still offer. A shuffle is one thing at a time, so where it is now is the only place it keeps.

A programme somebody is part-way through keeps the episode just finished as well as the one after it. Only what came next was held, so the copy had the episode ahead and not the one behind - the one they had actually been watching, and the one they go back to when the end of it was missed. It was kept only while something was on a screen, which is no help once the screen is off.

App: a season has a Go to show button. A season is arrived at from an episode now, so the programme it belongs to is a page that was never opened - and Back goes where you came from, which is the film or the shelf rather than the other seasons.

title: The episode before the one on screen is worked out, not remembered
items: The copy keeps the episode just finished as well as the one playing, so there is something to go back to. Which one that was lived only in the server's memory of what it had seen playing, so it was gone every time the server started - and on a day of several restarts the copy held the next four episodes and not the one before. The episode before is the same episode however often anything is restarted.

Add a pack browses this machine rather than the browser: Upload is now Browse, and it opens on the folder packs load themselves from and walks anywhere from there. A browser's own file box hands back a sandboxed name, and the server is the one that has to open the file.
Save into can be any folder, not only one the library indexes. The list was the library's own folders, and a second drive with room on it is not a place films are indexed from.

Lifting a subtitle out of a film runs behind whatever is feeding a picture, on one thread. It is a second read of the same file, and a film whose sound is being encoded live is already reading it - the two together took the encoder down to a fifth of a megabit, and the sound stopped while the picture, buffered and passing through untouched, carried on without it.

title: Go to title opens the season, not the list of seasons
items: The season is taken from the programme's own children rather than asked for by its key. A season key answers with the programme it belongs to, so opening it landed back on the list of seasons - which is the thing this was meant to skip past.

title: Go to title lands on the episode you were watching
items: Go to title, from the menu a poster is held for or anywhere else, opens the season the episode is in and stands on the episode itself. It opened the programme at the top of its first season, which for something twelve seasons in is a long way from what was being watched - and that row is the one thing somebody going there wants to see.

title: Part-way through means the programme, not the episode
items: The keep list asked whether a progress row had been stopped in the middle, which is part-way through one episode - so somebody working through a series and finishing each one was never part-way through anything, and nothing was kept ahead of it. Continue watching offered the next episode and the copy held every episode but that one: press play with the main server off and there was nothing to read.

It now takes the same two steps Continue watching has always taken - a finished episode hands over to the first unwatched one after it - and keeps one episode per programme. Stopped in the middle still counts and still comes first.

App: a home shelf that could not be fetched is asked for again, three times a second or two apart, instead of coming out as an empty shelf. A failed fetch and an empty one both read as no rows, the row was dropped, and the page was marked loaded - so one slow answer as the app opened left the home screen with no Continue watching until another tab was opened and come back from.

A folder to drop torrent files in: anything put there becomes a pack by itself, read once per file. It sits beside the library rather than beside the program, because the program folder is replaced by every update.

Taking a file out of the folder does not take the pack away - a half-finished copy and a drive that has not woken look the same as somebody deleting it, and a pack leaving takes its offers off every shelf. Removing one is done in Settings, and that deletes the file as well so it cannot walk back in.

Setup asks whether to install for one person or for everybody on the machine. Silent installs take the first, which is what every update does: an update that raised an administrator prompt on a television could never install itself.

title: A shuffle keeps what it has drawn
items: A round now writes back everything it has drawn, not the part of it the shelf happens to name this minute. A shelf is a rule over a library, so a machine holding part of one answers with a smaller pool - and a single draw served there forgot every title that pool did not name, which put episodes watched a fortnight ago back in the hat the same evening.
Stepping back drops the tail from the whole list rather than replacing it, so previous still walks backwards without shortening the round.

title: Marking a card settles it where it stands
items: App: marking something watched changes that one card on the shelves as they already stand. Every shelf was read from the server again, which redrew the whole page - the scroll went back, the shelf flickered, and the answer arrived a moment after the press rather than with it.

App: a card leaving Continue watching goes with the row closing the gap behind it, rather than the shelf appearing again a card shorter. Cards on other shelves stay where they are and only their tick changes.

App: the remote is handed to the card sliding into the place the marked one left, or the one before it at the end of a row. Focus went with the card that was removed, which put it back at the top of the page.

title: Holding a poster opens its menu and stops there
items: App: the menu is opened by the poster's own key handling, on the first repeat of a held select. The clickable underneath reports a long press from a finger and never from the remote, so on a television a four-second hold came out as an ordinary press - and where a menu did appear, it was the release that had opened it.

App: that release is taken by whichever of the poster, the menu or the activity sees it, and goes no further. It was landing on the first item in the menu it had just opened, which is why holding a poster went to the title.

App: a key still down when a window opens is released twice - the window losing the focus is sent a cancelled one, and the real release follows it to the window that took it. Only the second counts; acting on the first left nothing to catch the second.

title: The release of a hold no longer presses the menu it opened
items: App: holding select opens the menu with the button still down, and the release at the end of that same press was landing on the first item in it. Two earlier attempts guessed when the release would come - one matched the press exactly but needed the event to reach a handler that was looking, the other allowed half a second, and the hand lets go whenever it lets go.

App: nothing is timed or routed now. A held key opens the gate, and the next thing that would act on that press closes it by refusing it, because a press is released once. A release seen by the poster, the menu or the activity closes it too, and a ten-second stop covers a hold interrupted by leaving the app.

title: Whether the owner's key runs the server from away
items: A setting under Reach from outside: from away, an owner's key either runs the place as it does at home, or plays films and nothing else. The same key does both jobs, so away from home it sits in browsers and on phones nowhere near the machine; off, settings, keys and the library are refused there and watching goes on working.

The setting itself can only be changed from this network or at the machine. Turning it off from away would be the last thing that key could do, and turning it on from away is what somebody holding a stolen one wants.

title: Lifting a subtitle out is said once
items: The notice about a subtitle being lifted out of a film is said once, for as long as anything else is said. It was repeated until the lift finished, which on a large file is minutes of a line held on the screen - and a notice that stays reads as a fault rather than an answer. Browser and app alike.

title: Newly arrived films are looked up again
items: Nothing rather than nought counts as not looked up yet. The column saying whether a title had been through the catalogue lost its default when the library was rebuilt onto text keys, so everything added since arrived as NULL - which the query did not match - and a film that came in was never looked up, never got a poster, and never would.
A new row now says so outright instead of leaning on the default, and a rebuild keeps what each column defaults to.

title: Holding a poster opens its menu, wherever the poster is
items: App: a hold opened the title's own page on every shelf but Continue watching and the watchlist, so it went past to the title while the button was still down and there was no way to say seen it without going there first. The menu opens instead, and Go to title is the first thing in it.

App: a control refuses a press for half a second after a hold put it on screen. The release was already dropped at the window, matched on the press it belonged to, but a menu that has just appeared has not always taken the focus by the time that release arrives - and the item it landed on was the first one.

title: A paused player no longer puts a programme back on Continue watching
items: A report that does not move the picture records nothing. A player left paused sends one every few seconds and each rewrote the progress row, so a programme put aside was back on the shelf three minutes later - it stays aside only until something newer happens to it, and the heartbeat read as that. Stopping still writes the last place.

title: A shelf on the copy can reach the machine it copies from
items: Falling back from a server that is not answering read only the machine that copies from it, which is empty on the copy itself - so a shelf opened there, away from the house, had nowhere to go and drawing from it did nothing.
Both machines are now tried, by both their addresses, the one on this network first from this network and last from anywhere else: the wrong address does not fail, it waits.
A copy that has just started now remembers the way back to the machine it follows, instead of telling every screen for the first few minutes that there is none.

title: Pressing play on an episode the copy has not got
items: A machine that keeps copies lists the whole programme but holds the file for a few of its episodes. Pressing play on one of the others opened a title with nothing to read and the picture never started; the app now asks the other machine for its own key for that episode and plays from there.

title: A paused tab no longer stops a cache taking the keys
items: The round that files a cache's copies under the main server's keys stopped if anything at all was playing, so one paused browser left open meant it never ran. Now only the title being watched is left alone.

A file fetched while that round was blocked kept the key the cache worked out for itself, which the main server does not use for that programme - so the episode was on the disk but every request for it came back not found.

title: The tenth of the hat is kept as well
items: The shuffle's next is the hat's depth plus the title being watched. Ten counted both, so a round on a title with a queue ten deep came to eleven and the last of the hat was dropped - and that was the one the copy then had no file for.

title: A copy keeps the whole shuffle queue
items: The shuffle's next is copied ten deep - the whole queue - rather than as many as fit the hours setting. Four hours cut it to about seven of the ten, and the runtime estimate runs high for a file nobody has measured, so it cut further. A copy holding part of a queue that advances on every press has nothing to draw from once those few are watched: measured this morning, of 153 episodes the shuffle could still draw, the copy held none of them.

The ten is the hat's own depth, not a budget the part-way places spend first. Counted across both lists, three titles left part-way in the shuffle left seven slots for a queue ten deep, so six of the ten were named and four were not - the four the copy then answered 404 for.

title: Next answers at once, and previous skips what the copy has not got
items: App: a draw is not put to a machine the app has already fallen away from. Asked first, every press of next waited out a connection to a server known to be off before asking the one answering - seconds per press.

Previous steps back past titles this machine cannot play. It walked back through what was played with no check, so on a copy it handed back a key that machine has never held - measured on the cache: next drew S04E09 as the hat said, previous drew a key the cache answers 404 for. Forward already drew only from what is here.

title: The gain processor is out of the chain when it has nothing to do
items: App: reported active for every decoded film since 0.18.71, the gain processor sat in the audio chain of every direct play. A phone decodes to PCM and went through it and threw ERROR_CODE_FAILED_RUNTIME_CHECK at 0s, four attempts per press; a television passing Dolby to an amplifier never configures it, which is why the television played and the phone did not. Active again only when there is a correction to apply or an ease running.

The cost: a file measured while it plays corrects itself only if it opened with a correction already. The audio chain is built when the film opens and a processor left out of it then cannot be added later.

title: A shelf draw falls back to the copy
items: App: a draw that the shelf's own server cannot answer is put to the copy before giving up. Every object carries the machine it was listed from, so a shelf listed from the main server drew from it and nothing else - pressing Play with that machine off said "Nothing to play on that shelf". The fallback was in the player's next-episode step only, not on the Play button.

The drawn title carries the machine that answered, so its metadata, its stream and its subtitles are asked of the same one. Asked of the machine the shelf came from, the subtitle failed first and the film after it.

title: A copy lists what it can play
items: Films and TV listings name only titles the machine holds a file for. A copy carries the whole catalogue as names and posters so it can say what a key is, and listed all of it: with the main server off it offered 5442 films and could play about one in forty, so browsing to the copy and pressing play failed on nearly everything. On the main server every item has a file - 1057 films and 65 programmes before and after - so nothing changes there.

App: the player reports a playback failure to the server - the error code, the message, where it had got to, which machine it was reading from and the file. It handled its own errors and told nobody, so a film that would not start left the server with a stream cut after two megabytes and no reason for it. Once per code per playing, since the retries would otherwise send the same line six times in twenty seconds.

A draw looks at the whole shelf, not only the ten the hat had drawn. A copy holds part of a shelf and had a file for none of its ten, so the draw handed back the first of them - a title it cannot play. That is a shuffle that stops on a copy while the main server is off, which is the one time it has to work.

title: A film on a screen is kept while it is on the screen
items: What is playing this minute stays on the keep list whether or not it counts as watched. A title passes the watched mark with minutes still to run, left the list there, and the copy deleted its own file while somebody was still watching - so the machine that could have carried the last minute had nothing to carry it with.

And the one before it, per viewer. A title leaves the list the second its player stops reporting, and the copy sweeps what the list no longer names. The last two each are held instead: the episode just finished survives while the next is watched, and is there to go back to for anybody reminding themselves what happened. The disk cap decides when it finally goes.

A title fetched before anybody asked for it - the episodes after something watched, the shuffle's next draws - drops off the keep list after 30 days unwatched. What somebody chose by name is not held to this: a watchlist entry stays. When each was first named is kept on disk, because the server is restarted often enough that a clock in memory would never run out.

title: The player's info line reaches the server
items: Ten seconds into a film the player writes down whether the sound reaches the gain processor, what correction was wanted and whether it was applied. "It does not sound any louder" could not be told from "it is being passed through" without reading the television's own screen.

The whole line the player would show - where it is reading from, what is decoding it, the rate, the buffer, the subtitle, how the sound is handled - travels with each progress report and appears on the viewing in Now playing. It was on the television and nowhere else, so looking into a fault meant asking somebody to read it out.

Now playing shows how many seconds each screen is holding, and says STALLED when one has run out. Every player has reported its buffer since the reports started arriving; it was read only to decide how hard to hold a copy back, so a viewer running thin was visible to the throttle and to nobody else.

title: The info line says when a correction cannot be applied
items: Sound passed through to an amplifier never reaches the gain processor, so a correction could be held and do nothing while the line read "+6.7 dB". The processor now says whether it was ever configured, and the line reads "not applied - passed through" when it was not. A Dolby bitstream is not ours to change: correcting one means letting the server encode it, or setting the television to hand over PCM.

title: The player's info line shows a loudness measured while it plays
items: The answer to a progress report carries the file's measured loudness beside the gain, and the info line prefers it to what it was told when the film was opened. A file measured mid-play had its number on the server and nothing on the screen.
On a direct play the decibels shown are the ones the processor holds this instant, so an ease is visible while it happens; an encode still shows what was baked into it.

title: The file being watched is measured while it is watched
items: A progress report for an unmeasured file starts its measurement even though somebody is watching - it is that viewer's own file, already being read off that disk. Every other file still waits for a quiet machine. The rule was "not while anybody is watching", which made the one file whose loudness anybody was waiting for the one file that could never be measured.
With the gain now carried on every progress report, a file measured this way corrects itself part way through, eased in over 30 seconds.

title: The server's new version offers the app that goes with it
items: App: noticing the server has been replaced asks what build is on offer, and shows the install banner instead of the note when this app is behind. Updates.check answers only for a build newer than the one running, so the note still stands when the app is already current.

App: the remote starts on the install offer when there is one. The opening placement put it on Home 350 ms after the bar had asked for it, so a build waiting to be installed sat there with the cursor somewhere else.

Measuring asks whether anybody is watching rather than reading a list that is written when a file is served and never taken down again. Measuring stopped at the first viewing after a restart and did not start again until the next one, which is why 3381 files had 25 measured. The list is also put down now when the last viewing ends.

title: Loudness applied while a film is playing, and measured for the whole library
items: The answer to every progress report carries the gain the file needs, and the player eases into it over 30 seconds. The level was settled when the film was opened, so a file measured while it was playing stayed uncorrected to the end.

The gain processor is now always in the audio chain for 16-bit sound. A processor reported inactive is left out when the chain is built, so a level arriving later could never reach a film that started at nought; with nothing to do it hands the buffer on untouched.

Every file in the library is measured, one at a time, whenever nothing is playing and the disk is easy. A file that arrives later is picked up the same way. 3381 files, 25 of them measured before this.

Now playing shows a file being measured, on either machine: its name, how long it has been read, how many files are measured and how many are left. A disk busy for half a minute at a time all evening should say what it is doing.

title: The keyboard stays open while searching
items: App: nothing asks for the remote while the search box has the cursor. A typed letter narrows the list, which reloads it, which changes what the list was loaded for - and the effect that puts the cursor on the tab row of a freshly loaded tab fired on that change. One letter and the keyboard shut.

title: A kind set to night is no longer deleted every morning
items: The copy sweeps against everything the main server would keep, not the shorter list of what may be fetched this minute. The cache names the kinds its hours allow when it asks, so between 08:00 and 21:00 the answer held no shuffle rows at all - and the sweep deletes whatever it fetched that the answer does not name. Measured today: 149 rows during the day against 166 with every kind, the missing 17 being 6 the shuffle's next, 2 left part-way in the shuffle and 1 on a screen now. Everything fetched at 21:00 was deleted at 08:00 and fetched again the next evening.

/follow/playing returns both lists from one pass: holding, whatever the hour, and wanted, the part this copy will take now. A reason belonging to no kind - the episodes after a programme, the subtitles riding with a film - is in both, as it was before.

The web subtitle Download list stays open. It redrew the panel whenever the server's last finished subtitle job was ok, whoever asked for it and whenever it ran, so once anything had been made that day the list was replaced by the track list the moment it opened.
The download-complete notification names the file rather than the pack. qBittorrent passes the torrent name, so a film fetched out of a 5000-film pack was announced as the pack.

title: A shuffle carries on when the main server goes
items: App: a draw that fails is asked of the standby machine before giving up. It was asked of the server the film was opened from and given up on, so with the main server off the picture failed over to the copy and the next episode came back "Could not draw from the shelf" - while the copy, which holds the round and answers for itself when the main server cannot be reached, was never asked.

A draw prefers titles the machine answering it holds a file for. Every title on a shelf has a file on the main server, so this changes nothing there; a copy holds part of a shelf, and drawing one it has not got yet stops playback, since the film cannot be fetched from a server that is off.

title: One film read off two machines is one row again
items: Now playing drops a player's year label whether or not the title had to be rewritten to carry it. Rows from the two machines are gathered under key plus that label, and a title that already ended in its year kept the label - so the machine the player reported to had "key|2011" and the other had "key|", and one viewing appeared as two rows with the rate split between them.

What each client is doing is filed under the viewer and the device together. Under the device alone, two televisions calling themselves the same thing - every Google TV Streamer does - overwrote each other every five seconds, so of two people watching only the one that reported last had a position: the two rows took turns showing progress, and anything reading the list saw one of them blinking. Measured over three minutes: exactly one row carried a position at any sample, alternating.

title: Back from a title leaves the remote on the poster
items: App: three effects took the remote back after a title's page closed. The browse screen leaves the composition while a title is open and re-enters when it closes, so effects keyed on Unit or on values that change during the reload all ran again: the opening placement moved focus to Home 350 ms after back had put it on the poster, the per-tab placement moved it to the Films or TV button, and the update bar claimed it once per redraw rather than once per build. All three now run once and give way to a poster being restored.

title: Every measured file is levelled, not only the outliers
items: Loudness correction has no dead band: every measured file is brought to -18 LUFS, capped at 8 dB. The 4 dB band put two files measuring 0.2 dB apart 3.9 dB apart out of the speakers - one at -22.1 was corrected to -18.0 and one at -21.9 was left where it was.
Settings > Advanced drops the "Left alone within" row with the constant behind it.

App: backing out of a title returns the remote to the poster it was opened from. Coming back reloads the shelf or the tab, so the effect that restores it ran against an empty list, found nothing and cleared the key it needed a moment later - which left the remote on the tab row.

title: A shelf with an unresolvable key keeps its row
items: Continue watching tries the title a shuffle is on, then the next few in its queue, and shows the first the library can resolve. A player had reported a file id as the key it was playing; that went into the round as the current title, nothing could be looked up for it, and the shelf lost its row entirely.
A shuffle records a place only for a key the library holds, so a report naming something else cannot enter the round.
Torrents is its own tab under Settings, right of Library. It was a box at the foot of the folder lists.

title: Next-episode setting uses the same control as the rest
items: Settings > Library > Torrents: "Next episode" is now two buttons, Keep it ready and Only when asked, with the note under the row saying what the chosen one does. It was a browser checkbox - the styled switch in the stylesheet is scoped to the friends list, so class="onoff" elsewhere fell back to the platform's own tick box.

title: Focus ring only where something is steering by remote
items: App: the white focus ring on posters and pills is drawn only when a remote or keyboard is in use. Focus is handed out on a phone too - a tab asks for it when pressed - so the ring stayed on the last thing touched after the screen changed.

title: Copy queue on its own tab, episodes named in the download log
items: Settings > Advanced no longer lists hours ahead and episodes ahead. They are per-machine settings, and the page showed hardcoded defaults that disagreed with what was set.
The copy queue is its own sub-tab under Remote computer, and gives the number of titles and total GB. It sat at the foot of the cache settings page.

Download log names the episode: season, number and episode title beside the programme's name. The row carried the programme's name alone, which reads the same for every episode of it. Filled in from the pack entry for rows written before packs read episodes.

App: the indication under every control draws on press only. The default also draws a state layer for focus and hover, and on a phone something always holds focus, so a white patch sat on an untouched icon.
App: holding a poster on the watchlist offers Off the watchlist. Taking something off was only on the title's own page.
Advanced page text rewritten in plain technical language.

title: Hours-ahead window counts unmeasured episodes
items: More like this matches programmes against programmes. It asked the film section for any title's genres, so a series page listed films.

Web: an episode that is not downloaded opens its offer page with a Download button and carries the download mark in the season list. Clicking any episode called play(), which fails when there is no file.

how_long() falls back to the programme's average runtime when an episode has no measured file. Counted as zero, unmeasured episodes never filled the hours window, so a 4-hour setting queued 10 episodes of a 50-minute programme with 23 of its 55 unmeasured.
Changelog and today's code comments rewritten in plain technical language.

title: Loudness shown in the player's info line
items: Player info line shows the file's measured loudness and the gain applied: "-26.1 LUFS  +8.0 dB", or "+8.0 dB encoded" when the transcoder applied it. Unmeasured files show nothing.

title: Episode pages, queue limits, watched threshold
items: An offered episode now returns episode metadata (title, index, parentIndex, season) instead of movie metadata, so its page shows the episode and a Download button.
Part-way queue limited to 6 per viewer and places updated within 30 days. Was 40 per viewer with no age limit: 110 films queued, mostly abandoned starts. Now 39.

Watched threshold is now 95% or 3 minutes from the end, whichever is earlier, floor 85%. A 22-minute episode finishes at 86%, a 2-hour film stays at 95%. One helper, used by the watched mark, Continue watching, shelves, casual and the copy queue.
Repeated browser log lines are written at most once per 15 minutes (digits ignored when comparing). A stale tab was posting the same line every 15 seconds.
Loudness measuring waits until nothing is playing or copying, one file at a time. Two concurrent ffmpeg reads held a copy at 41 Mbit with the drive at 57 ms latency.

title: Volume normalisation, DVD subtitles burned in
items: Setting under Playback: even out volume. Each file is measured once (ffmpeg ebur128, 180 s from 5:00) and cached in loudness.json; files more than 4 dB from the -18 LUFS target are corrected by up to 8 dB. Direct play applies the gain in an ExoPlayer AudioProcessor, transcodes apply -af volume. Passthrough bitstreams are left alone.
Offered programmes merge into the library's own: opening a show lists its seasons plus seasons only a pack has, and a season lists held episodes alongside offered ones, in order.

DVD (VobSub) subtitles are burned in instead of being passed to the player. Media3 decodes PGS but has no VobSub decoder: selecting one threw "unsupported MIME type: application/vobsub" and playback stopped. Legacy subtitle decoding is also enabled on the text renderer.
Loudness thresholds are listed under Settings > Advanced.

title: Torrent packs understand episodes
items: Pack entries are parsed for SxxExx and matched against TMDB TV instead of movies; episode names come from one season lookup. All 34 files of a TV pack previously parsed as one film title and returned "not found".
A pack's programme appears in the TV section with its episodes, each fetchable, instead of one grouped movie row. Held and offered episodes are counted separately.
Existing packs are re-read once and their "not found" result cleared so they are matched again.

Setting under Downloads: keep the next episode ready. Past half an episode the next one is requested from its pack if a pack has it and the library does not. At a season end it takes the first of the next; once per episode.
Up from the top row moves to the tab above that card, measured from the card's position. The framework's search reached the server picker from the first two columns.
Holding select on a poster opens the menu and keeps it open: all events of that keypress (repeats and the release) are dropped, matched on downTime, in the activity and in the dialog window.

title: Guest writes, cache roles
items: /stream/buffer and /favorites added to the guest path list. They were in GUEST_MAY_POST but not in GUEST_PREFIXES, so the door refused them first: 208 buffer reports from one guest rejected in a day, and sync only ever yielded to local viewers.
Invite roles are copied to the cache and refreshed each round. Without them the owner's key was a plain guest there and the wall panel was refused /watching.
A stale page reports itself once instead of every 15 seconds.
Smoke test now exercises guest-writable and machine-key endpoints.

title: Focus and key handling on the title page
items: Down works on a film's page. The alike shelf loads after the page, and adding verticalScroll then rebuilt the column under the focused node; every direction key then threw ActiveParent must have a focusedChild and was dropped by the key guard. The column now scrolls from the start.
Up from the middle of a grid's top row goes straight up; only the left-hand card goes to the open tab.
"More" moved to the shelf heading: at the end of the row it was off-screen on a television.
Programme pages keep full text sizes; the reduced sizes are only for pages carrying a shelf.
Buffer reports are keyed per screen, not per viewer. One person watching on two devices overwrote their own last report.
A follower writes told titles under the post-rekey key. Written under the old key the update matched nothing, so titles just moved kept their file names.

title: More like this fits the screen
items: The alike shelf fits a 1080p screen: title, year, plot and spacing reduced on television layouts, shelf positioned under the text rather than at the screen foot, cards at 5/8 of shelf size.
Detail pages scroll when a shelf sits below the fold.
Holding select opens a poster's menu on the hold rather than on release.

title: Up from the left-hand card
items: Up from the leftmost card of the top shelf goes to the tab row. The framework's search found the server picker, which sits above and left of the tabs.

title: Buffer reports reach the server
items: /stream/buffer is answered on GET and POST and reads the seconds from body or query. It existed on GET only and read the body a GET does not have, so every report returned 404 into the caller's catch: AHEAD was always empty and sync never yielded. A viewer sat on 1 s of buffer while a copy took 270 Mbit.
Graded response instead of one threshold: 50 s is fed, under 40 s the ceiling stops climbing, under 30 s it halves, under 20 s it drops to the floor.
A transcode is judged by buffer direction, not depth - it holds whatever the encoder is ahead by - and only a falling buffer, or one under 5 s, counts as starved.
A player reporting a stall drops the ceiling to the floor regardless of depth.
Thresholds listed under Settings > Advanced.

title: A film is looked for by its key, not by its name
items: A player looking for the same film on another machine asks for it by number. Every machine works a key out from the title and the year for itself and they all arrive at the same one, which is the whole reason the keys are made that way - and the question being asked was the one thing that differs. The main server has its titles from the catalogue; a machine keeping copies reads them off the files it was sent, punctuation and misspellings and all, so a film both machines held under one key was two different names to a search. It was read off one machine when two had it.
The name is still asked for afterwards, for a machine that has not been given the same keys yet.

A machine keeping copies takes its titles from the one it follows, in the round where it already takes its keys. It had only the files it was sent to go on and named them as the releases did - no colon, the odd misspelling - so six of the twenty-seven films both machines held were filed under two different names.

A disk holding a picture up pulls a copy back before anybody has to notice. How much of each block's time went on getting it off the disk rather than handing it on was already measured, and used only to decide how much of the reading to hand over; above a third of it the copy now stands back as well.
The web and the server ask by key too. Three places asked another machine what it called a film by name; one was fixed and the other two would have gone on failing the same way.

Out of the top row of Films or TV, up goes to the row of buttons over the posters rather than past them. Straight up from the left-hand column reached the server picker, which sits above them and to the left.
A list opens with the cursor on that row. It opened with the focus nowhere in particular, so the first press of any direction went hunting rather than moving.

The answer a copy is given carries the title it asks about. It was added to what is sent without being fetched from the index, so the question a copy asks about every file it holds answered with nothing at all.

title: Two lines, and a ceiling that finds out
items: A copy gives way only to what shares its own path. A film going out to somebody's phone is on the line to the world and a copy to a machine in the next room is on the network here, and neither takes megabits from the other - but they were counted together, so somebody watching from away at seven megabits held a copy between two machines three metres apart to eleven. Each side is measured on its own now, and where nothing on the copy's own side is watching there is no ceiling at all.

The ceiling finds out how much there is rather than believing what it has seen. What had been seen was never the line's capacity - it was what the ceiling had allowed so far, and a ceiling that never exceeds its own measurements cannot learn a bigger number, because the traffic that would teach it is the traffic it prevents. It may climb to twice what that side has carried, which doubles every few seconds until the wire, a disk or somebody watching stops it: a copy sat at sixteen megabits on a network measured at a hundred.

A thin buffer counts on its own side only. A phone on mobile data running low says nothing about a copy between two machines in the house, and holding that copy back would not give the phone a single megabit.
Both rules are on the Advanced list under Settings, with the rest of the numbers.

title: One answer to when a copy is taken
items: Each kind of thing a copy keeps decides for itself when it may be taken, and nothing else does. Under the five of them sat a switch that could say nothing at all moves before night whatever they said - two answers to one question, and the quieter one won without saying so. It is gone, and everything set to Always is taken now.

Start the night now sits with the rows that offer Inside hours, which is where somebody reading those three words looks for the way to make them mean now. It also counts as the hours: a kind told to wait for them no longer waits through it.

The machine's own three rows stay on the page beside the cache's settings. What that machine is set to copy is drawn by clearing whatever box it is handed, and it was handed the one they had just been put in - so they were built, added and wiped off the page before anybody saw them.

title: What a copy keeps, one kind at a time
items: Each kind of thing a second machine keeps can be off, kept only through the hours that machine is the one awake, or kept always: what people are part-way through, watchlists and favourites, what has been watched lately, the shuffle's next, and whatever is on a screen this minute. It was all or nothing, so a machine wanting one person's watchlist took everybody's half-watched series with it and the only way to stop that was to stop copying. The machine keeping the copies decides which apply, because it is the one that knows what time it is there.

The sound is taken off the top before a picture is measured, and an old codec is not asked to spend what it used to. The library keeps the whole container's rate, so a film with DTS carried a megabit and a half that is not picture - and a broadcast MPEG-2 at twenty-one megabits was being re-encoded at twenty-one, where h264 holds the same picture at eight.

Settings has an Advanced button: every number the server settles on when nobody has said otherwise, in the places they belong and with a line each on what they do. Read from the running server rather than written out again, so the page cannot come to disagree with the machine.

title: Show more opens the filter
items: Show more, at the end of the shelf of what is like a film, hands its words to the tab they came from: Films or TV with those genres already marked, where one can be taken off or a decade put beside them. It is there however short the row is - a shelf of four is exactly where somebody wants to widen it - and a longer row of the same thing was not what anybody was after.
Show more clears whatever was last searched for. Left standing it narrowed the genres to whichever of them had that word in the title, which is two questions at once.

A re-encode is never asked for more than the picture carries. Away from home with no ceiling set, anything going out was given eight megabits whatever it was - a fallback in the code, not a setting anybody made. A fifty-minute episode of 367 megabytes, a DVD rip running at one megabit, was re-encoded at eight and had sent three times its own size before it was half watched, over mobile data, with nothing gained. Only an x265 encode is given more than the file holds, half as much again; anything else is held to what came in.

title: More like this, and a download button that is one
items: A film's page carries a shelf of what else is like it: the titles holding every one of its genres, written over the shelf as tags. In year order around this film - five from before it and five from after, newest at the left - and where one side has nothing, the other makes up the ten. It widens in time, never in words: letting a word go put films in the row that were not that kind of film at all.

The whole matching set is asked for rather than the first page of it. A page is a hundred and twenty and it arrives newest first, so for a common pair of words everything older was never fetched - and a film from 1987 cannot sit in the middle of a list that begins in 2015.
Show more opens the rest of them, and a button beside it makes a collection of what is shown.
A film that runs to its end comes back to its page at that shelf, with the remote on the first of them.

Download for subtitles is a button beside the menu rather than a choice inside it. It was written after the menu closed, so the browser dropped it out of the list and drew it as a line of text: there was nothing to press, and the thing listening for it could never hear a thing.

A poster that arrives too small to be a picture is asked for again. The same address answers with the real one and with a near-black stand-in depending on which edge of their network replies, and whatever arrived first was kept for good.
Marking a decade or a genre leaves the remote on the line it just ticked.

title: More like this, under a film
items: A film's page carries a shelf of what else is like it, newest first: the titles holding the same genres, matched the way the genre filter matches when those words are marked. The words are written over it as tags, and a rare one is dropped rather than leaving a shelf of two - one film was the only thing in the library that was science fiction, drama and a television film at once.

A poster that arrives too small to be a picture is asked for again. The same address answers with the real one and with a near-black stand-in depending on which edge of their network replies, and whatever arrived first was kept for good: one film in a library of four thousand had a black poster since the fifth of September.
The shelf is newest first, and its words wrap on a phone standing up rather than running off the side.

A film that runs to its end comes back to its page at that shelf, with the remote on the first of them. It came back to the top of the page with the play button under the remote, which is the one thing nobody wants next.
The web carries the same shelf under a film, with the same tags over it.

Marking a decade or a genre leaves the remote on the line it just ticked. The lists are read again when something is marked - that is what makes the numbers fall - and the row under the remote stopped existing, so the focus fell out of the menu onto the button beside it.

title: The copy keeps what the shuffle is on
items: A machine keeping copies holds on to the title a shuffle has drawn until it is finished. Drawing one writes it down as played, and the list of what to keep was the queue less what had been played - so the copy stopped wanting an episode at the very moment somebody started watching it, and swept it while they were. That is why a film read off one machine when both held it.

A shelf reads again when a film is backed out of, so pressing the poster carries on where it was left. It was told to read again and the instruction went nowhere unless the tab had changed as well - which is why going to another tab and back made it work.
The web marks several decades at once as it already did genres, and each list says how it joins them.
The numbers beside a genre or a decade in the web fall to what is left once something is marked, as they do in the app.
A film on offer keeps its colours in the web too, and its mark is drawn rather than typed.

title: One rule for where a press of the remote goes
items: Where the remote goes at the edge of a list is decided in one place now. It was four handlers and five hints to the framework's own search, all answering the same three questions differently: up out of a list, down into one, and shelf to shelf. The shelves on Home did it a press at a time and were right; the lists hinted at the search instead, and a hint fires from every row rather than the edge.
Up out of a list goes straight up, to whatever is over that poster, and down goes straight down. Both were being sent to one named button instead, so a press in a corner of the screen crossed it.

Down from a tab goes straight down, into whatever is under that button - the same as the sort, the genre and the search box beside it. Naming one poster for the whole row sent every tab to the first one, so two buttons on the same line did two different things.
A press at an edge is taken before the search runs rather than after it. Answering afterwards meant the focus had already moved.
The download mark is drawn rather than typed: an arrow into a tray, the shape everything else uses. It was a character the television rendered with whatever font it had.
A film on offer keeps its colours. Drained of them it read as broken rather than as something you can have.

A press of the remote no longer closes the app. A direction pointing at a row that has scrolled away throws inside the framework's focus search; one such failure was already survived and this is the other.
A download that finishes reads as arriving rather than blinking nought per cent.
Several decades can be marked at once, the way genres already could. A title need only be from one of them - a film has one year, so asking for all of them at once would answer nothing.
The genre button says what its number is: twelve matches, not twelve. A bare number beside the word read as how many genres were marked, which is the one thing it was not.
The decade list has a Clear, named and coloured as the one on genres is.
Up leaves an open genre or decade list, the same as it leaves anything else on the screen. Back was the only way out, and back on a remote means leave the app to most people.

Each filter says how it joins what is marked: genres want a title carrying all of them, decades want one from any of them. A tick-list reads as any of these to most people, which is why the number fell as more were marked and nobody could see why.

The number against a genre or a decade counts the films on offer as well, because that is what picking it shows. It counted only what was on the disk: three hundred against a word that then filled the screen with two thousand.

title: The app survives a press it cannot answer
items: A press of the remote no longer closes the app. A direction pointing at a row that has scrolled away throws inside the framework's own focus search; one such failure was already survived and this is the other, seen four times in three minutes on a television.

A download that finishes reads as arriving rather than blinking nought per cent. The live row goes the moment the file is complete and every screen fell back to the shelf's snapshot, which was taken before the download began.
From the top of Films or TV, up goes to the tab the screen is on. Home already did; these two let the search run, and it found the picker and the search box that sit above the tabs.
A film on offer keeps its colours. Its poster was drained of them, which on a shelf read as broken rather than as something you can have; the mark in the corner already says it is not here yet.

title: Copying gives way to the picture, and a copy can serve its episodes
items: A player says how many seconds of film it has in hand, and copying stands aside while that number is low. Until now a machine worked it out from the rate falling away, which is only true once the picture has already stopped; the same measure holds whether a film is read straight off the disk or made by the encoder.

A machine keeping copies can serve an episode it fetched after the programme was re-keyed. Every such file named an episode that did not exist, so the pair read as one machine and the second was never asked for it.
Files are pointed back at the episode they belong to wherever that link was broken, at every scan and after every re-key.
A place in an episode follows it when two copies of a programme are folded together.

title: Seasons say which season, and up goes to the tabs
items: A machine that keeps copies may ask the one it follows who is watching. It could not, so the pair could never draw itself: a film read off both machines is two streams and each machine sees only its own half.

A season carries its name under it, and an episode its number: the pictures alone could not say, because one programme's seasons are the same artwork four times over. Films stay as they are - their poster is their name.
From the top shelf, up goes to the tab the screen is on. The picker and the search box sit above the tabs, and the nearest thing upwards was one of those.
The container image is published: ghcr.io/grovestick/palladium, built from the source this build came from.

One viewing reads by one name whichever machine reports it. A machine keeping copies knows an episode as "Episode 32" until it is told otherwise, so the same film appeared under two names side by side.

The drawing keeps up with the list beside it: what the other machine is feeding was kept for half a minute and asked for every two seconds, so a film had been coming off both machines for twenty seconds before the line appeared.

title: Posters, and a screen that fits what is on it
items: No names under the pictures in the app. A poster is the title written large by somebody paid to make it recognisable, and a shelf of names cut off halfway said nothing the artwork had not. What the words took, the pictures get.

How big a poster is drawn is decided by the height of the screen rather than its width. A television is wide and short - 960 points by 540 - so it was being given the size meant for a tablet, and the second shelf began below the bottom of the screen. Two whole shelves on a television, five to a row on a phone lying down, three standing up, whatever size the phone is.
On a screen that short the name, the machine picker and the search box stand on one line, the tabs are the smaller size, and the air above each shelf name is one line of it.
The remote starts on Home, a press of down goes down rather than sideways, and down and up keep the column they are in - each shelf remembers where the remote was on it.

A machine that keeps copies can draw its own wiring again: asking the main server what it is feeding was written into the answer before the method that does the asking existed, so the whole answer failed and the drawing lost its way out and its second machine.

A machine that lists a title but holds no file for it is not a second source. The one that keeps copies mirrors the whole catalogue, so it answers for every episode of a programme and holds the file for three of them - and a film being played said the other machine had a different file when it had no file at all.

title: Both machines drawn, and every viewing says which one sends it
items: A machine that keeps copies draws the line from the main server to whoever is watching. It asks that machine what it is feeding, with the key it follows with - the key a browser holds there is that machine's own and the main server has never heard of it - so a film read off both showed the main server sitting idle while it carried half the picture.
Every row in Now playing says which machine is sending it.
The band that says a page has fallen behind stays off a film: not while something is playing, not while the player is open, and never in full screen.

title: A download's numbers move while you watch them
items: The percentage, the rate and the time left of a download move on screen instead of standing at whatever the first reading said. The title carries those figures in fields the language leaves out of its own equals, so a film at nought per cent and the same film at ninety-nine compared as equal - and the screen was told nothing had changed. Watched on a television: the rate went from 104 to 221 Mbit and the time left from five minutes to one, on screen, as it happened.

The cast button is a light glyph rather than a black square: Google's own element draws itself black whatever it is asked, which on a dark page reads as something broken. Nothing at all is drawn until that element is ready, and it never sits over a film.
In Now playing the drawing keeps up with the figures beside it - two seconds, as they do - and everything on the page ends on the same line down the right.
The name of a film leads to the film's page. On Continue watching the picture carries on where it left off, which is right for the picture and wrong for the words under it.
A machine that keeps copies draws the line from the main server to whoever is watching: it asks that machine what it is feeding, the way the viewer list already does.

title: A machine that goes away comes back to the film
items: A machine dropped mid-film is asked again every few seconds and rejoins as soon as it answers. Dropping one is what marked it not alive, and asking it again was the job of the very thread that ended when it did - so one connection that timed out put a machine out of the film for good, however well it answered a second later. Watched on a television: the main server stopped for forty seconds, was asked five times while it was down, and was carrying its share again three seconds after it came back, with the picture never stopping.

Every machine that has the film carries it, up to four, asked again every twenty seconds. That is the whole rule - the separate one that moved a film back to the main server is gone, and so is the one that kept a machine measured as slower off the work.
A viewing drawn from a player's report is named after the person and carries its year in brackets, like every other row.
The app waits six seconds to reach a server rather than three.

title: One rule for which machines carry a film
items: Every machine that has the film carries it, up to four, and is asked again every twenty seconds. That is the whole rule. After a machine has been away there is nothing to restore: it answers, it has the file, it takes its share again.
The rule that moved a film back to the main server is gone. It was a second way of saying the same thing, and it moved the picture to do it - a special case where the general one already applies.
The two ways a film could quietly end up on one machine now say so in the log, with every machine found and what became of its address.
The app waits six seconds to reach a server rather than three. Three was long enough for a machine beside it and not for a telephone on wi-fi, which then read its own main server as away.

title: A film says why it is coming off one machine
items: The two ways a film could quietly end up on one machine now say so. One returned without a word when splitting was turned off or the film was being encoded; the other when every machine found had been dropped for a reason nothing wrote down. A film that could have come off two machines and did not looked exactly like one where nothing had been asked - which is hours of an evening.
A viewing drawn from a player's report is named after the person, and its title carries the year in brackets like every other row.

title: Now playing says the same thing twice the same way
items: A viewing drawn from a player's report is named after the person, not after the telephone's model number. The same person watching one film appeared as themselves on one machine and as a part number on the other.
And a title reads the same whichever machine reports it: the film with its year in brackets, the way a file is named. A player sends the name and the year apart, so one film looked like two.
