The app waits six seconds to reach a server rather than three. Three was long enough for a machine beside it and not for a telephone on wi-fi, which then read its own main server as away and stayed on the machine keeping copies.

title: One rule: a machine holding the file carries the film
items: Every machine holding a film carries it, up to four of them, and a machine is left out only by not answering. The rule that kept a machine measured as slower off the stretch about to be played is gone: a speed is measured once and never decays, so a machine that happened to be busy for its first stretch was left out of every stretch after it - paired, connected and carrying nothing. What that rule was written for is already answered better: a stretch that has not arrived in about twice the time the quickest machine would have taken is given up and fetched again.

A film being played by the app is written down as the app. The player's own requests carried no name, so they were filed as a browser: one viewing appeared twice in Now playing under two different names.

Every machine known is asked whether it has the film every twenty seconds while it plays, rather than every minute - so one that has just come back joins what is already playing instead of being found a minute later.

title: The copy stops deleting what somebody is watching
items: A machine keeping copies never sweeps a file it is serving. It was meant to be safe because a file being read cannot be deleted - but a player reads a stretch, closes the connection and comes back a moment later, so for most of a film there is no handle on it at all. The sweep found one of those gaps and deleted a film being watched, which ended the pair carrying it and left one machine reading alone.
Every viewing writes down which file it is reading, which is how the sweep knows.

title: A film that moved to the copy comes back
items: A film reading from the machine that keeps copies moves back to the main server once that one is answering again, instead of staying there for the rest of the evening with the whole app following it onto a machine that holds a fraction of the library. The same move that took it there, the other way round - and only from a picture with fifteen seconds in hand, because a move costs a second of black and paying that to leave a machine that is coping is not worth it.

title: Both machines carrying one film again
items: A film held on both machines is read off both again. The two are paired by the name of the file, and the player took a shelf row with the title and the year on it as enough to go on - a row that carries no file name. So it matched on a name it did not have, found nothing, and settled for one machine while the other sat there holding the same copy.

title: Coming back to the main server, properly this time
items: A film listed while the machine keeping copies was answering is played from the main server once that one is back - by asking it for its own key for the title first, rather than handing it a key from somewhere else. If it does not know the title, nothing moves and the copy answers as before.
A stream that stops mid-film says which program was fetching it. One arrived from a machine with nothing but an address against it and there was no way to tell what had asked for it.

Two titles that come out under one key say so on the Index, with both names. A key is worked out from what a title is, so two different films that flatten to the same name and share a year land on the same one - the second was filed under the first without a word, one poster standing for both. The key stays as it is, because both machines work it out for themselves; what was missing was being told.
A title folded into another takes what was written down about it: places, the watch log, watchlists, shuffle queues. A merge dropped a key and everything naming it was left pointing at nothing.

title: A film is read from the machine that listed it
items: Playing a film no longer sends one machine's key to another. The last build moved playback back to the main server as soon as it was answering, using the key the title was listed under - and two machines hold the same film under different keys of their own, so the main server was asked for whatever that key meant there and played some other film under the right title. Taken out; coming back to the main server has to ask it for its own key first.

title: A film comes back to the main server
items: A film opened while the machine that keeps copies was answering is played from the main server again as soon as that one is back. The address a title was listed from is kept inside it, so a shelf read during a restart went on being played from the copy long after everything else had come home - until the app was started again.

The container carries every module. The list in its recipe was written out in full and fell behind the server twice; a module added after it was written is imported by name at startup, so the container restarted for ever, saying only which one it could not find.

A server in a container can be set up. Only somebody sitting at the machine could do it, and in a container nobody ever is - every request arrives off the network, so a new one refused the first page it was ever asked for and there was no way in at all. Until it has been set up, being on the same network is enough; finishing the wizard closes it again.

title: The app stops freezing on a download
items: A download's numbers move while the page is open instead of standing still until the app is started again. The reading was made with the thirty seconds any other question gets, and a reading that slow holds everything behind it - the wait cannot be cut short from outside, because it is the socket that is waiting. It asks for four seconds now, and reaches for three.

Settings answers at once on a machine Palladium has just been installed on. The firewall rule and what Windows calls this network were two separate starts of PowerShell, and on a machine that has never run it each one is seconds - so the first page a new owner opens sat there and then gave up. Asked together now.

A server that has been set up starts when the machine does. It was a switch nobody had been shown, so the first restart looked like the program had gone. Arranged once, when the setting up is finished; the switch is still in Settings, This computer, for anybody who wants it off.

title: Asking a finished torrent for one more film
items: A film asked for from a pack whose other films are all in now arrives instead of being cancelled a minute later. qBittorrent takes no notice of a file being asked for while it reads the torrent as finished - the request answers as though it worked and the file stays off - which read here as somebody having turned it off by hand. The asking is read back now, and anything that did not take is asked for again with the torrent stopped, which is when it listens.

title: A film that came in while nothing was looking
items: A finished download asks to be read into the library again if it never got there. The asking happened once, when the download finished; a restart during the minutes that scan takes lost it, and the film sat on the disk with its page saying "arriving" for as long as anybody cared to look. Asked again at most twice an hour.
The address that starts a scan refuses while one is running. Opening it twice started two walks of the same folders writing to one index, which is where a locked database comes from.

title: A download that keeps its numbers
items: The app kept the percentage, the time left and the rate of a download it could not reach for a moment. A poll that missed was written down as nothing downloading, so every minute or so the line under the tabs vanished and the poster fell back to the snapshot it was drawn with - which carries no time left at all, which is why there never seemed to be one.
It asks every two seconds rather than every second. A second poll against a server already converting a film is where the missed ones came from, and the numbers move no less for it.

The time left is worked out from the rate as it settles rather than from the moment it was read. A swarm handing out quarter-gigabyte pieces reads 200 Mbit one second and 3 the next, so the same download said three minutes and then three hours. The rate shown is still the live one.

title: The second machine is drawn again
items: The drawing on Now playing showed a live second machine as "no second machine - not answering". One answer replaced three there and names it differently; the drawing was still reading the old name and finding nothing.

title: Reports reach palladium.video, requests included
items: A report now says what program it is when it hands itself over. It went out under the name the library it is written with uses, which is turned away at the door as a robot - so every fault a server thought it had sent was refused before it got anywhere near being read.

A request can be sent to palladium.video as well as a fault, one at a time, by the person running the server. It was the one kind of report somebody actually sat down and wrote, and it was the one kind that could not leave.
Faults and requests are read in two tabs where they land, gathered by the machine that sent them.

title: Faults that were never sent say so
items: A fault is marked sent when palladium.video has taken it. It used to be marked as soon as the sending started, and whatever happened after that was thrown away - so a machine could show a fault as sent at a time when it had never left the house, and nobody went looking for it again.
A report that would not go keeps the reason and says it on the row, and the button offers to try again.

Everything a machine has not managed to hand over can be sent in one press, oldest first. A server that was told to report faults but had no way out keeps them, and they are worth nothing sitting there.

title: A restart nobody sees, and a cache that can update itself
items: A film being read straight from the server carries on through a restart: a broken read is asked again every second for up to a minute while what is already buffered plays, so a server being replaced never reaches the screen. Three tries across three seconds was less than a restart takes, and the picture stopped and started again at the same second.

A machine that keeps copies can fetch a build from the one it follows again. Being on the same network stopped counting as a key, and its own key opened only its copying - so following the other machine's build was refused at the door.

A machine keeping copies is written down as copying again, not as somebody watching: it calls itself a follower and the test asked whether it called itself a cache, so its files were listed as viewings at the speed of a copy and never gave way to a real viewer.

Mesh is gone. A meshed server could be added and a film could be read through this one, but no list ever carried the other library's titles - so it was a door with no catalogue behind it. The key kind and the setting go with it.

title: A way in from outside, and a poster behind a title
items: Settings - This computer - Reach from outside: forwarding the port stays the way it works and is the default. The other way fetches Caddy, which answers on 443 for a name you own, gets its certificate and hands what it receives to this server; a second name can point at the machine that keeps copies.

Caddy is fetched on request like ffmpeg, kept beside the library rather than installed, and started at sign-in if asked. Its configuration is written from the settings, with the timeouts and buffering a film needs.
A poster stands behind a title's own page and nowhere else unless asked: what used to be behind the shelves as well is now a choice rather than the default.

Two titles the library had under one match are folded together again: an item's key is twelve hex digits, reading it as a number threw, and duplicates had never merged. The one holding the most files keeps its key, so watchlists and places in an episode still point at it.
The site says again what the licence is: AGPL-3.0 in the footers, the licence in full on the server page, and the repository linked from both.

title: Keys, roles and what stands behind the page
items: Web: the genre menu has no checkboxes; a marked genre's name is drawn in the accent colour on a tinted row.

Web: each genre press redraws Films, TV, search or the watchlist at once, with the menu kept open at its scroll position; the old page stays up until the new list arrives, and a slower earlier load no longer draws over a newer one.
Settings: Subtitle language is the first box on the Subtitles tab.
Remote computer: Tonight sits under the night hours in the cache's own box, and the reading share and key buttons moved into that box too; the share is explained in five lines instead of eleven.
Web: a poster stands behind the page - the newest thing in Continue watching when it loads, and the title last opened after that. Dim behind the shelves, full on the title's own page.
Fixed: with no titles matching the marked genres, the genre menu was cut off at the header; the page clips sideways overflow with overflow-x: clip instead of hidden, which had made it a scroll box.
Users: every key in one list, grouped by what it is for - owner, admin, user, cache, mesh - and alphabetical inside each group. The tab opens on that list rather than on the invitation form.
Users: a key's role is set in one place, the dropdown on its row. The separate Owner button is gone.
New role, admin: a key that reads whatever the owner reads and writes nothing. For a panel on a wall rather than a person.
Keys are made under Users and nowhere else. The Remote computer tab no longer makes or revokes them.
A machine that keeps copies is set up with an ordinary invitation - its link, or an address and the five-character code - instead of a pasted setup line. Mark that key Cache under Users.
Fixed: a guest's own download showed no progress in the app. Asking how far it had got was refused as something a guest may not read, so the line stayed empty and nothing said why.
App: a poster stands behind the shelves - the title last opened, or failing that the newest thing in Continue watching, which is the film somebody stopped.

Two servers, two words: the one with the library on it is the main server and the one keeping copies is the cache, everywhere either is written about. Names on the wire are untouched, so an older app and a machine on an older build go on talking to this one.

Settings: Background poster - Always, Title page only, or Off. Always puts it behind the shelves as well; Title page only keeps it to a film or series' own page. Yours rather than the machine's, so the browser, the phone and the television agree.
Users: the Casual button is gone from each person's row - the casual shelf is a collection shuffle now, and what is kept for somebody is their half-watched films and their watchlist.

Fixed: every /follow call answered 500 and the machine keeping copies could not check in, copy, or take the invitations - it had been unable to reach any of them since the rename earlier in this release. The record of which machines follow this one was also being written to a file nobody read, so the list came back empty after a restart.
A key may only be marked Cache once a server has used it: the machine has to have announced itself here first. A person's key cannot be turned into a machine's by mistake.
Settings: Backdrop is set per screen - television, computer, phone - and per person, like the subtitle look. A television across the room is not a phone at arm's length.
Settings: This computer is no longer a tab of its own; the computer, its encoding, the add-ins, fault reporting and a word to the screens all read as settings.
Users: the invitation list is sorted with the owner first and the rest by name, and a rule separates each group of keys.
The cache's own box calls the shuffle by its name rather than casual watching.
Remote computer has two halves, Server and Cache: what another machine keeps of this library, and what this machine keeps of another. They were one long page reading as a single subject.

Under Server: one card for caching in general - how much of the reading is handed over, the keys sent, starting the night early - and one listing the machines that keep a cache, each with its own settings. A machine with a key that was also announcing itself used to be drawn twice.

Users: a key for a machine is laid out like a key for a person - the same name column, the same note under it, the same boxes and the same rule beneath - and every role dropdown sits in the same place, wide enough for the word in it.
Every key that is marked Cache is listed as a machine, whether or not the flag underneath it was ever set.
Fixed: a season or an episode number kept as text took a whole answer down rather than one title - "Season" and the year are read as numbers now, and fall back to nothing when they are not.

Remote computer: Test and Sync now sit at the top of the machine's own box, and there is one of each rather than two. The box says it is managed from here, with a button that asks the machine whether that is still true.

A key is needed on the home network too. Being on the same network is no longer a credential: the machine itself still needs none, and every other screen carries an invitation, whether it is in the kitchen or on a train.
App: the themes sit under the row rather than beside it and wrap onto as many lines as they need - five of them never fitted across a phone.
App: Settings has the same Background poster choice under Appearance, for the kind of screen it is running on.
Settings: Performance is no longer a tab of its own - what the computer is doing and game mode sit under Settings, with the rest of what that machine is set to.

Fixed: App - the poster behind the shelves was stretched to fill the screen, so only the middle of it was left and what somebody had stopped watching was unrecognisable. It keeps its shape and stands at the height it has.
App: the Theme row no longer names the theme above the pills that already show it, which is a shorter box on a phone held upright.
Remote computer: the caches are a list. Press one to see what it is set to copy; with one cache it reads as it always did.

Downloads are asked after every second while anything is arriving, in the browser and in the app alike, so the percentage, the rate and the time left move as they happen. Nothing arriving, and it goes back to asking every ten seconds.

Fixed: a new episode of a programme the catalogue already knows started a second, unidentified programme of its own - a season on its own, with no air date and nothing in Recently released. An episode's filename carries no year and the catalogue's row does, and the two were only ever compared when the years matched.

Fixed: asking every screen for a key stopped the machine that keeps copies as well. It was owner here only because it sat on the same network, so its own rounds were turned away at the door and caching halted. A key marked Cache reaches the copying endpoints again, which check for themselves that it follows this server and has not been stopped.
Settings: the box giving the other server's address is gone, and the Android app note no longer points at a source repository.
Remote computer: both halves say what they are for - one computer keeping copies of this library, and this computer keeping copies of another - and how to set each up.

title: Several genres in the browser
items: Web: Films, TV, search, the watchlist and collections take several genres from a checkbox menu with Clear; a title must carry all of them, and with two or more marked the button shows the match count.
Collections: a rule's genre may list several, comma-joined, matched the same way.
Settings: Library > Index shows Downloadable, the films on offer from torrent packs that the library does not hold.
Followers: a machine announcing with the same key from a new port on the same host replaces its old row; a cache that moved port was listed twice.

title: Download refresh reports what it gets
items: App: the download list is asked of each server separately, and the app writes a trace line to the server log whenever the list or a server's error changes; a failed refresh used to leave the list empty with nothing logged.
Fixed: Back and a title page's own Back could both close the page, and the second one crashed on an empty page stack (IndexOutOfBoundsException, index -1).
App: a poster or film page showing Arriving re-reads that film every 10 s and turns into the library's own entry once it has come in, on every screen that shows it.

title: Live download progress
items: App: download progress is refreshed app-wide, every 3 s while something downloads and every 10 s otherwise, on every screen; the film page, its poster badge, shelf posters and the download line all read that list. The refresh ran inside the home screen's download line, so a film page kept the 0% it opened with.
App: poster download badges show Mbit/s beside % and ETA.

title: Genre match count, download progress
items: Genre filter in the app: with several genres marked the button shows how many titles carry all of them (Genres · 66), not how many genres are marked. Films and TV take the server's totalSize; watchlists and collections count the filtered list.
App: the download line shows progress and ETA before the title; beside search on a television the title took the width and the numbers were clipped.
App: the download badge on a poster reads the live download list (refreshed every 10 s) instead of the shelf snapshot, which kept showing Queued or 0% while the film came in.

title: Several genres narrow the shelf
items: Genre filter: with several genres marked, a title has to carry all of them (science fiction and comedy together), not any one; on the server's shelves and in the app's watchlist and collection filter.

title: Back exits from Home
items: Fixed: Back on Home exits with two presses from the tabs again. The list's Back handler was enabled while the list was scrolled as well as while it had focus, so a scrolled list kept moving focus to the tab and never reached the exit.

title: Grouped changelog, several genres, copy window per series
items: Reports: What is new is grouped by minor version (0.18, 0.17), newest group open; web and app.
App: on a television or a phone on its side the download line sits beside search instead of on a row of its own.
App: Up from the download line moves focus to the current tab; it had no target and held the focus.
Genre filter in the app: several genres can be marked, and a title in any of them is shown; Clear at the top of the menu.

Fixed: episodes kept ahead on the copy follow Episodes ahead and Hours ahead once per series and viewer. Each source a series was reached from (on screen, watched lately, part-way) walked its own window, and a watchlist added every marked episode with Whole list off; Episodes ahead 10 queued 21 and 32.

title: Moved files and back focus
items: Fixed: a file moved to another folder or drive keeps its title's added date; it is re-indexed and re-probed but does not reappear in Recently added.
App: back from a title page puts focus on the poster it was opened from, in the Films and TV grids and in the home rows, with each home row keeping its scroll.

title: One download at a time, and downloads in the log
items: Downloads go one at a time: a film asked for while another is coming in waits its turn with its file off in qBittorrent, and starts when the one before it finishes or is cancelled; its page and the download line say how many are ahead.

The download line says how fast the film is coming in, in Mbit/s, beside how far and how long. In the app it has a row of its own under the tabs and says who asked; at the end of the tabs it was off the side of a phone.
Where it all goes shows the server downloading - the film, how far, how fast, how long and how many wait behind it - instead of nothing going out.
The Watch log lists downloads among the viewings: who asked for which film, when, and how far it got.
Editing a collection puts its sort, genre and decade in the edit box, set as the collection has them, instead of showing them above the list as well; a change of genre or decade is tested at once.
A collection's genre is found in the genre list whatever case it was saved in.

A film whose download has finished turns into its own page once it has come into the library, in the web and the app, rather than staying on Downloaded - arriving; its offer opens the film from then on.
In the Users tab, each person's weekly download limit shows what they have downloaded this week.
The boxes in the Users tab are drawn dark like the rest of the page rather than white.

Log > Downloads opens with what was downloaded this week, this month and altogether - gigabytes, films, what is still coming in, the largest, and who took most - for everyone or the person picked, as the Watch log does for viewings.
In Settings the Log tab sits beside Now playing.
In the web, back from a title opened inside a collection returns to the collection, scrolled to that title, rather than to the list of collections.

title: A pack downloads only the films asked for
items: A pack already in qBittorrent - picked up by its own watched folder, or added by hand - downloads only the films asked for in Palladium. Every other file is set to not download; before, Download turned the one film on and left the rest of the pack on with it.

A pack in qBittorrent that nobody has asked for anything from is stopped with all of its files off, and packs are checked every twenty seconds so one qBittorrent picks up by itself is turned down before it has taken much.
The watchlist button on a title page in the web steps through three states, as in the app: off, on the watchlist, and a favorite with a red heart.
Back from a title lands on it in the list it was opened from - Films, TV, a category or the watchlist - in the web and in the app, rather than at the top.
Now playing shows films downloading from a torrent pack: who asked, how far, the size, the speed and the time left.
A downloaded film takes the TMDB match it was offered under, so its poster, summary and genres arrive with it.
The app's poster badge on a downloading film shows the time left beside the percent.
Fix match works with the library's hex keys; it kept only the digits and named a different title, or none.
A film still downloading is left out of the library until it has finished, and one indexed halfway is taken out again; indexed, it would not play and its title page showed no progress.
A film its torrent pack carries more than once (a restored cut, a second disc, its trailers) shows as one poster; its page, in the web and the app, lists the releases to choose from before Download.
Pack films are matched to TMDB by first release year, so a remake no longer takes the original's poster; films matched to another year are matched again.
The Films count says how many of its films are there to download.
A film being downloaded shows its progress and time left across the poster on its own page, as on its card, in the web and the app.
A download can be cancelled from the film's page by the owner or whoever asked for it: its file is turned off in qBittorrent and the film is offered again.
A download whose file is turned off in qBittorrent, or whose torrent is removed from it, is reset: the film is offered again and waits for the next request.
A film asked for from a torrent pack joins Recently added at once and stays there once scanned in; cancelled, it leaves.
While something downloads, a line beside the tabs says what, how far and how long, in the web and the app; it opens the film. The owner sees every download, a guest their own.
A follower takes its house's torrent packs and matches, and offers those films itself while the house is off, fetching with its own qBittorrent into its own library.
Downloads go into a folder the library scans: a save folder outside the library's folders is added to its film folders.

While a collection is being edited, the genre and decade picked above its list become its rule's genre and years, shown in the form; saved, the collection holds only those titles and opens in the sort chosen.
Search lists films to download among the films, greyed, and follows the sort, genre and decade of the Films or TV tab, which can be changed from the search itself.
The favorite button keeps the highlight every chosen button has, with the heart in red, in the web and the app.
Changing the sort or a filter while a collection is being edited no longer closes the edit form.
In the app, back from a title opened from a grid of posters returns to the exact place the grid was scrolled to; a list drawn again differently scrolls to the poster.
In the app, back from a title page no longer jumps to the top of Home: a return to the front was taken to have happened again every time the library was drawn after a title page.

title: Torrents in one box, and the piece limit asked of qBittorrent
items: Settings, Library has one Torrents box: how qBittorrent is reached, where films are saved, the room there and whether it is connected, then the packs - add one, each pack's stats (downloaded of how many, gigabytes fetched, on offer, already in the library) and remove it.
The watchlist button on a title page in the app steps through three states: off, on the watchlist, and a favorite with a red heart, which stays on the watchlist when watched.

A pack is refused only when its pieces are larger than the connected qBittorrent's own limit, asked of it each time: just under 256 MiB on qBittorrent built with libtorrent 1.2, just under 512 MiB on libtorrent 2.0. It was fixed at 128 MiB and written down, so a pack stayed refused after qBittorrent was updated.
The refusal says which libtorrent the qBittorrent runs, its limit, and that the libtorrent 2.0 build takes up to 512 MiB.

title: Films on offer in collections, torrent stats, and room on the download drive
items: A film on offer from a torrent pack joins any collection whose filters match it - words, genre, years - greyed until it is here, and can be put on a collection by hand.
A shuffle never draws a film on offer, Play in order starts with the first film that is here, and a collection's cover is a film that is here.
Free space on the drive downloads go to is shown in the torrent settings, on a film on offer's page and on Download in the app. A film that does not fit is refused before anything starts.
A green dot says Palladium is connected to qBittorrent; a red one says it is not.
A pack cut into pieces larger than 128 MiB is marked as one qBittorrent cannot load as soon as it is added. Download on its films says so, instead of failing on every press.
qBittorrent's refusal of a torrent file is reported in words rather than as HTTP error 415.
While a film downloads, its page in the web and in the app shows how far it has got, its speed in Mbit/s and the time left, read again every few seconds.

title: Favorites in the watchlist, films to download, the tray inside the server
items: Favorites live in the watchlist: hold a poster there, or right-click it in the web, to make it a favorite. Favorites have their own row under the watchlist and a red heart on the poster, above the copy dot.
The heart button on title pages and the Favorites tab are gone.
A watched title leaves the watchlist unless it is a favorite. The Remove what is watched setting is gone.
A favorite that was also watched lately is copied to the other machine again; the first reason reached won and dropped it as watched.

A shuffled collection resumes only the title its round is on and starts the next title from the beginning. Continue watching shows that title, not whichever title on the shelf was left part-way most recently.
Users: a weekly limit per person, in gigabytes, for what is copied to the other machine for them and for what they download.
Torrent packs: add a pack's .torrent under Settings, Library, Downloads. Its films are matched to TMDB and shown greyed in Films and in search until they are here.
A film on offer has a page with Download. Download fetches that film alone through qBittorrent: every other file in the pack is set to not download, and the film lands in a library film folder.
Log, Downloads lists every download with who asked for it and when, and can be narrowed to one person.
The tray icon is shown by the server itself and no palladium.exe is built. Windows Defender took the separate launcher for malware and quarantined it on every install, which left the server stopped.
Start at sign-in, the Start menu entry and the installer start palladium-server.exe.
The player's sources line no longer shows the previous film's split share on a stream from one machine.

title: Only the sound is made when the picture plays as it is
items: A film whose picture the device plays but whose sound it cannot, such as DTS on a phone, is sent with the picture untouched and only the sound encoded, instead of the whole film re-encoded.
The app asks where such a stream starts: a copied picture begins on the keyframe before the second asked for, and the timeline and subtitles count from there.
Subtitles for an encoded stream are cut to the millisecond, not the second.
Now playing says direct video, sound encoded for these streams.
A collection saved in edit mode keeps the sort, genre and decade showing, and opens with them in the web and in the app.
Settings: This computer holds this machine's own settings, name and port included; Remote computer holds everything about the other machine. Each setting is shown in one place.
Settings that do not apply are greyed out instead of hidden or repeated, with a tooltip saying why.
A copy with Managed from the house on has its copying settings on the house's Remote computer tab, set through the house. On the copy they are greyed out with a tooltip naming where they are set.
Managed from the house read its switch from the wrong settings file and never took effect.
Now playing measures a viewing's rate over the last 20 seconds across all its requests. A direct play read in chunks showed several times its bitrate.

A copy asked to play a title it holds no file for encodes it with its own encoder, reading the file from the house. Subtitles for it are cut by the house. An app that had moved to the copy got an error for every title not copied.

Settings, This computer, Encoding: Encode on This computer or Connected computer. Connected computer sends encodes to the computer this one copies from, or the one copying from it, and encodes here when it does not answer.
Holding a Continue watching poster on the television opens its menu when the button is let go. It opened while the button was still down, and the release pressed Go to title.
The app's title page and the line over the picture say Direct video, sound encoded when only the sound is encoded.
On a title page in the app, Play, Mark watched and Go to show are the same height and line up; Mark watched was drawn smaller than Play when there was nothing to resume.

title: Watchlist, favorite and collections as three buttons
items: A title page has three buttons in one control: watchlist, favorite and collections, with no words beside them, in the app and in the web.
The collections button lights when the title is on any collection.
Play on a title page keeps its full size when there is nothing to resume; it was shrunk as if From start stood beside it.

title: Hold a poster to open its title
items: Holding any poster in the app opens its title page, and an episode opens its programme; a long press of the remote select button counts as a hold on the television.
Continue watching keeps a menu when held: Go to title, Watched and Not watched, and End this shuffle on a shuffle row.
A title page has a Collection button, in the app and in the web; the hold menu no longer lists collections.

title: Genre and decade on watchlists and collections
items: Watchlist, Favorites and an open collection have Genre and Decade, built from what is on the list, beside the sort, in the web and in the app.
Films, programmes, seasons and episodes carry their genres in every list, so a list can be narrowed without asking again.
A title leaves the watchlist once watched, and stops being copied, unless Remove what is watched is turned off. Favorites are copied whether watched or not.
Holding a poster in the app offers Go to title: the page of a film or a programme, and for an episode its programme.

title: Favorites: kept on both machines
items: The poster and title-page button is a favourite heart: a favourite is copied to the other machine whether or not it has been watched, so it plays from either and reads from both.
Watchlist has two lists, Watchlist and Favorites, in the web and in the app.
Adding a title to a collection moved to the hold menu in the app and to a right-click on posters, hearts and episode rows in the web.

title: Collections by genre and year, and watchlists kept on the copy
items: The Casual collection page opened with an error: a season card turned a title key into a number.
The copy checks whether a title is watched against the person it is kept for. The owner having seen a film dropped it from a guest part-way through it.
Everything on a watchlist is copied, watched or not.
A setting removes a title from your watchlist when you finish it or mark it watched; off unless turned on.
The collection editor has Holds, Genre and Years at the top, ahead of the title words, for Save and for Test filter.

title: Per-title subtitle looks stick, and the copy keeps its settings
items: A per-title subtitle look keeps its height and its placement together. One saved with only a height took its placement from the default, so changing the default moved it.
Very bottom is kept as chosen; the server cut every height above 0.4 down to 0.4.
A look set on a programme page applies to its episodes; it was filed under the programme and never read.
The copy no longer empties its settings file when it reads it mid-write: an unreadable file is left alone, and what the house sends is laid over the file as it is now.
The player shows how much each machine carried only while two are connected; with one dropped it read 95/5 beside one source.
Playing an episode off a shelf counts it as drawn however it was started, so the next draw cannot hand the same episode back.
The shuffle row on Continue watching offers an episode only when it was left past the first half minute; otherwise it offers the next draw.
Removed Goes to sleep at: it only set the extra hour before the house sleeps, which is gone.

title: The collection button asks which collection
items: The shuffle button on titles, seasons and episodes opens your collections, each marked for holding all or part of the title; picking one adds or removes it, and a new collection can be made from the same list.
Taking a title off a filter collection strikes it out, and putting it back lifts the strike, instead of pinning it.
Removed the Casual-only mark: /casual, its green poster badge and the casual field in /marks.
The copy takes what is on a screen only in its set night hours or after Start the night now; the extra hour before the house sleeps is gone.

title: Old casual round removed; the shuffle mark edits the Casual shelf
items: The shuffle mark on titles, seasons and episodes adds to and removes from the Casual shelf; since casual became a shelf it wrote a list nothing played from.
Removed the old casual round: /casual/next, /peek, /back, /reset and /queue, the casual watchlist tab with its Casual play and Start over, and the settings they kept.
During a shelf shuffle the next-up name and the next subtitle fetch read that shelf's round; they peeked the old casual round.
The copy keeps what shelf shuffles have queued or left part-way; it read the old round's fields, which no longer move.
Shelf shuffle rounds sync between the house and the copy per shelf, newest wins, both ways; they were copied once and never updated.
Playing a title again more than a minute after it was marked watched clears the mark once past 30 seconds, so it shows on Continue watching.
A shuffled playing that restarted itself - a source switch, a subtitle or a quality change - lost which shelf it came off, so the next draw failed.
The copy files its titles under the house keys. A copy keeps no year, so its programmes had keys of their own and shelves, shuffle rounds and progress did not match between the machines.
Per-title subtitle looks follow a key move; they were all left on the old row numbers and no longer applied.
The app draws subtitles as the server says whenever the server answers. A look kept on the device won over a changed setting, so a television kept yellow subtitles after they were set back to white.

title: Verified subtitles show as verified again
items: Verification was saved under the episode key but read back with a second e in front of it, so every verified subtitle - track or file - showed as unverified, and verifying by hand looked like it did nothing.

title: Title-key conversion fixes, and reaching the house past a downed copy
items: Conversion looked episodes up first, so a film sharing a row number with an episode moved onto it; on the copy two such rows collided and the conversion rolled back. Old keys now move by kind, seasons with their programme.
Each viewer's subtitle picks, put-aside cards, casual places and subSince are converted; only the top-level copies were.
A failed conversion is written to debug.log instead of lost on stderr.
Update install reads library.json directly, so a server whose library will not open can still update itself.
App: away from home, a server filed under its LAN address is tried on the copy's outside address with its own port before falling back to the copy, and the row is saved there so posters load.
Making subtitles from the soundtrack found no file for a title key; fixed.

title: Converting the library to title keys is all or nothing
items: The conversion ran as a series of separate statements, and sqlite commits a CREATE TABLE on its own. On the copy a lock stopped it after the first new table was made, and every start after that fell over trying to make it again, so the copy answered no library request at all. It now takes the write lock before touching anything, clears anything a stopped attempt left behind, and rolls back on failure to try again next start.

Seasons, posters, matches and renumbering read a title key as hex. A season is a title key with -s and a number after it, and eight places still took the title half as digits: a programme opened onto seasons with nothing in them, and every poster fell back to the plain P. Choosing another match for a title and renumbering a season passed the key through int() and would have failed too.

title: The e on an episode's key is not added twice
items: An episode's key is stored whole now, the letter with it, and two dozen places still put another one in front - so Continue watching, the seasons of a programme and the artwork behind them asked for keys that were not there. A season and a poster address were built with %d as well, which a key made of hex is not.

title: Keys come from the title, not from the order things were scanned
items: A key was a row number, so it meant whatever that machine happened to insert first: key 3 was one film here and a different film on the copy. Anything falling back to the copy asked for a key it had no business asking for and got silence, or somebody else's film. Keys are now twelve hex digits worked out from the title and the year - an episode from its programme, season and number - so both machines arrive at the same key without asking each other.

The library, the watchlist, the shelves, every shuffle round, what has been watched and where each viewing got to were all rewritten in one pass. A key is never shown in the interface; it appears in fault reports and logs.

title: What the copy holds can go down as well as up
items: The copy sends two reports - one built by looking at the files on its disk, which is the whole truth, and a short one when copying starts so the queue reads right from the first minute. The house could not tell them apart and added both to what it already knew, so nothing was ever taken away: a film swept out of the cache stayed on the list for good, the dot stayed on its poster, and with the house switched off somebody chose it and there was nothing at the other end. The whole report now says so, and replaces.

title: No grey box behind a card
items: Resuming from Continue watching in the app asks for the film in full first. A row on that shelf is brief - no codecs, no part, nothing about the file - and a film that cannot say what it is cannot be played as it is, so every resume from there went through the encoder. Choosing a subtitle made the player fetch the details and rebuild the stream, which is why turning subtitles on turned the encoder off.

Giving a card something to do on a long press brought the default press highlight with it, and that is drawn over the whole card - poster, title and the line under it - so it came up as a grey square larger than the poster. The white ring already says where the remote is.

And the two buttons on a shuffle row in the browser say what they do there: the tick marks the episode the hat drew and the shelf moves on, the cross ends the round. The cross already did that and still called itself "forget where I was".

title: The app says which condition sent a film to the encoder
items: A film that could have been played as it is comes back re-encoded and says nothing about why. There are six conditions and any one of them decides it; the one that refused is now written to the log, with the track numbers it was given.

title: The shuffle badge is the word, not a sticker
items: It was set on a filled rounded box, which over a bright poster reads as a grey square somebody has left there. The artwork is what is being covered and the badge only has to be legible over it, so the word carries itself now, with a shadow heavy enough to hold on a pale poster as well as a dark one. Both the app and the browser.

title: The line and Now playing say what is connected
items: The line counts the machines connected to this film: two of them reads 2/2, one reads 1/1. It counted machines that hold the file against machines that had brought something in the last ten seconds - two different questions, neither of them the one being asked - so on an easy film, where the quick machine keeps up alone and the slow one is left out of the near work on purpose, it read 1/2 and back while nothing was wrong.

Now playing asks both machines and folds the answers into one row per viewing. It asked whichever machine the page was pointed at; a film read off two is served by both and reported to one, so the page showed a row with no position, or nothing at all while somebody was plainly watching. The megabits of both are added up, because both are carrying it.

And it folds those rows on the film rather than on the name. A stream raises a row named for the viewer; a player's report raises one named for the device - so one person watching one thing arrived twice, as a viewer with no position and a device with one, and the viewer's row was drawn greyed out while nine megabits were going to it.

title: Backing out of a film shows where it actually got to
items: The closing report went out on the player's own scope and the player was being torn down as it went, so the last and most accurate position was the one least likely to arrive. It is sent on a scope that belongs to the process instead, and draws nothing, because there is no screen left to draw on.

And the shelves are read after it lands rather than at the same moment. Both happen at once when somebody backs out and the read was winning, so Continue watching was drawn from what the server knew a moment before the film ended - faithfully drawn, and the old position. It waits up to two seconds.

title: The line counts the machines feeding the film
items: It said "sources 1/2" on a film being encoded, which reads as a split that has half failed. There was never a second half: an encode is one machine's ffmpeg with its own position, the pipe cannot be read in stretches, and two machines encoding the same film do not produce the same bytes. The second number was a fact about who holds the file, not about the stream. The pair is now shown only while the film is actually being read off more than one machine; otherwise it says one source, and why.

title: Two faults off the reports page
items: The copy's settings pane read a variable declared in two other functions and none of them this one, so opening it threw and everything below the line went undrawn. It reads the keys this house holds from the library's own config, where the rest of the page reads them.
Pressing previous on the casual shelf threw: the run counter is kept per order now, like the history beside it, and one line still read it as a number and handed a dict to int().

title: Continue watching is in the order things were watched
items: Every row now says when it was last watched. Only the shuffled shelves carried that, and both the browser and the app sort the shelf by it - so every ordinary row sorted as nought, the thing watched five minutes ago landed anywhere among them, and where the list is cut at forty it was arbitrary which forty. The server had the answer all along and was ordering correctly before the clients undid it.

title: Coming out of a film never shows the page from before it
items: In the app the key that decides whether to read the lists again is built out of the tab and the filters, not out of having been away - so leaving a film back onto Home, which is where a film is nearly always started, changed nothing and the page stood as it was when the film began. Home is now read again on every return.
In the browser the back button stopped the film and left whatever was behind it on screen; it now draws the homepage again, as closing the player does.

The back arrow puts an episode on its own page rather than replaying it. Opening an episode sends it straight into play, so walking back into that entry started the film again at the position it had when the entry was made. Everything else on that stack is stored as a key and read again.

title: The cross on a shuffle row ends that shuffle
items: A row for a shuffled shelf is the shelf, not the episode showing on it - that is only whatever the hat drew last. The cross put that episode aside, so the row came straight back under the next draw and could not be got rid of. It now ends the round: everything back in the hat and the row goes. The tick still means the episode was watched.

title: Hold a poster on Continue watching
items: Holding a card on Continue watching offers what the browser already offers there: watched and off the shelf, or not watched and forget where I was. Both put it aside, because marking one episode watched otherwise hands the shelf to the next episode of the programme and looks like nothing happened.
Pressing that card resumes, so there was nowhere else in the app to say either.

A shuffle row there is the shelf, not the title showing on it, so holding one offers to end that shuffle: everything back in the hat and the row leaves Continue watching. Putting the title aside only brought the row back under whatever the hat drew next.

Finishing something now takes it off every shelf keeping its place. A shelf drops the place at 95%, but only when the report names the shelf, and only a playing started off that shelf does - so an episode watched from its own page stayed on Continue watching as half-watched for ever, and watching it again changed nothing. Marking it watched does the same.

title: Hold a poster on Watch later
items: Holding a poster on the Watch later shelf offers the two things done with one: mark it watched, or take it off the list. Both meant opening the title's page, where the marks live - two screens and a scroll on a phone for a decision made in a second.

title: Back in a collection shuffle steps back through that shelf
items: Next was moved to the shelf when the casual tab was replaced; Back was not. The browser still asked /casual/back, a different round on a shelf that is no longer there, so it answered about a shelf that does not exist. The app sent no direction at all, so Back drew a new title forwards.
The server has taken a back flag on /collections/shuffle all along; both clients now send it.

title: A guest may draw from a shelf again
items: Drawing from a collection shuffle was refused for anybody who is not the owner, which includes the owner from outside the house: /collections/shuffle replaced /casual/next and was never added to the list a guest may post to. Pressing Next in a shuffle answered 403 and the player reported it as the server being unreachable.
That message now says the shelf could not be drawn from, and the reason is written to the log.

title: Continue watching resumes in the app instead of opening the page
items: Every card on Home opened its page, so resuming took a second press and a shuffle lost its shelf on the way - the page carries no shelf, so Next handed over the next episode of the programme rather than drawing. The browser has resumed from that row for a while; the app now does the same.

title: The machine still answering is allowed to fetch the lump the picture is waiting on
items: A machine stopped while holding one lump. The other fetched the six behind it, which filled the window, and the window then refused the one lump that would have emptied it. Nothing came in for ninety seconds while a live machine sat idle, and the picture ran on its buffer until the film moved house. That lump is now claimed whatever the window says.
A machine that has brought nothing in for five seconds no longer counts as the quick one, so the near work stops being left to a machine that has gone.

The reader has room for four machines and counted all four whether or not they were there, so two machines looked like four and one looked like three. Down to one machine that let the reader put aside the only machine carrying the film.

title: A film being read off two machines does not move house when one goes
items: There are two things watching a stalled picture. The reader hands a dropped machine's work to whichever machine is left and takes the whole film off it, and the picture carries on. The other restarts the film on the other machine, which throws away everything in hand and fills from nothing - so what looks like a failover curing an empty buffer is the thing that emptied it.

While the reader still has a machine and film is still arriving, the film stays where it is. The mover was interrupting after fourteen seconds of a picture that had already stopped, which is exactly when the reader was in the middle of taking over.
It still moves when nothing has arrived at all for twenty-five seconds, because then there is nothing left to protect.

And a reader that has gone quiet says what it is waiting for, once a second: which stretch, which machine was given it, how much is in hand, and what each machine is thought to be doing. The only account of a reader going quiet was that the picture stopped, which says nothing about why.

title: The player's account of a server going away is not sent to that server
items: What the player did when a machine went is the one thing worth having written down, and it was being written to the machine that had gone - so the whole account of the moment was lost every time. A trace goes to the house, and to the machine keeping copies when the house will not take it.

Nothing else changed. A share rule shipped earlier today was withdrawn after being measured: driving the same arithmetic with a four-hundred megabit machine and a forty megabit one carrying a nine megabit film gives ninety-seven to three either way, because one machine can carry the film several times over and there is nothing left for the second to do. The split is redundancy, not speed, and the stalls were the retrying and the guard rather than the share.

title: Answering about itself is not the same as sending a film
items: A stalled picture asks the machine it is reading from whether it is still there, and stays put when it says yes. A server on its way out - one that has just been replaced, or is being shut down - answers that question cheerfully while sending nothing at all, so the picture stood still being reassured for the whole of the stall before it moved. It now has to have brought something in within the last twelve seconds as well.

Next on the television draws from the shelf the playing came off. It asked the old casual shelf instead, which drew a plausible title from somebody's marks and left the shelf's own round exactly where it was.
And a badged row played from a phone stays the shelf's: the row carries which shelf it belongs to, the title's page keeps it, and the film is told.

title: A shuffled row stays the shelf's when it is played from a phone
items: Pressing a badged poster opens the title's own page, and playing from there wrote an ordinary place - so the shelf lost track of its evening and Next handed over the next episode of the programme rather than drawing. The row carries which shelf it belongs to, the page keeps it, and the film is told.

Down to one machine, the other is asked for every five seconds rather than at a wait that doubles to a minute. Backing off further and further suits a machine nobody needs; it is exactly wrong when the machine still answering has nothing behind it - which is how a restart of the second one cost twenty-three seconds of stopped picture.

title: A machine that has gone is asked whether it is back before it is let back in
items: Reading a film off two machines survives one of them going: what it had taken on goes back to the other, which holds the whole film. What it did not survive was being asked again. A machine that has been switched off drops the packets rather than refusing them, so letting it straight back into the rotation handed it the very stretch the picture was waiting on and then spent five seconds finding out - over and over, ten seconds apart, while the machine that was answering sat there able to fetch it.

So the picture ran dry and the film moved house, with a live machine holding all of it. The side is asked whether it is there first, on a thread nobody is waiting on and with a second and a half to answer, and only let back in when it says yes.

title: Next draws from the shelf that is playing
items: Next asked the old casual shelf for its next card, which is not where a collection's round lives - so even a playing that knew perfectly well which shelf it came off had nowhere to ask, and fell through to the next episode of whatever programme it happened to be. It draws from that shelf now.

And pressing a row on Continue watching says what it saw - the shelf, and whether it took the playing to be a shuffled one - because that is the whole question and it cannot be seen from outside the browser.

title: The shuffle badge sits over the poster rather than behind it
items: It was drawn on the card, and a card is a poster with a title under it - the poster is painted with its own ground on top, so the badge went underneath and could not be seen at all. It is drawn inside the poster now, over the picture, and centred on the picture rather than on the picture and its title together.
And it shrinks with a small poster, so a phone shows the whole word instead of the middle of it.

title: The shuffle row stays put, and resuming one stays in the shuffle
items: The row had no date on it. A shelf ordered by when things were last watched put it at the very end, where a page of a dozen cards cuts it off - so the badge showed for as long as the first answer was on screen and then went. It carries the moment the shelf was last played, and sorts among the rest by it.

Pressing a badged row carries on being the shelf's. Next then draws the next thing out of that hat rather than handing over the next episode of whatever programme it happens to be - resuming a shuffle and then being given a series in order is not a shuffle at all.
The television says which shelf a playing came off, the way the browser does, so the shelf keeps its place and Next means the same thing there.

title: Both places stand on Continue watching, and the badge says which is the shelf's
items: Putting a film on with the shuffle and later choosing it by hand are two viewings of one title at two different seconds. Collapsing them into a single row made it impossible to see which was which, which is the one thing the badge is for. Both stand, and only the shelf's wears it.

So on Continue watching a poster with SHUFFLE across it is a place the hat is holding, and the same title without it is where somebody sat down with it. Nowhere else is marked - a title is not casual, a viewing is.

title: The shuffle badge is big, and it means what came out of a shuffle
items: One film, one row. Putting something on with the shuffle and then choosing it by hand wrote an ordinary place beside the shuffle's own, and the shelf showed both - the same title twice, nine seconds apart, arguing with itself about where somebody had got to.

Whichever place is the newer one is what the viewing is. Started by the shuffle, it wears the badge; chosen by hand afterwards, it is an ordinary viewing and wears none - which is the difference between a title that is in a shuffle and one that came out of it.
And the badge is big enough to be told apart at a glance, in the browser and on the television. Small print across a poster is something to notice afterwards.
A shelf says where its round was left, so the button reads Resume with the second it would start at rather than Play.

title: Play works on a shelf without shuffling, and a film lets out onto the homepage
items: The television reads a shelf through a different door than the browser does, and its season cards carried nothing but the season - so asking the library for one answered with the programme, and Play opened the show and started nothing. They carry the episodes they stand for now, in order.

Coming out of a film lands on the homepage, drawn again, in the browser and on the television both. Whatever was on screen when the film started is a page from before it: Continue watching still says the place it was at, a shelf still says what it said when the draw was made, and a shuffle that has moved on says nothing at all.

title: The Casual shelf is written into the settings that were changed
items: It was written by reading the settings a second time, which fetches a fresh copy without the shelf in it - so the file kept being written exactly as it was. The shelf existed in every answer and in no file, and the row on Continue watching had no name to show for it and said only "Shuffle".

title: Continue watching gets its row for a shelf being shuffled
items: The row was written and never appeared. The shelves were handed to the library api as a plain attribute and read back through the accessor every other setting uses, which reads somewhere else - so the deck was always told there were no shelves, however plainly one had a place in it.

A season card on a shelf stands for the episodes under it, and those are what plays. Asking the library for the season answers with the programme, so Play opened the show and started nothing - in the browser and on the television both.

And the television says the shelf across the poster, the way the browser does: one row for the shelf, turned forty-five degrees, because the row otherwise reads as the episode it happens to be showing.

title: A shelf is known by either of its names
items: The library numbers a shelf "coll:f592640" so that a shelf and a film cannot collide, and the shuffle was asked for one called "f592640". Being strict about which of its two names had been sent is how a television came to say there was nothing to play on a shelf full of films.
The server takes either now, and the app sends the plain one.

title: A shelf is asked of the server it belongs to
items: Shelves are gathered from every server anybody has a key to, and the draw was asked of whichever server the app happened to be talking to - so a shelf from one machine, asked for by name on another, was a shelf that did not exist. It said there was nothing to play, which was true of the machine it asked.

On a phone the shelf's name takes one line and the controls take the next. Five things across three hundred and sixty points put the buttons off the edge, and a button off the edge cannot be pressed at all.

title: The buttons on a shelf fit a phone, and Shuffle there means the same thing
items: A shelf's row holds a name, a count, two controls and the sort. At the full width of a phone the buttons were pushed off the edge, where nothing can press them - they are narrow on a narrow screen now.

One Play, and a Shuffle switch beside it, the same as in the browser. It drew a title at random before, which is a fresh evening every time it is pressed; it draws from the round the house keeps for that shelf and that person now - carrying on with whatever was left part-way, nothing twice until the hat is empty.

title: A shelf keeps the place of what it put on
items: The round advanced and the place never did. Drawing marked something played, and nothing wrote down where it got to - the one thing that does needs to know which shelf is playing, and nobody was telling it. So there was nothing to resume, and Continue watching had nothing to show, because that row is built out of exactly that.

The player says which shelf it drew from on every report, the way it already says whether the playing was chosen. The shelf keeps the place; what has been watched is still left alone, because putting something on is not watching it.
Choosing a title by hand forgets the shelf, and so does playing a collection in order: a queue is not a round.
And a season card carries the episodes it stands for, so playing a shelf plays them. Playing the season's own key opened the programme's page instead - Play took somebody to the show.

title: One Play on a shelf, with a switch for how
items: Two play buttons asked somebody to choose the way of playing before there was anything to play, and both of them said Play - so which was the ordinary one had to be worked out by reading. There is one, and a Shuffle switch beside it that stays as it was left for that shelf.

And shuffling now opens what it drew. The draw describes the title; the player wants the library's own answer with its files and its tracks on it, and being handed the first where it wanted the second is why pressing it did nothing anybody could see. It asks again by key, the way playing a collection in order already did.

title: A rolled-up card is the season, counted against the season
items: The key for a season answers with the programme it belongs to, so nineteen cards all read as the same programme and counted their episodes against the whole of it: "7 of 179" for a season of twelve, nineteen times over. Each card says which season it is and counts against that season.

title: A shelf of episodes reads as seasons, and the copy opens rather than asking who you are
items: Episodes on a shelf stand as the seasons they belong to. Four episodes of a fifty-six episode programme showed four episode cards and said nothing about the programme; one season card saying four of fifty-six is what somebody reading the shelf wants to know. The episodes are still what the shelf holds - this is how it is read, not what it is.

The way in to the other machine carries the viewer's own key. A cookie belongs to the machine that set it, so arriving at the copy with one for the house is arriving with nothing - which is why the owner, who has every right to be there, was shown the way in for a stranger.
The Casual shelf is written down rather than rebuilt for each answer. It existed in every reply and in no file, so anything reading the settings directly could not see it at all.
And a shuffle that draws something and then cannot start it says so. Failing silently on the way to playing is indistinguishable from a button that does nothing.

title: The other machine is offered by name, and only when it is there
items: "The machine that keeps copies" is what it does, not what it is called. The line that offers it appears at the one moment somebody is anxious, which is the worst moment to be vague, so it says what that machine calls itself.

And it is asked whether it is there before being offered. Both machines restart during an update, so the line came up saying the copy was still there at the one moment it was not, with a button that opened a page which could not load. If neither answers it says so, and says they may both be restarting.
The button falls back to this window when a pop-up is blocked. A blocked pop-up is silence, and silence reads as a broken button.

title: One Shuffle on a shelf, and it is the one that remembers
items: A second Shuffle was added to the heading of a shelf that already had one, so the page offered the same thing twice and meant something different by each.

The button that was already there does the remembered kind now. It used to shuffle the order of a playlist, which starts a fresh evening every time it is pressed; it keeps a round for this shelf and this person instead - carrying on with whatever was left part-way, never repeating until the hat is empty, and showing as one row on Continue watching rather than filling it.

title: Go to show stands on the episode it was sent to
items: It scrolled the row to the episode and left the highlight where it had been, so the first press of a direction key took the row back to the start of the season - which is indistinguishable from never having gone there. The episode is stood on now as well as scrolled to.
A poster can be handed a modifier by whatever is drawing it, which is what lets one of them be the one focus lands on.

title: A collection played in shuffle, in place of a shelf of its own
items: Casual watching was a second list beside the collections - marked a different way, drawn a different way, kept in its own corner of the settings - and it is the same idea: a set of titles and a hat. The hat moves onto the collections, where the sets already are, and putting something on becomes a way of playing one rather than a place to go.
A round belongs to one person and one shelf. Two people shuffling the same shelf are two evenings, and one person shuffling two shelves is two rounds - which the one shelf casual had could not say.

What was marked for casual watching becomes a shelf called Casual on the first run, carrying its hat, its history and everywhere it was left. Nobody is asked to mark a hundred and eighty episodes again because the idea was renamed.

And a shelf being shuffled has a row on Continue watching: what is being carried on with, or what the hat has drawn next, with the word said across the poster at forty-five degrees. One row for the shelf, per person - a hat of two hundred episodes putting each one it touched on the shelf is what made that list unreadable in the first place.

The Casual tab is gone from both the browser and the television. A shelf is shuffled by the button on its own page, which carries on with whatever was left part-way and otherwise draws - no page in between pressing it and something playing.

title: Casual play opens on a page, not straight into a film
items: Pressing it started something playing at once, which is right when the answer is "put anything on" and wrong every other time: there was no way to see what was about to play, no way to carry on with the one left half-watched, and no way to look at what is in the hat without leaving for the watchlist.

It opens the way any other title does now - the poster, and a button that says what pressing it will do. Resume names the place it would start at, because the shuffle keeps that place and nothing else does.
Underneath it: the ten already drawn, in the order they will play, and what the hat has already used this round. The shelf itself is a button at the end of the row.

title: One evening, kept by the house
items: Two machines each drawing from their own copy of a round are two evenings. Walking from the television to a phone gave a different episode and both machines were right locally, which is what a copy of a round always comes to mean. Reconciling faster narrows that window; it does not close it.

So the house owns it. A machine keeping copies puts the question there under the same person's key and hands the answer back untouched - a draw, a peek, going back, starting over, marking a title. It answers for itself only when the house cannot be reached, which is the night that copy exists for, and hands its round back when the house returns.

And a round can be looked at: what was left part-way, the ten already drawn, and what the hat has used this time round. The first of those is a shelf of its own - a casual playing writes no row Continue watching reads, so nothing else could ever offer to carry one on.

title: The shuffle can be carried on with when the house is off
items: What the shuffle was in the middle of is copied, and it comes first. A casual playing writes no row that Continue watching reads - that is the point of it - so nothing ever put a half-watched shuffled episode on the other machine, and the one thing it could not do when the house went off was carry on with what was actually on.

How many are kept follows the two settings that govern everything else kept ahead - Episodes ahead, and Hours ahead at most - rather than a number of its own. A shelf of half-hour comedies and one of hour-long drama are not the same number of files, and the settings already say so. Ten is the ceiling whatever those say, because ten is all the shuffle knows: the queue is drawn ten deep and the eleventh has not been decided.

Hours of casual play is the shuffle's own limit and is used at last. It was asked for by the machine keeping the copies, sent over, and dropped on the floor - the hours that govern a series somebody is part-way through are about the night ahead, and an evening of putting something on is a different question.

Where the evening had got to travels both ways, and the shelf it was drawn from does not. The machine keeping copies knows only the part of the shelf that fits on its disk - sixty episodes of a hundred and eighty-two - so the first time it had the newer round it would have handed that back as the whole shelf.
It sends the round alone now, and the house refuses a shelf or a watchlist arriving that way in any case.

title: The words are read where both machines can reach them
items: Describing a shuffle and reading one back were written on the server and called from the copy, which has no such thing - so every attempt failed quietly and the shelf arrived as numbers again. They live beside the rest of the translating now, where both machines use them.

And a shelf of numbers nobody can place is replaced whatever the stamps say. The two machines agreed about when the round last moved and disagreed about what it was, which comparing stamps would have left that way for ever.

title: A shuffle described in words, because a number means nothing on the other machine
items: Every library numbers its own titles. The marks travelled as numbers, so a hundred and eighty-two episodes arrived at the other machine as a hundred and eighty-two numbers it could not place - and the shelf, which is those numbers looked up in the library, came out empty. A phone on the copy said nothing was marked for casual watching.

The shuffle now travels the way a viewing already did: a programme, a season and a number, which both libraries recognise. The marks, the queue, what has been played and where anything was left, all of it, in both directions.

The watchlist crossed the same water and was numbered too - nine titles on the copy, none of which it could place. It is described now as well. One made sitting at that machine is still left alone; one that is only numbers is replaced.

title: A shuffle belongs to the person, not to the machine it is played on
items: The round went one way, house to copy, so an evening carried on properly until somebody picked up a phone - and then the copy played its own round and the house never heard about it.
It is stamped whenever it moves now, and the newer stamp wins in either direction. Taken whole or not at all: a queue half from one machine and half from the other is not a queue anybody drew.
The two machines compare rounds every two minutes rather than every ten, because where somebody is in an evening moves every twenty minutes and a watchlist does not.

title: The shuffle is kept as it was drawn, and travels to the other machine
items: Ten episodes, which is the depth of the queue the shuffle actually keeps. It used to pad that list out of the marked pool until it had twenty, and the pool is in library order - so half of what was copied was the first episodes of a programme in sequence, which is the one thing a shuffle will not play.

And nothing is taken after a draw. Six episodes follow anything somebody is part-way through, because that is what they will want in twenty minutes; what follows a shuffled episode is whatever the shuffle draws next, and that is already on the list. Ten draws had become a hundred and forty files.
One person's shuffle is now ten files rather than a hundred and forty.

And the round travels with the marks. The other machine was given the shelf and none of the state - no queue, no history, nowhere anything was left - so a phone on the copy drew a fresh shuffle from the top instead of carrying on where the evening was, and could not resume an episode left part-way.

Where somebody is in a round is kept up to date on the copy rather than written once. A preference set on that machine is still theirs and is left alone; a place in a round is one moving thing both machines have to agree on.

title: The machine keeping the copies decides whether it keeps the shuffle
items: It was asked and then overruled. The follower's own setting said keep two hours of the shuffle ahead, and the house threw the number away before answering - so the row on that machine's own page did nothing anybody could see, and there was no way to tell which of the two switches was the one that mattered.
One switch, on the machine whose disk it is: Casual watching, under Follow another server.
And no word on the line between the machines in the drawing. The line is already dashed and moving while a copy is going, and the box at the end of it says it is taking one.

title: Copying gives way to a film that is struggling
items: Taking what the films are drawing away from what the line can carry is arithmetic, not watching. It assumes the line behaves, and a wireless one does not: the number it carried an hour ago is not the number it carries when somebody walks between the aerials.

So the allowance is steered by what the films are getting. A viewer whose rate has fallen away from its own running average, with a socket still open, is being starved - and the copy gives up nearly half of what it had, in one step. When everybody is comfortable it takes eight megabits more each time. Down in one step and up in small ones is the only way round that ends with the film winning.
