Measured against each viewer's own average rather than the bitrate of what they are watching: a direct play reads in bursts and idles between them, so "below what the film needs" is true of a healthy one half the time. A viewer with nothing open is holding a full buffer, which is the opposite of starved.

title: Copying takes what the line has spare
items: A number typed into a settings file knows nothing about the line it is on. Twenty megabits is slower than the film it is meant to have ready, so the copy loses the race it exists to win; no ceiling at all takes the line out from under whoever is watching.

So it is measured. The most this machine has been seen to shift at once is what the line can carry - nobody can ask a network how fast it is, and what it has actually carried is the only honest answer. What the films are drawing this second is what they need. A copy may have what is left, less a margin for the bursts a filling buffer asks in, and never less than four megabits.
The high-water mark halves after ten quiet minutes, so a line that has got slower is believed within the hour.
A number in the settings still wins, and nought still means no ceiling at all. What the line was seen to carry and what a copy is allowed against it are both on the traffic page.

title: No ceiling on copying means no ceiling
items: Nought is how somebody says there should be no limit while a film is playing, and nought was read as twenty - the one value anybody sets on purpose was the one the setting could not hold. So a copy crawled at exactly twenty megabits and the film it was meant to have ready finished first.
Leaving it unset still means twenty.

title: The film being watched is never the one deleted
items: Two changes met badly. The cache deletes what the house has no reason to hold, and a shuffled playing had just stopped being a reason for anything - so a film put on by the shuffle was deleted off the disk it was being read from, and playback stopped where it stood.
Nothing refused the deletion. A film is read in two-megabyte stretches, so the file is closed between them and there was no open handle to object.
What is on a screen is named on the list again, shuffled or not, and marked: keep this where it is, do not fetch it, and do not take the six episodes after it.

title: Taking something off Continue watching drops the place as well
items: It used to be remembered behind a date: the shelf was told to ignore the row and the row stayed. So a film left at eighty-nine per cent went on drawing a bar across its poster, and went on being copied to the other machine as something somebody was part-way through - thirty titles of them.
The place is now cleared when the title is put aside, for the programme's episodes as well as the film. A tick made by hand says something else and is left alone.
The places already put aside were cleared once, where nothing had been played since.
Now playing opens with the drawing of what is talking to what. It is the one picture of what is happening this minute, and it was on the last tab anybody would look at for that.
The other machine's queue and its own row leave Now playing for Remote computer. Neither is somebody watching something, and between them they pushed what is on a screen below the fold.

title: A shuffled playing is on a screen without being a reason to copy
items: What is on a screen now leads the copy queue and takes six episodes with it, and a shuffled playing was answering that. It is still in Now playing, which is what Now playing is for; the row says whether anybody chose it, and only the queue reads that.
That was the third way the shuffle reached the queue, after the progress row and the watch log.
And what is on a screen is named. It was the one reason in the list with a blank where every other one has a person.
The sweep runs before the fetching rather than after it. At the end of a pass it ran once a pass, and a pass with a backlog runs for hours - so on a busy night it never ran at all.

title: Adding a title to the casual shelf no longer starts the round over
items: A title marked casual is unplayed because it is not in the history, and that is all it takes to reach it. Emptying the history made every episode already watched that evening eligible again, so the shelf repeated itself an hour later - and marking one title did it.
Starting the round over is what the reset button is for.

title: One tab called Log, with the watch log and the transfers under it
items: What has been watched and what has been copied are one question asked of two books. The transfers were filed under Now playing, beside the machine that fetched them rather than beside the log they belong to. Log now carries Watch log, Transferred and Versions.
And the transfer log credits a person. Twenty entries said "the house", which was never anybody: they are the owner's, which is whose viewing they were.

title: The cache keeps what there is a reason to keep
items: A copy is deleted when the house stops wanting it. The cap answered "is there room" and nothing answered "is there a reason", so a film copied because somebody was part-way through it stayed after they finished, and a season copied for a watchlist stayed after the list was cleared - until the cap reached it, which on a disk with room to spare is never.
What it tests against is what the house wants at all, taken before the hour decides what may move tonight. Testing against the night's list would empty the disk every morning.
It deletes only files this machine fetched, never a part-file arriving now, and never on an empty list from the other server. A file somebody is watching refuses to be deleted and stays.

The follow settings are greyed out on a machine that follows nothing. They write to whichever server the page is open on, so an hour typed on the machine with the library was accepted, stored where nothing reads it, and shown back as though it had been set.

title: The copy queue names who watched, and the night hours are kept when they are set
items: The queue names whoever watched it. "The house" was standing in for a person: no filter could match it and no cache could be kept for it.
"Night from" is written down. The page has always offered the hour and the server dropped it, so an owner who typed 21 was left with 22 and nothing on screen to say so.

title: Nor does the shuffle count as the house having watched something
items: The copy queue asks what the house watched lately and keeps the rest of the series behind it. A shuffled playing was answering that question. Five episodes of a season went to the other machine at twenty to nine in the evening for a programme nobody had chosen.
A casual playing still writes its line in the watch log - Now playing and the log would be wrong otherwise - but it is no longer a reason to copy anything.

title: A shuffled playing keeps its place without joining Continue watching
items: Putting something on is not choosing it. A casual playing now writes down where it got to, marked as casual: it resumes, and Continue watching, the copy queue and watched state all pass over it.

Before this a casual playing wrote nothing, which left whatever row was already there. One episode sat at 341 seconds of 1297 while the shuffle carried it to the credits, and was copied to the other machine as something part-way through for a fortnight.
Choosing a film clears the mark. A tick made by hand is never overwritten.
The mark travels between servers with the row, and survives renaming a viewer.

title: A film being encoded is not read in stretches, and so no longer restarts for ever
items: Reading a film off several machines works by asking for two megabytes at a time. Against a file that is exactly right. Against an encode, which is made as it is sent, every one of those asks starts the encoder again from that point - and starting it again stops the one before. So the picture waited for an encode that was replaced every two seconds, and waited for ever: two hundred and thirty encodes were begun for one episode that never played a frame.
The reader was handed the film before anything asked whether it was a file or an encode. It is asked first now.

title: A film is never re-encoded at more than it was made with
items: Re-encoding something already compressed, at a quality target rather than a bitrate, spends far more than the original did: an episode made at six megabits was going out at forty-seven. That is worse than the film it came from, and it floods any line thinner than this house's own - which is what was stopping the picture.
The film's own bitrate is the ceiling now, with a fifth again for a busy scene, unless somebody asks for a particular number. A film with no bitrate recorded falls back to what it did before.

title: One file at a time to a machine taking copies
items: The copy asks for one file at a time, but a fetch it gives up on left this side still sending - so two, three, four files went out at once, each taking its share of the line and the air, for a machine that had stopped listening to all but the last. Whoever asked last is the one still listening; anything older now stops.

That matters more than it sounds. A copy on the same wireless channel as a television is not using bandwidth beside it, it is taking airtime from it - and four transfers at once take four times as much.

title: A screen away from the house is told an address it can actually reach
items: Asked where the other machine is, this server answered with its address on the home network - to anybody allowed that address, wherever they were standing. Somebody away from the house was handed 192.168.x, asked it, and waited for an answer that could never arrive: so from away the second machine had no version, no build and no way to be reached. Being allowed the address on this network and being able to use it are two questions, and only the first was being asked.
In the watch log, what to show is chosen by machine name rather than by a switch called "On the copy" - which is a job rather than a machine, and says nothing on a screen with two servers on it.

title: A key reaches the other machine at once instead of within the quarter-hour
items: The machine that copies this library takes its invitations a quarter of an hour at a time. So a key handed to somebody was refused by that machine for up to fifteen minutes - and since it is the machine that answers when this one is off, that is exactly when a new key is most likely to be tried.
The house now says when its keys last changed, in an answer the copy already asks for every minute. When they have changed the copy comes back for them there and then.

title: What each machine is running can be seen from anywhere; replacing it cannot
items: Asking a machine what build it is running was the owner's business, and owner means being in the same house as it. So a screen away from home was refused, and where the machines should have been listed there was nothing at all - not even the machine that screen was talking to. A version number is worth showing to anybody holding a key, and it is now shown.

Replacing the program stays exactly where it was: the owner, from the same house as the machine. The answer says which of the two the asker is, so a screen that may not press is not offered the button.

title: The other machine is asked of the server, not of the app's own notes
items: A server names two things: the machine that copies from it, and the machine it copies from. On the house the first is filled and on the copy the second, so between them there is always an answer - and the app was reading only the first. From the copy there was nothing to read, so the house was missing from the list of machines to update.

The app was then made to fall back to the servers it had written down, which depends on it having written both down. It asks the server itself now, which knows, and keeps its own notes only as a last resort.

title: The second machine in the list is never the one already in the first
items: Which machine to offer beside this one was taken from what the server had said about its copy, and that is remembered against each server and can be out of date. On the copy it pointed at the copy itself - so the second row named the machine already named in the first, and the other machine appeared nowhere. The machine offered is now one the app knows to be a different machine from the one it is standing on.

title: Both machines can be updated from the app, whichever one it is on
items: The second row was found by asking the server for the machine that keeps copies of it. A copy keeps no copies of its own, so with the app on the copy there was no second row at all - and the house itself could not be updated from the app while the app was standing on the other machine. It now takes the other machine from the ones the app already knows, whichever way round the two are standing.

It is also asked with its own key rather than with this server's. A key belongs to the machine that issued it, so asking one machine with another's was refused - which is why a row that did appear could say nothing about what that machine was running.

title: Both servers are offered for updating under their own names
items: They were "The server" and "The other server", which name nothing on a screen that has two of them on it - and which one is about to be stood down and replaced is exactly what somebody pressing Update needs to be sure of. Each row carries the machine's name, falling back to its address only where no name is known.
This app keeps its own row, as it had.

title: The name somebody goes by is theirs; the name on their key is the owner's record
items: Renaming yourself rewrote the invitation, so the name the owner wrote when they made the key - which is how they know whose key it is - was quietly replaced by whatever the holder chose. The two are separate now. What somebody calls themselves is kept with their own settings and is what shows against whatever they are watching; the key keeps the name it was written with.
In the list of people, a key shows both: the name it was made under, and the name its holder goes by where those differ.

title: Settings is the first tab, and holds what a person actually changes
items: Quality is called Settings and comes first, since it is where somebody goes. Under it: what you are called, shown as it stands; the picture size and megabits you watch at; how a film is fetched; and the other server.
The other server has no tab of its own any more. What it is, whether it is awake and what it is holding is a box under Settings, named after the machine rather than after the job it does.

title: How films are fetched sits under Quality
items: Reading a film off several machines, and moving to another when one stops, are decisions about how a film reaches a screen - so they belong beside the picture size and the megabits rather than beside the subtitles.

title: The app names the machine even before it has found it
items: A machine was named from the copy once one had been found, or from what the server had said about where its copy is. Both are empty for the first seconds of a film - and a message arriving in those seconds called a machine with a perfectly good name "the other server". The app falls back to the machines it already knows, which is where the name was all along.

title: Reading off several machines, and moving between them, are each a choice
items: Two switches of your own, under Subtitles. Reading a film off every machine that holds it, so losing one does not stop the picture; and carrying on from another machine when the one serving it stops answering. Both on unless you say otherwise.
They belong to the person watching rather than to the machine: one house may want every machine used at once, and somebody on a thin line would rather a film came off one and stayed there.

title: Everyone is called what they say they are called
items: A name was something only whoever wrote the invitation could give, so everybody wore whatever they were christened at the moment they were invited, for ever. Anybody can set their own now, under Subtitles, and it is written back onto their key - so what shows against what they are watching, and what the owner sees in the list of people, is the name they chose.
"Me" is what a server calls whoever installed it before anybody has said who that is. It is a placeholder, not a person, and it no longer appears on a screen: the owner's row wears their name.

title: A viewer's own watchlist follows them to the other machine
items: A watchlist, the shelves somebody arranged, the collections they made: these live beside the library and were never copied. So the one moment a viewer needs the other machine - this one being off - was the moment their own list was empty and the shelves were somebody's defaults. What each viewer keeps is now copied along with the films, under the same key they watch by.
Only what a screen would show goes over - a list, a shelf, how their subtitles look. No password and no key travels with it.

What somebody set on the other machine, sitting at it, is theirs and is not written over by the house. And the house's own owner is known there by the same key, so the person who owns the library is not the one viewer it treats as a stranger.

title: Whoever sits at this machine is a person, not an address
items: A guest is known by the name on their invitation, and everybody else was known by the address they came from - so the owner's own screens stood among named guests as bare numbers, which is the one person the server is certain of shown as the one thing nobody recognises. Anybody on this network with no key of their own is now shown under the owner's name, in the list of who is watching and in the drawing alike.

title: No machine is called by what it does for a living
items: "The machine that keeps copies" is a job, not a name, and it named nothing on a screen with two servers on it. Every heading, note, tooltip and message that used it now says the machine's own name, and falls back to "another server" only where no name is known yet.
A copy going out is logged under the name of the machine taking it, or its address, rather than under the job.

title: A player away from the house can say what it is doing
items: What a player reports - which machines it found, what it chose, why it stopped - was listed among the things a guest may write, and not among the things that make somebody a guest at all. So every report from anybody but the owner was refused. The only players whose word could be heard were the ones sitting at the machine, and the trouble is nearly always somewhere else. Crash reports were refused for the same reason and are allowed now too.

In the list of what was transferred, why a file went has a column of its own. It was crowded onto the end of the file's name, where it read as part of the name; how fast the file managed now sits under it.

title: A copy gives way to a film somebody is watching
items: Copying to the other machine took its share of the disk, the line and the router from whatever was being watched at the time, and there was nothing to say which mattered more. A copy is never in a hurry - it is for an evening that has not happened yet - so while anybody is watching it goes at a walk rather than a run, and has the line to itself again the moment the last film ends. Nothing is stopped or dropped; it simply waits its turn.
Twenty megabits while somebody is watching, which leaves a 4K film its twenty-five and the rest of the line besides. Set it as syncMbitWhileWatching, or nought to let a copy run flat out as before.

title: Choosing a soundtrack no longer re-encodes the film
items: Every soundtrack is already in the file, and the player can pick one out of it. Asking for the second one had the whole film made again to hand over something it already held - which costs the card a film's work, and turns a film that would have played untouched into one that cannot be read off two machines, cannot be seeked cheaply, and is sized by an encoder's guess.

The chosen track is matched by where it sits among the film's soundtracks rather than by the number the server gave it: those numbers count every stream in the file, pictures and subtitles included, and the player only ever sees the sound. It is chosen again whenever the film is opened afresh, since a seek makes new tracks of the same sound.

If the chosen track turns out to be one the device cannot decode, it asks for the film in AAC as it always did. Burning a subtitle into the picture, or asking for the sound in a particular coding, still needs an encode - those genuinely change what is in the film.

title: A film encoded for somebody outside the house is sized for the line they are on
items: With no number asked for anywhere, the encoder was given a quality to hit and a ceiling meant for this network - twenty-four megabits, or forty from a 4K source - and it used them. An 800p picture went out at more megabits than the film it was made from, to a phone on mobile data, which is why the same film played straight through without trouble and stopped when it was encoded. Somebody outside the house now gets eight megabits unless they or the server has said otherwise; inside the house nothing changes.
The figure can be set, under the library's settings, as awayMbit.

title: A film that moves machines keeps the soundtrack it was asked for
items: Only the picture was carried across. A phone that had asked for stereo AAC - because nothing passes through a Bluetooth pair, and the film's own track is Dolby Digital Plus - was handed the original by the machine that took over, and got sound it could not play. The soundtrack and the number of channels go with the film now, as the picture size and the megabits already did.

title: A film stays on the main server unless that server has actually gone
items: A picture that has stopped was taken as proof the server was at fault, and the film was moved to the machine that keeps copies. It is not proof. The line to the screen stalls too - and then the trouble travels with the viewer, so moving cannot help and puts them on the slower of the two machines. The server is asked whether it is still there: if it answers, the film stays where it is.
A stall four times longer than that still moves it, without waiting to ask. By then nothing else explains it and there is nothing to lose by trying the other machine.
Coming back was already there and is unchanged: the way home is remembered, and the first request after the main server answers again goes to it.

title: One icon in the tray, not one per update
items: Updating killed the program outright, and a program killed outright never tells Windows to take its tray icon away - Windows then leaves the icon sitting there until somebody happens to hover over it. Every update left another dead P behind, and after a run of them there were ten. It is asked to close first and takes its icon with it; being killed outright is still there a moment later for one that will not go.
The program answers being asked to close, by an update or by Windows shutting down, by taking the icon off the tray on its way out.

title: Every file copied says how fast it went
items: A list of what moved and when cannot answer why a night was slow: the same file at eighty megabits and at seventeen looks identical in it, and which of the two it was is the whole question. Each copy now records the rate it managed and its best moment, and the list of what was transferred shows them beside the reason it was wanted.

title: The check that stops a server going backwards no longer stops it going forwards
items: Refusing an older build was put at the door itself, and it asked the site what the current version was before deciding anything. The site is announcing a build from weeks ago, so every install was refused - including installers made on this machine, which are the ones that were newer. The check now sits on the one path that can go backwards: what is fetched from the site. An installer made here is judged where it is found, as it was.

title: Moving a film to another machine keeps the quality it was asked for
items: Whatever picture size or megabits somebody had settled on was dropped at the moment of moving, so a viewer who had turned the quality down - usually because their line could not carry it - was handed the whole file by the machine that took over. The move asks for the film the way it was being asked for before.

title: A server will not replace itself with an older build
items: What the site publishes is what it publishes, and a site left announcing an old build had this server replace itself with one from weeks ago. That is a working install of the wrong thing, so nothing afterwards notices: the program runs, the library opens, and every fault of the intervening month is back. Installing now refuses anything not newer than what is running, and says both numbers.

title: Somebody watching one film is not put on to another
items: A number that names a film names it in one library only, and two machines number their own. A film that moved to the other machine and was asked for again by that machine's number was a different film here, so somebody watching was moved on to something else entirely, mid-evening, by the server. A number that comes back naming a different film is refused.

Moving a film to another machine checks it is the same film first. Splitting one has always checked that both machines hold the same file; moving one never did, so whatever had been found stood as the same film over there with nothing testing the claim.

A film being encoded is no longer moved for a thin buffer. An encode is made as it is sent and keeps a few seconds in front of itself however well it is going, so running out was true for the whole of every encoded film and a viewer was moved to another machine with nothing wrong. The picture actually stopping still moves it.

title: The router box opens the router
items: It was a box with a press hung on it by hand, and the drawing is made again every few seconds - the box was replaced and the press went with it, so pressing between two drawings did nothing. It is a link now, and the browser opens it in a new tab whether or not anything else has run.

title: A film on a meshed server, handed on by this one
items: A mesh is a catalogue made of several libraries rather than copies of one. Servers meshed with this one are added by pasting the line another server made with a Mesh key, and are asked who they are before being written down. Nothing is fetched and nothing is kept.

A film held on a meshed server is read from that server as it is asked for and passed straight out, ranges and all, so somebody watching holds one key to one server and never learns the film came from anywhere else. When the far server does not answer, the fault says which server it was, so a film that will not play is not blamed on the machine that was passing it on.
Still to come: the catalogue itself. What a meshed server holds does not yet appear in the shelves here, so today this carries films it cannot yet list.

title: One list of keys, each with what it is for
items: Every key is an ordinary invitation with a role on it, chosen from the row it sits on: User watches; Owner has the run of the server, as though sitting at it; Cache is another server keeping copies of this library; Mesh is a cache meant to read both ways. A key for a machine was a different sort of thing in a different list, which put the same question in three places.
An Owner key is honoured as an owner from anywhere, not only from this network - and is asked for out loud before it is given, since it can change the library and the keys, that one included.
The flags underneath a key are kept in step with its role, so everything that asks whether a key follows this server goes on working. Keys made before this take the role their old flags imply.

title: Every key this server has given out, under Users, by what it is for
items: Three kinds, three lists: people, machines that keep copies of this library, and machines meshed with it. Every key was drawn as a person, so a server sat in the list of viewers being asked whose half-watched films it ought to keep.

A machine's row carries what it may hold - a figure in gigabytes, or empty for no limit from this end - whether it may copy at all or only read, and a button to take the key back. One machine at a time, not all of them.
Keys for machines are made from the same page they are read on, named after the machine they are for.

Mesh keys can be made and revoked. They are meant to make two libraries read as one in both directions; the merging itself is not built, and a mesh key behaves as a copy key until it is. The page says so rather than implying otherwise.

title: A key for each machine that copies from here, on its own terms
items: Keys for machines are listed the way invitations for people are: one row each, with how much of the library that machine may hold, whether it may copy at all or only read, when it was last used, and a button to revoke it. There was a single key for the house and a single ceiling for whoever held it - so lending a library to a second machine re-lent the first one's allowance, and taking the key away took it from every machine at once.
The ceiling belongs to the key. Empty means no limit from this end and the other machine's own setting stands. A library's old single figure still applies to keys made before this.
A key may be for reading only. A machine holding one still knows the library and still answers for it, and takes no copies of anything.

title: Watching and copying on a line each
items: A machine's box gives what is being watched off it on one line and what is being copied off it on the next, each only while it is happening, and "nothing going out" when neither is. Added together on one line, a machine sending somebody a film and a machine filling the other one read as the same thing.

title: Copying counts towards what a machine is shifting, and the file being fetched says why
items: The drawing counted only what people were watching. Copying to the other machine was left out of it, and on a night of copying that is most of what a machine shifts - so a server working hard read as idle. Its box now says how many are watching, how many files are going over, and the megabits of both together. Only the number of files being copied was sent to the page at all; the rate goes with it now.

In the copying queue, the file being fetched said "being fetched" and nothing else - dropping the reason it is wanted, which is that column's whole purpose and the one row somebody is most likely to be asking about. It says both.

title: A server that comes back appears without restarting the app
items: The list of servers and the knocking on each of them were both done once, when the list was opened. So a machine switched off and switched on again was missing from it until the app itself was started again - nothing that happened afterwards could put it back on the screen. Both are done again every ten seconds while the list is open.

title: The server stops refusing connections it is perfectly able to answer
items: Five connections could be waiting to be accepted, which is Python's own figure and was plenty while a film was one long connection. Reading a film off several machines asks for every two megabytes on a connection of its own - several a second from each screen for a 4K film - with a copy taking files and a settings page asking how things are going on top. Past five the rest were refused, and what the player saw was a machine that would not answer: it waited five seconds, gave up on it, and the picture stopped for that long, over and over, on a server that was perfectly well. A hundred and twenty-eight may wait now.

The count of machines carrying a film counts only machines that have brought something in the last ten seconds. A machine that has been switched off is still counted as there until whatever it was holding times out, so the line said two sources with one of them off.

title: The machine that copies from this one is not also drawn as a viewer
items: It was drawn twice: once as its own machine and once as somebody watching, under the name of the key it uses. What keeps machines out of the list of screens tested for the word "following", and the machine calls itself a "follower" - so it went straight past. It is matched on any of the words it uses and on its address, which it cannot describe itself out of.

A key for a machine that copies from this one takes that machine's name as soon as the machine says what it is called. It was called "a following server" - made before anybody knew which computer would use it - and that is what the drawing and the list of keys then called the machine.

title: A machine sharing a film says how many, and what it is sending
items: "1 split", with the megabits it is carrying, inside its own box - which is where a figure belongs and the one place it was missing.

title: Nothing is written outside a box, and the drawing can be asked to redraw
items: A machine carrying part of a film says "split 1" - how many screens it is sharing, and nothing else.

No figures along the lines. They crossed each other and the boxes both, and a screen fed by two machines had a number on one line and not the other. The screen's own box gives what it is taking, both machines added together.
A Refresh button on the drawing. It redraws itself every few seconds, which suits watching something happen and is no use when something has just been changed and you want to see it now.

title: Screens keep their place in the drawing
items: The screens were listed freshest first and the drawing is made again every few seconds, so every card moved whenever any other screen started or stopped - and the thing could not be read while it was being watched. A screen keeps the row it was given until it goes quiet, and a new one takes the lowest empty row.

title: A machine carrying part of a film says it is split
items: The drawing called it "second source for 1 screen". It is a split, and that is the word used everywhere else for it.

title: A machine dropping out of a film says so
items: A machine that stopped answering mid-film was set aside without a word, and asked again later without a word. So a film coming off one machine while two were holding it looked exactly like one where the other machine had never been asked - and a picture stopping now and then had nothing behind it to read. Both are written down now, with which machine, at what point in the film, and what went wrong.

title: What the second machine is carrying, in megabits
items: A machine acting as a second source for a film says how much it is sending and to which screen. It has to be asked - a player reading part of a film off it talks to it directly, and this machine sees none of that - so it reports the address, the rate and the title for each screen it is feeding.
The drawing puts that rate on the line running from it to the screen it feeds, and the total in its own box beside "second source".

title: Why a file was copied is written down, and the drawing shows who is feeding whom
items: Every copy carried a place for why it was taken and it was empty on every one of them: the reason is worked out when the queue is made and was never carried through to the file going out. It travels with the file now and stands beside it in the list of what was transferred - what put it in the queue, and whose watching asked for it.

A film looked for on another machine is now looked for from where the film is coming from rather than from where the app is. Only the player moves when a film moves machines; the shelves stay behind, and the two were each using a different idea of where "here" was - so after a film moved it offered the machine it had just moved to as its own second source, and read the film off one machine while two of them held it.

In the drawing, a line runs from a machine only to the screen it is actually feeding. Every machine had a line to every screen, so one carrying a single film looked as though it were carrying all of them.
"Outside" is called WAN.
Installing a new version says it is restarting, and that anything playing from that machine stops for a moment. It said only "installing".

title: What a screen is taking is written in the screen's own box
items: It sat on the line running to the screen, which worked while one machine fed it. With two machines carrying one film there are two lines into that screen and only one of them could carry the figure, so it read as though half the film were arriving. The screen's box says what that screen is taking, and how it is playing it.

title: A film that has moved machines can move again, and everything is called by its name
items: Moving a film to another machine was once per film. So a picture that stopped on the machine it had just moved to stayed stopped - there was nowhere left to go - while the machine it came from sat there answering. It is once a minute now, not once ever.

What the app knew about other machines was kept across a move, and the machine it had just moved to was the other machine a moment before. So it found itself as its own second source and read the film off one machine while two of them held it. It asks again from where it now stands.

Machines are called by their names. "The other machine", "the machine that keeps copies" and "night server" named nothing on a screen with two servers on it; every message, dot and label now says which one it means.

The drawing on the settings page reads left to right, the way a film travels: the way in from outside, the router it arrives at, the machines the films are on, and the screens watching them. Both machines are drawn feeding the screens, because both of them can be - only one line was drawn before, so a machine carrying half a picture looked idle.

It also says when a machine is a second source for something playing, rather than "standing by". A player reading part of a film off it talks to it directly and says nothing here, so this machine asks it.
Keys for machines that copy from this one are made and taken away one machine at a time. There was a single key for all of them: a new key took it away from every machine at once.
The decoder is set under This computer rather than under Quality, with the processor offered beside the card - the answer for a card that is full, busy, or making a mess of one file.
How much this server may read off the copy is set on the same page, and says plainly that the app's own reading from several machines is a separate thing that needs no setting.

title: What this computer encodes with, and how much it shares, are set together
items: The decoder was set under Quality, among settings about how a film should look. It is a fact about this computer and it is set there now.

The processor is offered beside the card. Only what a screen cannot play as it stands is ever re-encoded; the card is quicker and is what this uses, and the processor is the answer for a card that is full, busy, or making a mess of one particular file.

How much of a film may be read off the machine that keeps copies is set on the same page, with what it does and when it is worth setting. The number used to sit on the page about the other computer, and it is about this one - and what is actually handed over is decided as the film is read, from how long this machine spends getting a stretch off its disk against how long it spends sending it.

title: The chip above the server list is rounded like the list below it
items: The press was drawn into the chip before its rounded shape was painted, so the press left a square over a rounded chip - and the picker showed two grey boxes with different corners, one above the other. It is clipped first now, and ringed in white while the remote is on it, as the rows below it are.

When a film is read off one machine while another holds it too, the log said only that nothing else held it. Three separate reasons all printed that same sentence, so a film that had found its second machine and then set it aside read exactly like one that had found nothing. The log now names which of them it was, with the addresses and file names it compared.

title: A machine answering short no longer ends the film
items: A machine that returns fewer bytes than it was asked for - which a busy one does - was taken to mean the file ended there. The player was told the film had finished, dropped back to the shelf, and playing it again started from the beginning. Nothing appeared in any log because as far as the player was concerned the film had simply ended. When the length is known from the open, a short answer is now a fault: the stretch goes back and is fetched again from whichever machine will have it.

How long a machine holding up the picture is waited for is no longer a flat eight seconds but about twice what the quickest machine standing would need to fetch that stretch instead - a fraction of a second, usually. Eight seconds was several times the whole run of film in hand, so a machine that went busy mid-stretch - somebody else starting a film on it - stopped the picture for six seconds before anything was done.

title: The slower machine keeps to the far end of the queue
items: Deciding what a slow machine may take on was done by weighing how long it needs for one stretch against how fast the quick machine could clear everything claimed. That second figure is not how much time the player has - the player uses film at the rate the film runs - so the sum meant nothing, and it could both starve the slow machine and still hand it the very stretch the picture was waiting for.

No arithmetic now: a slow machine may take work from the far half of what is in hand and never the stretch about to be read. If the quick machine stops, its speed stops counting and the slow one takes everything - which is what it is there for.

title: The server chips are rounded, and the one the remote is on is ringed
items: The press was drawn into the chip before the rounded panel was painted, so what the press drew was a square laid over rounded corners. The chip is clipped first now, and ringed in white while the remote is anywhere on it - which the television was otherwise showing almost nothing for.

An address on this network is only preferred over the way in from outside once the machine answering there has proved it is the right one. Houses number their machines from the same small range, so a server whose home address is 192.168.0.25 is somebody else's machine from anywhere but its own house. Any mix of addresses works: two from outside, one of each, or two on the network.

title: A machine in the same house is read from across the house
items: A server is filed under whichever of its two addresses last answered, and one that had been filed under its way in from outside was then read from there - out through the router and back in over the same wireless, while the machine sat on the same network. Half of a 4K film was coming that way and what was left to play ran down to nothing. The address on this network is preferred whenever it answers, both for opening a server and for reading a share of a film off one.

Being read off several machines no longer stands the move to another machine down for ever. It was right that a film carrying on well should not move house over a thin buffer, but a machine can be answering and slow, or reached by a bad road - and then the picture stops with nothing coming to its rescue. A picture that has actually stood still long enough to empty what was in hand moves, as it did before.

title: The server the remote is on is ringed in white
items: The ring was drawn from whether the panel itself held the remote, and it never does: each row carries buttons, and on a television the remote lands on one of those rather than on the panel around them. It follows the remote anywhere inside the row now.

title: The slower machine takes only the work it can finish in time
items: Stretches of film reach the player in order, so one taken on by a slow machine holds up every stretch behind it while the quick one waits with nothing to do. A machine many times slower was still being handed one stretch in six, and a 4K film stopped on each of them: the picture froze, and what was left to play fell to nothing.

Each machine's speed is measured as it goes, and a machine is handed a stretch only when it can bring it back inside the run of film already in hand. A slow one gets the work when there is slack for it and none when there is not - and still takes everything the moment the quick one stops, which is what it is there for.
Finding a second machine no longer puts a message across the picture. The line along the top says so, and a message belongs to something going wrong.

title: A film now finds itself on the other machine, which it never once did
items: The same film on another machine is looked for by title and year. What the player had in hand was often the row off the shelf it was started from, and that row carries what draws a poster rather than what identifies a film - the year is not on it. So the question went out asking for year nought, which matches nothing, and every film read as being held by no other machine however many held it. An episode is looked for by programme, season and number, all of which the row does carry, which is why episodes found their second machine and films never did.
What is playing is now asked for in full whenever the row in hand is short of what the question needs.

title: The app says what it knew when it went looking for a second machine
items: A film held on two machines was being read off one of them about two times in three, and off one of them always when it was a film rather than an episode. Every explanation at the far end has been ruled out: the other machine finds the title, reports the same file of the same size, and answers in fifteen milliseconds. What is left is the list of machines the app is holding at the moment it asks, so that list now goes into the log with what was asked of it and what came back.

title: The line along the top is grouped, and reads the same in a browser
items: Where the film is coming from, then what it is, then how it is flowing, then anything wrong with it. It used to be the order each thing was added over the years: whether the film was being encoded sat behind two decoder names, and how many frames had been dropped sat between the buffer and the subtitle.

A browser never said which machine was serving the film, which is the first thing worth knowing on a page that can move house halfway through. It says it now, and carries the same fields in the same order as the app.

Two fields on the browser's line - a warning about stray subtitle tracks and the count of subtitle lines drawn - were added to it after it had already been written out, so neither had ever appeared. Both are on it now.

title: The second machine is looked for sooner, and the looking never stops
items: Other machines holding the film were looked for only while none had been found, so the first one found was the last one ever looked for: a third machine with the same film, or one switched on halfway through, was never picked up. It asks for the whole of the film now, once a minute.

And it starts asking straight away rather than waiting fifteen seconds for playback to settle first. That wait belongs to the buffer, not to the question of who else has the film, and it put the first answer half a minute into a film that a copy was holding all along.

title: The line along the top counts the machines instead of describing them
items: It said "looking for a second machine" while it was asking, and named a machine when it found none - a paragraph about something that wants a number. It reads "sources 1/1", "1/2", "2/2": how many machines are carrying the film, of how many are known to hold it. The share each one has carried follows it when there is more than one.

A reason is kept only where there is nothing to be done about it - casting, or a film being encoded rather than sent as it is. A film being encoded cannot be split at all: what is sent is made as it goes, so two machines would not be making the same bytes.

title: A film takes all of its subtitles across, and the server list shows what is picked
items: Copying a film sent only the subtitles in the languages being kept for, plus whichever one had been chosen. It sends every subtitle beside the film now - downloaded and already there alike - because the one wanted on the night is not always the one the languages say, and a subtitle is kilobytes against gigabytes. Episodes still take the languages being kept for: a series is hundreds of files where a film is one.
Each one carries its size and both its ends, so a subtitle that changes here is fetched again there rather than left as it was.

In the app, a row in the server picker is ringed in white while the remote is on it, and its corners stay round - the panel was rounded and what was drawn over it on a press was not, so the corners squared off at the moment of pressing.

title: How much of a film the other machine reads is decided where the reading happens
items: The share handed to the machine that keeps copies was worked out from what the viewer had left to play. Nothing ever sent that figure, so the share sat at nothing and the second machine was never once asked for a block - and the figure would have been useless anyway, since a browser keeps about two seconds in front of itself however well it is fed.

It is measured at the disk now: the time spent getting a block off this machine against the time spent handing it on. A disk keeping well ahead of the line is worth nothing to share and the share winds down to nothing; a disk the line is waiting on hands over more, up to the ceiling set in settings under "Read from it as well".

title: In a browser, moving to the other machine needs a reason
items: What is left to play decided whether to move house, and in a browser that number means nothing: a film streamed from a file keeps about two seconds in front of itself however well it is being fed. So "running low" was true for the whole of every film on either machine, and it moved house over and over on a stream that was working - to the slower of the two, which cannot help. The picture standing still decides it now: the stream is opened again first, and only a second stall moves anything.
The server counts how much of a film each machine carried, ready for the line along the top to say so.

title: In a browser, the machine it is already on is not somewhere to move to
items: The address of the machine that keeps copies is remembered between visits, so a browser opened on that machine held its own address as somewhere to go. Every dip in the buffer started the moving-house routine to arrive where it already was, and said so. An address belonging to the machine serving the page is no longer offered as anywhere.
A machine that will not take the film is left alone for half a minute rather than asked again on every tick, which was a line of toasts and a request a second at the moment there is least to spare.
Both messages name the machine instead of calling it "the other machine".

title: A film being read off two machines is not moved to one of them
items: A server filed under its address from outside was not recognised as the machine the film was already playing from, so it was offered as a second machine and the film was moved to where it already was - restarting every few minutes. A machine is matched by all of its addresses now, and the move refuses a destination that is the machine in use.

Moving the film to another machine used to happen whenever the buffer ran thin, and being read off two machines only made it wait longer before doing it. So a film carrying on perfectly well off the slower of the two ran its buffer down, waited out the longer count, and moved house - to the machine it was already reading from, restarting the film to arrive where it was. While the reader still has a machine it is left to get on with it; the move is kept for having run out of machines altogether.
The line along the top says "single source" when there is only one machine, rather than naming the machine it is already playing from as one that has not got the film.

title: Reading off a machine that has been switched off no longer fills memory
items: Each two-megabyte stretch is held until the player has taken it, and the limit on how many were in hand was written as a distance rather than a count. Dropping a machine winds that distance back to where the player is, so with one server off and being retried the limit said there was room while the heap filled - and the film ended at a quarter of a gigabyte with the app gone and the home page back. It counts what is held now.

A reader that fails now takes only its own machine out. It threw, and a thread that throws takes the whole app with it, so the one fault this is built to survive was also the one that closed the film.
A machine that is not answering is tried again after five seconds, then ten, then twenty, up to a minute, instead of every five seconds for the rest of the film.

title: A film is read off every machine that has it, for as long as it has it
items: The second machine was decided when the stream opened, and finding it takes about fifteen seconds of the film - so it was never known in time and every film was read off one machine however many held it. That is why the share never appeared on the screen and why a server switched off mid-film was a hand-over with a stop in it rather than the split this was built to be. The reader is asked which machines to use as it goes, and picks up a machine found after the film started.
It is no longer two: up to four machines are read from at once, and the line along the top gives each one's share - 100/0 at the start, then whatever they settle at.

Every server the app knows is asked once a minute for the film that is playing, rather than the copy being asked once at the start. A machine switched on halfway through joins what is already running.
A machine that stops answering is dropped and asked again five seconds later, so one switched off and on again during a film comes back instead of being gone for the rest of it.

title: The share each machine is carrying is on the screen while it is happening
items: The two-source line waited until both machines had carried something before it appeared, so the opening stretch - read entirely off one of them - showed nothing, and a split that was working looked like no split at all. It shows the share from the moment the second machine is set up: 100/0 first, then whatever the two of them settle at.

title: The line about the second machine says which machine, and waits to be sure
items: The stats line called the other machine "the copy", which names nothing on a screen that has both machines on it. It says the name now.

It also announced that the copy did not hold the film before it had finished asking - the answer takes about twenty seconds - so a film that was about to be read off both machines was announced as one that could not be. While the question is open it says so.

title: The list stops losing a server to the one that copies it
items: A copy learned from a server was written down carrying that server's id, so the two rows read as one machine and the list folded them together on the next start - the server disappeared, the app sat on the copy, and the picker offered no way back. The id now belongs to whichever address answered with it: a row moved to another machine's address loses it, a row holding an id that another row has just proved has it cleared, and every row is asked at startup rather than only the ones with no id at all.

title: A film that runs out of server carries on, without stopping
items: One film is read off both machines at once, and when one of them is switched off mid-film the other was supposed to pick up its share. It gave up instead: the reader waited its eight seconds for a lump the dead machine had taken on, asked whether more than one machine was still standing, and - since one had just died - stopped, with the survivor sitting there idle. A machine that has gone now hands back everything it was holding, not only the lump it died on, and one machine left is a machine to ask rather than a reason to stop.
The bar names the machine that is answering rather than the one that was chosen. A film that moves to the copy is on the copy, and every screen went on naming the other one.
Two rows for the same machine become one, on any address they share. It asked whether one row's way in was the other's way out, which misses two rows written down with the same address.

A server on the list is named by whatever answers there. The name a row was added under can come to belong to another machine, and the list stood with two rows under the main server's name, one of which was the cache.

The queue of what is being copied answered with an error rather than a queue - a name left behind when moving a title to the front by hand was taken out. Nothing asked it, so nothing said so; the pages about the machine that keeps copies are now among the ones checked before a build goes out.

The player says what it is doing to the server as well as to the device's own log. A television has no console and nothing to ask, so why a film came off one machine rather than two was written where nobody could read it.

title: The app lost the subtitles when the film changed machines
items: Carrying on from the machine that keeps copies started the film again with nothing but the film and the place in it. The subtitle, the soundtrack, the picture size and the rate were all dropped, so an evening that moved machines lost its subtitles at the one moment nobody can work out why. All four go with it now - and because two libraries number their streams for themselves, the track is looked for again over there by its language and its name rather than by a number that means something else.
How the subtitles are drawn is put to the other machine before it is asked for anything, so its menus open on what is on the screen instead of its own defaults.

A screen says how much it has left to play, and that is what decides whether the machine keeping copies is asked to help with the reading. A buffer going down is the one honest sign that a machine is not keeping up - a quick disk and a clear line are both beside the point if the picture is about to stop.

A film coming off one machine when it could come off two says why, on the line along the top of the picture: it is being encoded, the copy has not got it, the copy has a different file, or the copy is this machine. It said so only into the system log, where nobody was reading, so a film that could have been split and was not looked exactly like one that could not.

title: Reading one film off two machines
items: A share of the blocks of a film can be read off the machine that keeps copies while this one hands the film to a screen. It is set as a percentage and spread evenly through the film - a fifth means one block in five, not the first fifth - and the viewer sees one unbroken answer either way: this is which disk a block came off, not anything about the stream. A block that does not arrive quickly is read here instead, so the other machine can slow down or go away in the middle without the picture knowing.
Off unless somebody sets it. It is worth having when the two machines are about as quick as each other and worth nothing when they are not: one a tenth the speed adds a tenth.

Before that, and whatever the share: the film moves to the other machine when what is left to play starts falling rather than when the picture stops. Twelve seconds in hand is a pause nobody sees; nought is a stall.

title: An evening that changes machines keeps its subtitles
items: Carrying on from the machine that keeps copies asked it for subtitle nought - none at all - so the subtitle went off at the moment the film moved, which is the moment nobody is in a position to work out why. The track that was on screen is looked for in the other machine's list by its language and its name, because a track number belongs to the machine that numbered it.

How the subtitles are drawn goes over with it, before anything else is asked of the other machine, so its own menus open on what is on the screen rather than on its defaults. Size, colour, background and position survive the change of machine.

title: Taking one poster off a shelf
items: Marking something watched or forgotten on Continue watching takes that poster off the shelf and leaves the rest of the page alone. It drew the whole front page again for the sake of one card, which threw away where you were on it and blinked every other shelf. The page is only drawn again when a shelf empties, because then its heading has to go too.

title: Films and programmes by decade
items: Films and TV can be narrowed to a decade, beside the genre, in the app and on the web. The list is built from what the shelves actually hold and says how many are in each, so it never offers a decade with nothing in it - here that is the fifties through the twenties, with the eighties, nineties and two-thousands ninety-odd films apiece.
A shelf narrowed by hand can still be kept as a collection, and the rule is the narrowing: a decade becomes a span of years, so what is added later joins it by itself.

title: Being named cost you your shelves
items: A server calls its owner "me" until somebody says who they are. Naming them - by giving them an invitation of their own, so they are the same person on the television as at the desk - moves everything they had onto that name. The list of what to move left out their collections and the arrangement of their front page, so those stayed behind under the old name, still in the file and read by nothing: twelve collections vanished off the shelves and were made again from nothing. The list is the list of what a viewer owns now, and there is only one of it.
A server already in that state puts it right the first time its owner is asked for, and what they watched before they were named comes with it.

The owner's own viewing is kept by the machine that holds copies whether or not they have a key. It was kept only while they were still called "me", so the moment they were named, the one person certain to be watching was left out of their own cache.

title: The queue, written once - and it stops asking for what cannot come
items: A file that fails the same way three times is given up on. A file that fails the check on arrival fails it again every time, because nothing about it has changed - and it was asked for again every pass, all night. Twenty-three damaged episodes had been fetched between fifteen and a hundred and eighty times each and deleted on arrival: seven hundred and twenty-nine gigabytes moved to deliver thirteen. It is asked for again the moment the file changes at the other end, because a different size or hash is a different file, and a different complaint does not count towards giving up - a bad minute is not a bad file.

What is worth copying is decided in three steps that can be read one at a time: what the house wants and why, the episodes that follow it, and the rows a copy can act on. It was one function of two hundred and sixty lines carrying three generations of contradictory rules, with the comments of all three still in it.

A programme's episodes are in season and episode order, in the place the programme stands. They arrive from three places - a watchlist, somebody part-way through, and the walk ahead of both - and each was added where it landed, so a series read as S01E01, S01E04, S01E02.

Moving a title to the front of the queue by hand is gone. One thing lifts anything above the list - a screen that is on this minute - and everything else keeps the place the list gave it. Two kinds of priority make a queue nobody can predict, which is the whole of what a queue is for.

title: The server list, written once
items: The list of servers is one idea again. A machine is a set of addresses; machines fold together where their addresses overlap; the open one is the one holding this page's address, and it is called whatever that server calls itself; you reach a machine by trying its addresses with the kind you are already using first, knocking before leaving so a machine that does not answer cannot strand you. Five overlapping pieces and two disagreeing notes of which address answers became one of each, and a third of the code went.

Which address answers is remembered against the address. It was remembered against the machine, and a row that had never been asked which machine it is shared that with whatever was serving the page - so pressing such a row was answered with this page's own address and went nowhere.
Both of a machine's addresses appear once. The address you are on is also one of the two the machine names, and it was listed twice.

title: Both of a machine's addresses, nearest first
items: The other address of the machine you are on was listed and did nothing when pressed. The row for this machine has no server behind it, and that was being read as "you are already here" whichever of its addresses you pressed - so the one address needed to get from outside back onto the network could not be used.

Addresses are offered with the kind you are already using first. On the network the network address is the quick one and always there; from outside it cannot be reached at all. Pressing a machine's name takes the first that answers, so on the network it stays on the network.
The list is tested as a guest as well as the owner. A guest is what a friend's link makes you, and it is the only way most people ever see this list.

title: No way back to a machine's other address
items: The row for the machine you are on was built from the address you arrived at and no other, so opening a server from outside left no way back to its address on this network. A machine knows both of its addresses and says so; the list shows both, and pressing one that cannot be reached from where you are says so rather than leaving you on a blank page.

title: A machine with no name shows its address
items: Two rows in the server list are ones nobody added: the machine keeping copies of this one, and the machine this one copies from. They are there because the list a browser keeps belongs to the address it is on, so opening the copy starts with an empty list and no way back. Until the machine's own name is known they were called "The house" and "Night server", which say nothing about which computer they mean. They show the address instead.

title: Every button in the server list, pressed
items: Pressing one of a machine's addresses said you were now on it and stayed where it was - it only changed which library the shelves read - so the bar named one machine while every request went to another. It goes to that address now, and knocks first: an address on the house network cannot be reached from a train, and going there anyway leaves a blank page with no list on it to press.

Finding out where the house is, and finding out whether it is running something newer, were both asked inside the round that mirrors the app - which does nothing at all unless there is a folder to mirror into and half an hour has passed. A machine with nothing to mirror never learned where the house was and never looked for a newer build. Each is its own round now.

The list is tested by pressing it. The drawing code runs against a stand-in for a browser, so the buttons are the buttons - the same labels, the same handlers - and the test says where each press leads, standing on either machine, at either of its addresses, at home and away.

The bar names the machine you are on. It was drawn before the server had said what it is called, read "This server", and stayed that way - and on two machines answering the same pages, not knowing which one you are on is the whole difficulty.

Two rows for one machine are one row. Rows that share an address are the same computer written down twice, and the list showed both under the same name - one saying you were on it, the other offering to take you there.

The shelf of recently released episodes is empty on a machine that keeps copies, because a copied episode arrived with no idea when it went out. The house sends the date with the rest of what it knows about the file.

title: Opening the copy stranded you on it
items: A machine says what it is called, where else it can be reached, and which machine it copies from. It said none of that if nothing was copying from it - which is true of every copy - so a page opened on the copy was told nothing about anywhere else and had no row to press to get back. Those are facts about the machine answering, not about any follower of its own, and they are always sent now.

The list is tested against both machines as they actually answer, from every address either of them has: one row is the open one, it is called what that server calls itself, and from anywhere there is a way to everywhere else. Every fault in this list so far has been in what a server said rather than in how the list was drawn, which a test made of invented answers cannot see.

title: A row named after a machine it is not
items: A server on the list keeps the name it was added under, and an address can come to belong to another machine - a link handed on, a port moved, a row written down while the copy was answering for the house. Each address is asked what it is when the page opens, and the answer was used to file the row and not to name it. So the row was right by its address and wrong by its name: pressing the house said you were already on the house, while the copy was what had answered all along. Rows are renamed by whatever answers there.

title: The server list, decided in one place and tested
items: Which machines the list offers and which of them is the one answering is worked out in one place now, apart from the drawing of it. The only way to find out what the list would do was to press it, and it was wrong in ways that depended on which library was on screen.

Exactly one row is ever the open one, and it is the row whose address is this page's address. With the other machine's library showing, its row claimed to be the open one and refused to go there - and the plain row stopped claiming anything, so the list said nothing was open while offering the machine you were standing on.
Moving to the machine that keeps copies says its name. What it does is not what it is called, and its name is what the bar shows a moment later.

A row knows which machine it is by the addresses on the row itself, not by the table this browser keeps of which machine answers where. That table is a guess about where else to knock, and a failover can write the house's name against the copy's addresses - which made the house's row contain the address of the page it was drawn on, so it said you were already there and would not go.

title: An evening that moves to the copy keeps its subtitles
items: How each person has their subtitles drawn - size, colour, background, the language they want - is sent to the machine that keeps copies along with the invitations, and kept there under the same name. A film that carried on from the copy changed size and language halfway through, and the menus over there had that machine's defaults behind them rather than the person's, so setting anything meant setting it twice.

title: Pressing a machine's name went nowhere; pressing its address worked
items: Which of a machine's addresses answers is remembered for two minutes, in a slot named after the machine - and a row that was never asked which machine it is had no name to use, so it shared the slot with whatever is serving the page. Both rows that a server offers rather than a person adding them are like that: the copy a server names, and the house a copy names. Within two minutes of the page knocking on itself, pressing one of those names was answered with this page's own address and went nowhere.

A subtitle key is sent to the machine that keeps copies with the login that goes with it. A key searches and only a login downloads, so the copy could list subtitles for everything and fetch none of them.

title: The list said you were on a machine you were not on
items: Pressing a server said you were already on it and stayed where it was. It was deciding by which machine's shelves you had chosen to look at, which is a different question from which machine is answering the page - and with both libraries showing, the shelves were the other one's. A row is now the open one only when its address is this page's address.

title: No soundtrack to choose, on three thousand files
items: A film with a dub in front of the original played the dub, and the soundtrack list would not let you change it. What each file's soundtracks are is written down the first time somebody opens the title - unless something is written down already, and a probe from before the library knew about soundtracks had written an empty list for every file it touched. Empty and never asked look the same from the outside, so those files were never asked: no numbered tracks, nothing to pick between, and whatever the encoder took first. Three thousand of three and a half thousand files were in that state; they are asked now, one at a time as they are opened.
The soundtrack list is sized for the screen it is on. It was drawn for a television read from a sofa, which on a telephone is enormous.

What a cache keeps, who it keeps it for, whether the cap may clear it, and how many episodes to keep ahead are all saved when they are changed. The page sent them and the server kept a fixed list of names it would accept, which those were not on - so four switches moved on the screen, said nothing, and went back to what they were on the next drawing.

title: A cache that was keeping the house's copies went on keeping them
items: Keeping copies for one person rather than for the whole house arrived as the way a new machine starts, and was applied to machines already set up as well. One that had been holding the whole house's viewing quietly became one person's, and everything on anybody else's list stopped being copied - the queue full, the machine idle, and nothing anywhere saying why. Only a following that has not been set up yet starts as one person's.

title: The bar named a machine the page was not on
items: Which machine's shelves you had chosen is remembered by the browser against the address you chose it at. Opening the copy is opening a different address, and the choice made on the house was restored there anyway: the bar named the house, its row said you were already on it, and every request on the page went to the copy. A choice is only put back on the machine it was made on.

title: No way back from the machine that keeps the copies
items: Switching to the copy took you there and stranded you. A browser's list of servers belongs to the address it is on, so a page opened on the copy starts with an empty list, and the only other machine it offers is the one that copies from it - which the copy has not got. It now says where the house is, and the house is on the list.

A machine that follows another was answering that it followed nobody. It was looking for the setting in the viewer's own settings file, and the following is set up in the library's - so the question had never once been answered correctly by a machine that was in fact following one.

Where the house is gets asked for however the copy is set to handle updates. It was learned only as a side effect of checking for a newer build, so a machine told not to update itself never found out where the house was.

title: A follower set to keep up with the house never could
items: A machine that keeps copies can be told to replace itself when the server it follows moves on. It compares two numbers to decide - what the house is running and what it is running - and the answer it reads them from carried neither. Both were absent, the comparison was nothing against nothing, and the machine sat on the build it was installed with for as long as it ran. Both numbers are sent now.

A machine deciding whether to update reads its own version from itself rather than from the answer the house sent back. For the first minutes after the house restarted it had no record of the other machine yet, so the comparison was against nothing and the update was declined.
The list of who a house has says each name once. The owner's name is also an invitation name when they hold a key of their own, and the list is read by people.

Each server on the list says whether it holds a key. Whether a row has one is the single thing that decides if it works from anywhere but the house, and it was nowhere on the screen - so a row that would be refused everywhere else looked exactly like one that would not.

title: Nothing to type on the end of the install code
items: The address for Downloader on a Google TV ended in .apk, which is four more characters to spell out with a remote control and the part people got wrong. The file arrives named the same either way - the server says what it is in the response - so the line to type is now just the address and the code, and says so: no http, nothing on the end.

title: The app held an invitation it never sent
items: A server typed in at home is saved without a key, because none is needed there. The invitation that arrives later is a second row for the same machine with the key on it. The app opened the first row, sent nothing, and was refused everything from outside the house - which reads as the server being empty rather than as the app being nobody: a green dot and bare shelves.

A row is now opened carrying whatever key any row of that machine has, on every path that chooses a server - the one the app starts on as well as the one somebody presses. Folding two rows into one for the screen keeps the key as well, which it had been dropping along with the row it came on.

A guest who is not on the house network is no longer shown the address on it, in the app or on the web. It is no use from where they are standing, and the inside of somebody else's house is not theirs to be told about.

title: A server that answers is not the same as a server that lets you in
items: The dot beside a server on the phone meant the machine answered a knock, and the knock lands on one of the few doors open to anybody. A server with no password set takes the address for the proof of who you are, so away from the house it answered every knock and refused everything behind it: a green dot and an empty library. The dot now asks the second question too, and turns amber with a line saying to set a password on that server or open it with an invitation link.
The server list is drawn folded after it is knocked on. It was being written back unfolded, so a machine known by both its addresses appeared twice a quarter of a minute after the screen opened.

title: Add-ins stay on the list after they are fetched
items: ffmpeg, the app and the subtitle tools each disappeared from the add-ins list the moment they worked, so there was nowhere to see where one had come from, where it sits, or to change your mind about it. All three stay on the list with what they are and where they came from.
