The old gold is in the row, last, marked "don't use this" - it is there so nobody wonders where it went.
The launcher icon keeps the blue - that one is baked into the app when it is built.

title: The tick turns as the credits arrive
items: Nothing verified itself any more, and the reason was blunt: the players report that a subtitle is on, not which one, and a rule added this morning compared that word with the name of the file that had been fetched, found them different and refused. Every automatic verification since then was lost that way.

The reports now name the subtitle - a number for a track inside the film, the release name for a file beside it - so any subtitle can earn its mark by carrying an episode to the end, not only one the server fetched itself.

And the answer to that last report carries the news, so a panel that is open turns its tick green as it happens and the player says so for a moment. It used to appear the next time the panel was opened.

title: Verifying survives a restart
items: When a subtitle came on was held in memory only, so a server restart in the middle of an episode looked exactly like a subtitle chosen at the end: the rule that stops a track picked in the last minute from being credited with the whole film then refused it, however far the episode was watched. On a ten-minute episode the window is three minutes, so almost any restart lost it.
It is written down now, in the settings file, and only when the subtitle changes. A restart picks up where it left off, and a position that cannot be known is treated as unknown rather than as late.

title: A colour of its own
items: The accent was #E5A00D, carried over from what this program started life as. Too close to another media server's for comfort: a dark theme and that colour read as a reskin of it.

It is now #4A90F0, sampled from a poster in the library: the mean of the bright blue on it, nudged up for contrast. Dark text on the accent and the accent as text on the page both come out at 5.8 to 1, comfortably past the 4.5 that counts as readable.
Everywhere at once: the mark, the app icon and the television banner, the tabs and buttons, the setup and sign-in pages the server draws, and the television web app.

title: Laid out for the phone most people hold
items: The rows were measured on a Pixel, which is 411 points across; most phones are 360. Everything that had just been made to fit went back over the edge there - Mark watched onto a line of its own, the genre off the right of the tab row.

A pill on a narrow phone is smaller again: ten points of padding either side, four to the next one. Measured at 360 points: Resume 47:15, From start and Mark watched all stand on one row, ending well inside the screen.

title: The order and the genre fit across a phone
items: Pills on a phone are the same height with less width either side, so Home, Films, TV, the order and the genre all stand on one line at 1080 pixels instead of the genre hanging off the right. The television keeps the wider pills, which is the target a remote wants.

On a title's page Resume, From start and Mark watched stand on one row held upright, at any resume time: an hour and a half in the button says "Resume 1:37:04" and that was three points over the room, which put Mark watched on a line of its own. An episode's fourth button, Go to show, still takes the second line.

title: Search follows the tab it was typed on
items: In the browser, a search from the TV tab lists series and episodes before films, and one from Films lists films first. Somebody looking through TV who searches is looking for a programme, not for the film of the same name. From Home the server's own order stands, which puts first whatever the words asked for.
Reports hides itself while a library list is open, as it was meant to: the test named two tabs - "films" and "tv" - that the page does not have, so it never hid.

title: Search sits on the top row, and works from Home
items: The search box has moved up beside the name, where there is room for it, and it is on Home as well as Films and TV. From Home it looks through everything - films, series and episodes - rather than one section, since Home is not one.
The version number sits on a line above the name, which is the width the search box wanted; the P and the word keep the height and the spacing they had.

Typing dropped the fetch that the last letter started, and the screen said "the coroutine scope left the composition" instead of showing the results. A dropped fetch is not a failure and is passed on rather than reported.

title: The sort and the genre sit among the tabs
items: On Films and TV the order the list is in is fourth along and the genre fifth, straight after the TV tab, rather than at the end of a row that does not fit across a phone. They are the two controls somebody reaches for on the way into a list and the two that had to be scrolled to.
The search box stays at the end of the row.

title: Series with no date sort last in the app
items: Sorting television by Released or by Year put the unidentified series at the top. The server has always ordered its own share with those last; the app sorts the joined list again - several servers, one list - and that pass did not know about them. It does now, in both directions.

A series with no aired episode reported its date as the four letters "null", which the cards printed as "last aired null" and the sort read as a date. The server sends nothing instead, and the app reads a null as nothing.

title: 100% is a share of a 16:9 picture
items: Subtitle size is measured against a 16:9 picture as wide as the player rather than against the screen. A phone held upright is three times taller than the picture on it, so a share of the screen was text the height of a thumb; a browser window dragged tall and narrow had the same fault. On a television and a maximised window the two are the same number, so nothing moves there.
A scope film and a 16:9 film now draw the same size of text on the same screen.

Nothing is drawn until the shape of the picture is known. The black bar is worked out from the video's own width and height, and until the file has been read those are zero: the first cues were drawn in the wrong place and at the wrong size, and then jumped. Both clients hold them back instead - the browser until the metadata lands, the app until the first frame reports a size.

title: Subtitles draw with the phone upright
items: No cue was painted at all in portrait. Media3 draws into a child view of the subtitle view, and that child was left nought pixels tall - measured before the picture had a shape and never measured again. The view itself was the right size, the cues were there, and nothing was drawn. It is given the room the view has whenever the two disagree.

Cue heights are a share of the picture with the bottom of the box anchored at it, rather than a count of text rows. A row is still the step: one press of Position moves the text by one row of its own size, worked out from the size rather than counted by the player.
Reproduced and verified on a Pixel 6 emulator, upright and on its side, on a 16:9 file and a 2.4:1 one.

title: The subtitle language is the viewer's, not the browser's
items: The browser kept the language in its own storage and nowhere else, so a browser that had never been asked - a second machine, a cleared profile, a private window - started every title with subtitles off while the television had English. It now falls back to the language the server keeps for the viewer, which is the one the app already reads, and choosing here writes it there.
"Off" stays a choice of the browser that made it: the server keeps a language, not the absence of one.

Cue heights are worked out from the space the browser actually slides the box across, not from the height of the element. In a narrow window - a big black bar - the text sat a few pixels below the bottom edge of the picture.

title: A word while a track is being lifted out
items: A subtitle inside the film has to be extracted before it can be drawn, and on a large file that is minutes the first time. Both clients drew nothing and said nothing, which reads as broken subtitles - and rotating the phone, or anything else that happened to take that long, looked like the fix.

The player now says "Lifting the subtitles out of the film" after two and a half seconds, and stops as soon as the cues arrive. Every later playing of that track is served from the cache in about a tenth of a second.

title: Text size is measured from the picture, not the padding
items: Media3 measures a fractional text size against the view less its padding, and the padding carries the black bar. A phone held upright drew the first cues at 5% of the whole screen - several times the height of the picture - and they shrank as soon as the bar was padded out.
The fraction ignores the padding now and the picture is measured directly, so 100% is 5% of the height of the picture whatever shape the window is and whenever it settles.

title: Subtitles start at the right size in the app
items: The look is applied when the player view is built, not when the server answers. Until then the subtitle view used the file's own styling and Media3's default size and bottom padding, so the first cues were drawn too large and high and then jumped.
The look each title was drawn with is kept on the device and used as the starting point, so the first cue matches what the server is about to say.
A title never opened on this device starts at the general size for this kind of screen rather than the built-in default, which on a phone is a quarter smaller than most people watch with.

title: Heights are worked out again when the window changes
items: The browser now re-places the cues when the video element resizes, when full screen is entered or left, and when a stream of another shape arrives. The black bar under the picture is a number measured from the element, so a resized window was drawing subtitles with the old window's arithmetic.

In the app the same measurement is taken again on every layout of the subtitle view. It was taken once, when the picture size was first reported, and a layout listener left over from an earlier design then cleared it - so "bottom of the film" stopped counting from the film.

title: The subtitle look panel in the browser
items: No button in the Aa panel worked. The panel was built without the class the outside-press handler tests for, so every press inside it counted as a press outside: the panel closed and the click was swallowed. Both the class and the panel ids are tested now.
"Bottom of" - the film or the whole screen - is in the Aa panel, not only on the settings page.

A height or a base changed on the settings page with a film open now re-places the cues on screen. It used to take effect on the next film only, because those two settings live on the cues rather than in the stylesheet.
The panel's footer is one button: it resets this title's settings when there are any, and opens the defaults when there are not. The gear beside it is gone.

title: Subtitles are lifted out before they are wanted
items: Measured on a 7.6 GB film: 472 seconds to pull one text track out of the container the first time, 72 milliseconds every time after. That is where the waiting went - not in the listening, which is six seconds for the whole film, nor the correlating, which is under two.
The server now lifts every embedded text track out while nothing is playing and keeps it. It stops the moment somebody presses play, and picks up again when the machine is idle.
pd-warm-subs.py does the same on demand, for somebody who has just added a lot of films and would rather wait now than later.

App: Stop is in the subtitle menu while a measurement runs, not only over the picture; Reset appears whenever there is a correction to undo, even one made on another day. The verified tick moved to the right of the name.

Heights are measured from the picture by default, not the screen. On a film wider than the television the black bar under it is about 13% of the height and a line of text is 5%, so "Just up" was still inside the bar and looked like the very bottom - the setting and the screen disagreeing for a reason nobody could see. Where there is no bar nothing changes, and the Aa menu still offers either.
The film's page keeps to choosing a subtitle and saying which one: placing it and the auto tick are the player's, where the film is on screen to judge them against.

A subtitle inside the container is never measured by itself. It came with the release and is in step with it; measuring one costs minutes of reading the film to be told nought. Auto now applies to files fetched from elsewhere, which are the ones cut for another release. Sync to film still places anything, when pressed.

The subtitle panel opened from a film's page leaves the timing controls out entirely - the tenths, Sync to film and the auto tick. They were drawn there but wired to nothing, so the tick could not be marked; and there is no film on screen to judge a correction by. In the player they are unchanged.

Fixed: a film's own subtitle settings were not used while it played. The player asked the server for them by the bare rating key; every other client, including the Aa dialog on the same screen, asks with the "l" in front. Without it the server finds no exception and answers with the general settings - which is why the menu said Bottom and the screen drew Just up.

A disc marks a subtitle that came inside the film, in both clients' choosers, and the key in the app says what it means. Which side a track is on decides whether it is measured automatically, so it is worth seeing at a glance.

Fixed: tracks with no name of their own were offered as "null". A nameless track arrives as a JSON null and Android's optString hands back the four letters rather than nothing; the server now sends an empty string, and the app treats "null" as empty either way.

Subtitles are offered in an order rather than the container's: a file that was fetched first - it was fetched because what came with the film would not do - then your own language, then a full track before a forced one or one that describes sounds. Both clients.

The Bottom of setting can be set to the screen: the server was reading five keys out of what a client sent and base was not one of them, so choosing it changed nothing. The black bar is also measured again when the picture appears, since its size is not known before the first frame.

The Aa menu fits a television screen again: the choice pills are smaller, which is what five rows of them cost. The Bottom of choices are called The film and The whole screen, with a line saying that a wide film is drawn with black above and below it and that heights count from whichever edge is chosen.

Fixed: skipping to the next or previous episode, and starting something from the casual shelf, turned subtitles off. playIntent was called without a subtitle index, so the player opened with none however many the episode had, verified or not. Both now fetch the full metadata and choose the same way the film's page does.
One subtitle extraction at a time across the whole server. Five at once on the same disk made each five times slower, with a viewer waiting on one of them.

A film verifies its subtitle the same way an episode does: watched to within ten minutes of the end, with at least 70% gone, using a subtitle that was fetched for it. Before, only episodes did - the attempt was not even recorded for a film.

Verifying by watching now requires the same subtitle throughout: the track named in the progress reports must be the one that was fetched, and it must have been chosen in the first third of the film. Switching to something else halfway through, or picking a file with ten minutes left, says nothing about it. Tested: on throughout verifies, a different track at the end does not, chosen near the end does not.

Fixed: a subtitle fetched ahead for the next episode could never be verified by watching. auto_subtitle called fetch_subtitle with remember=False, so no attempt was recorded and there was nothing to promote when the episode finished - which is most downloads, since fetching ahead is the usual path.

Bottom of is in Settings as well as the Aa menu, per screen, and the browser honours it: cues counted from the film sit above the black bar under a wide film, cues counted from the screen sit at the element's edge.

Any subtitle can now be verified by watching, not only one this server fetched: a file that was already beside the film, or a track inside it. The track named in the progress reports is the evidence - a file by its name, an embedded track by its stream number. The series' remembered choice is still only set from a fetched file, since a stream number means nothing on the next episode's release.
Fixed: the verify tick never turned green in the browser. The rule was #subpanel .track .mark.tick and the dropdown rewrite moved the button out of .track and into #ccpanel.

title: Placing a subtitle: from the film's page, and stoppable
items: Fixed: a measurement could sit there for minutes. Three ffmpegs were reading the same eight-gigabyte film at once - the player asking for the subtitle, the measurement asking for the same one, a seek asking again - because none had finished to fill the cache. One extraction per track now, and everybody else waits for it and takes the same answer.
The first extraction of a track is given fifteen minutes rather than five: it competes with the film being streamed off the same disk, and it happens once.

Sync to film and the auto tick are on a film's own page, next to the subtitle chooser - before pressing play, rather than a minute in with a menu over the picture. The pill becomes Stop while it runs.
Reset stops a measurement that is running, instead of waiting for an answer nobody wants any more.
The film's page names the language of the subtitle that is chosen.

New in the Aa menu: whether Bottom means the bottom of the screen or the bottom of the picture. On a wide film the two are a black bar apart, and every other height counts up from whichever is chosen.

The Aa dialog says whose settings it is showing: a title with its own says so at the top, and a title without says that changing one will make it its own. A title set to Bottom while the general setting is Just up looked like a fault; it was an override nobody could see.
The auto tick on a film's page sits on the line with the pills rather than above them.

title: A drift has to earn it
items: Fixed: a subtitle that was already in step was reported as drifting nineteen seconds early to twenty-two seconds late across a film. A line has a free parameter a constant does not, so it can always be fitted through noise - and it was, through the second- and fourth-best peaks of three windows, while the two most confident windows said -0.1 and +0.1.

Two independent windows whose own best answer agrees to within half a second now settle the question: that is a constant, and no line drawn through weaker peaks may argue with it. Where no such pair exists, a line still has to be believed by more windows than the best single number, or by as many with markedly more agreement.
Checked against the case it must not break: the episode that genuinely drifts still measures 0.997756, -1.83s to -4.79s, which is what was seen on screen.

App: a track's name is coloured for how it reaches the screen - blue drawn over the picture, amber burned into it - and green is left to mean one thing only. The text colour was a green close enough to the verified green that every track looked vouched for after a measurement.

The verified tick is drawn in the dropdown beside each track that has earned it, in its own green. One per language, and earned only two ways: pressed by hand, or given automatically to the subtitle that carried an episode to the credits. Measuring a subtitle has never granted it and still does not.

title: Which subtitle opens, and what it is called
items: Fixed: the app opened the first subtitle track in the file. On one release that is a German forced track with six cues in two hours, chosen automatically for an English viewer who then saw nothing for twenty minutes at a stretch. The order is now: a file put beside the video, then your own language in full, then your language with the sounds described, then your language forced, then any full track.
Tracks are named by language and kind - "German - forced", "English - SDH" - rather than by whatever word the release put on them. "Forced" alone does not say which language it is forced into.
The server records which tracks are forced from the container's own disposition, and works it out from the name where the container is silent.
The text / burned in / verified key is back under the chooser in the app.

The wait and the answer are one pill in one place: "Analysing the film" becomes "Subtitles: static +0.2s" where it stood, and goes after five seconds. It was a system toast before, which cannot be coloured and lands wherever Android puts it.

In the chooser, a track's colour says how it reaches the screen - green drawn over the picture, amber burned into it - which is what the key underneath has always said. The words at the end of every name said it a second time and are gone.

title: No subtitles in the first hour of a film
items: Fixed: every cue in the first hour of a long film was thrown away. ffmpeg writes WebVTT the way the specification allows - MM:SS.mmm below an hour, H:MM:SS.mmm above it - and the code assumed the second shape everywhere. On one 146-minute film that turned 1992 cues into 947, the first one at 58:58. Timestamps are now read in either shape, written in one, and normalised where the subtitle enters the program.

Embedded subtitles are pulled out of the film once and kept. The whole track, not the part after the seek, so one copy answers every seek in the film. A cold 8 GB file took over the 90 seconds the extraction was allowed and the player showed nothing at all; from the cache it is 60 milliseconds.

Subtitle placement across the library, 14 films: 11 placed, 1 refused, 2 with nothing readable in the chosen track. Measurements from 20 to 326 seconds - the slow ones are the first read of a large file.
App: the "Analysing the film" mark waits at the bottom of the picture, where the answer appears, instead of the top. The always tick is called auto, as in the browser. 0.14.15, code 243.

title: "Could not place it" was the app giving up too early
items: Fixed: the app waited 30 seconds for a subtitle measurement and reported "could not place it" when that ran out - while the server went on and succeeded. Measured on a 106-minute film with nothing cached: 33 seconds. Sync now gets five minutes; every other request keeps the old limit. 0.14.14, code 242.

pd-soak.py: 25 minutes, 546 rounds of streaming, seeking, subtitle fetches and polling. Memory 51.0 to 48.5 MB (worst 52.6), handles 228 to 225, threads flat, no sessions left open, no ffmpeg left running, no tracebacks.

pd-subcheck.py: places the subtitles of every film in turn and reports what happened - how many placed, how many refused, and how long each took. Nothing is saved; the library's own corrections are untouched.

title: AVPlay on Samsung sets
items: Where a television offers Samsung's AVPlay, the client plays through it instead of the browser's video element: the panel decodes MKV and HEVC that the engine refuses, so files play untouched rather than being re-encoded by the server. Subtitles are drawn by the client over it, since AVPlay has no cue layer of its own. The player's information line names which player has the film.
All of it is behind one test for the AVPlay API, so nothing changes anywhere else. Unproven on a real set - the calls follow Samsung's documentation and have not been run on a television.
pd-soak.py: leaves a server playing against a copy of the real library for as long as asked, sampling memory, handles, threads and stray ffmpeg processes.

title: Samsung TV, and the app can give a password
items: App: a server with a password says so, and the address screen asks for it rather than showing an error nobody can act on. /auth/state tells a password apart from somebody else's server; /login returns a token the app keeps the way it keeps an invitation. 0.14.13, code 241.

Samsung TVs: the invite page now says how to get Palladium onto one. The shortest route is the television's own browser and the invitation link - the client is a web page. For an icon on the home row there is /tizen.zip: the source of a Tizen web app with this server's address already written in, or a guest's invitation if downloaded from their row. Build and sign it in Tizen Studio with your own certificate - Samsung installs nothing signed by anybody else - and the page lists the five commands.

title: An owner password, and who counts as the owner
items: There is now an owner password. Optional and off until set - a server with one person on the network needs none - and offered as the fourth step of the first run and in Settings.

Before: anyone whose address looked private was the owner. That is a decision on a home network and no decision at all behind a reverse proxy or in a container, where every request arrives from the gateway and so every caller was the owner. With a password set, the address proves nothing: only this machine gets in without asking, and only when the request did not come through a proxy (X-Forwarded-For, Forwarded or X-Real-IP).

Login is rate limited: eight wrong tries per address, then five minutes of refusals including the right one. Stored as PBKDF2-SHA256, 200k rounds, with a random salt. Sessions are random 48-character tokens with a six-month life, kept server-side and dropped when the password changes.
The locked page offers a password box when one is set, so an owner away from home has a way in rather than a refusal.

Fixed: a password could be set and never removed. Settings are written by merging top-level keys, so a key left out of the write is restored from the file - removal had to be an empty value, not a missing one. Anything else that deletes a top-level setting has the same trap.

title: First run
items: A new install opens a setup page instead of an empty library: pick the folders your films and series are in, paste a TMDB key, fetch ffmpeg if the machine has none, scan. It appears until there is something in the library, and never after.
Fetching ffmpeg is one press - a static build, ~80 MB, unpacked into the papers folder and used without a restart. Remembered for the next run.
Fixed: /config answered 500 on a machine with no config.json. It is the first thing any page asks for, so a new install drew nothing at all - including the setup page. The smoke test now asks for it.
The folder browser lists mount points where there are no drive letters, for Linux and for the container.

title: Stability: a fresh install answers everything
items: No request can close a connection without an answer. Any unhandled fault is a 500 with one line and a full traceback in the log; the browser saw a dead connection before, which is indistinguishable from the server having died.
Fixed: every page touching the transcoder crashed on a new install, because engine() read config.json unconditionally and a new install has none.
Fixed: a rating key that is not a number ("l1", empty) crashed /subs/plan and /subs/reset. Keys come from clients and are now checked.

pd-smoke.py: starts a server with an empty folder on a free port and walks 40 endpoints, failing on any 500 or traceback. An empty folder is what a new install is, which is the state hardest to test by using the program.
pd-server.py takes --port and --root, so a second copy disturbs nothing.
README rewritten - it still described the program as a client for somebody else's server.
The Windows installer builds, for the first time: Nuitka compiles the server and the tray to native executables and Inno Setup wraps them. 32 MB, no Python needed on the machine it lands on.
The build proves itself before it is wrapped - the smoke test runs against the compiled server, and a failure stops the release rather than shipping.

Fixed: ffmpeg was only looked for in WinGet's package folder. It is now looked for beside the program and on PATH first, which is how every other install puts it - and the only way it can be found at all on Linux.
Dockerfile and a compose example: python:3.13-slim plus ffmpeg, runs as its own user, everything it writes on a volume, films mounted read-only.

The installer is tested, not just built: pd-try-installer.py installs it silently to a temporary folder with no Startup shortcut and no firewall rule, walks the 40 endpoints against the installed server, and uninstalls. Result: 49 files, no UAC prompt, 0 failures, and %APPDATA% untouched.
A silent uninstall no longer asks whether to remove your settings - it keeps them and says nothing. The prompt hung any scripted uninstall, including one done by a later installer replacing this one.

title: Fetched ahead, placed ahead
items: A subtitle fetched for the next episode is measured against the film as soon as it lands, when auto is on - five minutes before the episode is reached, so the first line is already in step. Server-side and silent; failures say nothing, as with everything about fetching ahead.
App: a measurement nobody asked for draws no overlay and raises no toast. Only a press on Sync to film reports back.

title: Timing row in the app
items: -1s and +1s removed; the tenths buttons repeat while held, starting at one step and speeding up to twenty a second. Touch and the remote's centre key both.
Sync to film is drawn as a filled button, not a bare word.
Web: pressing anywhere outside the CC, Aa, sound or quality panel closes it. Presses inside it do not, including ones that redraw the panel.

Web: choosing a subtitle file, or downloading one (which selects it), reads that file's own correction and analyses the film when auto is on. Only a track change that restarts the stream did it before; swapping a sidecar in kept the previous file's timing. The CC panel redraws when the measurement lands.

title: Subtitle panel layout
items: Tracks are a dropdown instead of a row of pills, with verify and delete beside it. Release names run 40+ characters and wrapped over several lines.
App: the same dropdown. Off is its first entry, the tick beside it verifies whichever track is showing, and the colour key is gone - text or burned in is written in the entry.

One row per job: Show, Get, Timing, and the line stating what is applied. Timing carries the tenths, Sync to film and the auto checkbox (was "automatically"). Eight controls shared one wrapping row in a 460 px panel before.
Off is the first entry in the dropdown; the separate Off button is gone.
Delete is a waste-bin icon, not a cross - the cross is the glyph the panels use for close - and asks a second time: Delete file / Cancel, with the filename shown.

title: Phone player controls
items: Phone: CC moved into the bottom row next to Aa; picture-size (F/Z) moved to the top corner with cast and quality. TV layout unchanged.

title: Subtitle menus mark the setting in use
items: Size and Height mark the nearest option instead of requiring an exact match. Stored values are not always one of the offered ones (older files, other clients, the 0.14.6 rescale), which left the row with nothing marked. App, Aa panel and settings page.
TV: focus starts on the option in use, not the first in the row. Leanback only.
Phone default height 0.05 -> 0.08. 0.05 matched none of the four options.

title: Subtitle position
items: Bottom now sits at the bottom in the browser. cue.line is the bottom of the text box; the code subtracted a fixed 6% of height as a height allowance, leaving the last line that far up.
1% of height kept clear under the last line, browser and app, so descenders are not cut by the panel edge. Measured at 1262x624: 1% clear, second line grows upward.
Position steps are one text row, as in the app. Were 0/8/16/28% of height = 1.25, 1.25, 1.9 rows. Now 31, 37, 37 px against a 40 px row. A two-line cue keeps the same bottom row.
Row height is measured, not set: Chrome ignores line-height on ::cue. 1.32 x font size. snapToLines is not usable - Chrome draws a two-line cue at the bottom for line -1 and -2 alike.
Settings states the size scale: 100% = 5% of screen height, with each screen's setting in per cent and in pixels at 1080 and 4K.
CC and Aa moved next to each other in the web player controls.

title: One scale for subtitle size
items: 100% = 5% of the height of the screen it is drawn on, everywhere. Was 2.7% in the browser, 5.33% in the app (Media3 default), and burned-in bitmaps scaled 0.60 to match the browser - so one setting came out ~2x larger on a TV.
5% is WebVTT's default; CEA-608 is 5.33%.

Stored sizes are rescaled once at server start by the ratio of the old base to the new, so nothing changes on screen. settings.json records the base. Measured: web 1.5 -> 0.81 = 4.05% of the window before and after.
Burn factor 0.60 -> 1.11 (a PGS plane is authored at ~4.5% of frame height).

title: Subtitle sync: drift, steps, reset
items: Sync reports the shape it found - static, drift or steps - and the numbers, in both clients. A drift is given as both ends, e.g. -1.8s -> -4.5s.

Drift is fitted by a line through the readings that agree, not the loudest window: best four peaks per window, a line through every pair, keep the line at least three windows sit within 0.6s of. Rates snapped to standard framerate ratios.
Claims over 10s need a second window or are refused. Killed a -104s reading from one lucky match.
Sound-only cues ([door slams], music notes) dropped before correlating.
Steps: window readings clustered, boundary found by bisection. Verified plans stored per subtitle file and reapplied without measuring again.
Reset restores the file's own timing, beside the line stating what is applied.
Embedded tracks read and synced in both clients. Sidecar indices no longer discarded. Guests may verify a fit.
AMD AMF and Intel Quick Sync encoders alongside NVENC, picked by what the machine has.
Watch log: newest first, 24- or 12-hour by setting, device type shown, titles link to the poster or the season.
ffmpeg and ffprobe no longer open console windows.

Search takes an episode code: s4e9, S04E09, s4 e9, 4x09. Alone it lists that place in every series; after a series name it narrows to that series. Episodes lead the results for a code, titles for words.

Fixed: subtitles ran early on a resumed re-encode. The stream is asked for a whole second; the browser measured cues against the fractional resume point (208.7 vs 208), so every line ran 0.7s early. Direct play was unaffected, so it only showed up off the LAN.
Fixed: a sync plan was applied in the stream's clock, not the film's. A track pulled from a live encode starts at zero; 20 min in, a 0.2%/min drift came out 2.7s under-corrected.
Fixed: a plan on a double episode was discarded when its two subtitle files were joined.

Fixed: the library flashed through the picture when a stream restarted (seek past the encoded window, quality or subtitle change, next episode). The teardown hid the player and redrew the page behind it.

title: Subtitle timing measured across the film
items: The film is swept in five windows of four minutes, evenly spread, and each is placed on its own. One answer says how late the subtitle is; five say whether it stays that way.

A correction can be in parts. Measured on one episode: +1.10, +1.20, +1.00, +3.70, +3.90 across the film - not a slope but a step, because the release carries something the subtitle's master did not. The plan is +1.2 s from the start and +3.8 s from 11:15, and the server serves the file mended that way. Verified against the served text: 193 cues moved +1.20, the other 223 moved +3.80.
The CC menu says which it is: "static +1.2s", or "+1.2s, then +3.8s from 11:15". A drift or a step is named by its numbers rather than by the method.
A single correction is still kept as a plain number the viewer can see and undo; only a correction in parts is applied to the file as it is served.
Windows that could not be placed are dropped, and a lone window disagreeing with both its neighbours is treated as a bad reading rather than a third part.
Measuring always starts from the file on disk: it ignores any correction already stored, so running it twice gives the same answer and nothing compounds.

The foot of the CC menu is three rows: timing and "Sync to film" together on the first, what the measurement decided on its own row beneath when there is anything to say, and Download and Close last. The note used to sit among the buttons and push them along as it appeared.

A file corrected in parts can still be nudged by hand, and the menu says so: the number reads "Extra" rather than "Timing", with the correction in force printed underneath. The two add up - the server's plan puts the subtitle in the right place, and the nudge is what somebody adds on top of it.
The player asks what is already in force on the way in, so the menu shows it before anything is pressed rather than only after a measurement.
The label on the timing row sits level with the buttons beside it.

Three kinds of correction can be in force. Static: one offset, kept as the number in the CC menu, which anybody can see and undo. Parts: two or more offsets with the point they change at, for a release carrying something the subtitle's master did not. Rate: a framerate ratio applied to the whole file, for a subtitle written for 25 fps and played against 23.976.

A framerate mismatch cannot be measured window by window - four per cent adrift is ten seconds inside a four-minute window, so every reading is noise - so the ratios anybody actually ships are tried by name instead, and the one that makes both ends of the film agree wins. Recovered 25-against-23.976 exactly, in 0.8 s.
Each window is searched around what the window before it found rather than around nought, so a correction that grows through the film stays inside the search.
The CC menu is wider, so the timing controls, "Sync to film" and its tick stay on one line.

"In force" is shown whenever a correction is being applied - one worked out automatically on the way in, one pressed for, or a plain number somebody set by hand - not only after a measurement in this sitting.

A plan already worked out is kept: the film is not listened to again for an answer somebody already has. Automatic timing skips a subtitle that has a plan or a correction against it; "Sync to film" still measures from scratch whenever it is pressed.

Where a step happens is pinned by listening inside the gap between the two windows that disagree, halving it three times - so the boundary is known to under a minute instead of to the five minutes between windows. It moved 11:15 -> 10:35 on the episode this was found on.

A stored plan is shown on the way in, whether it was worked out a moment ago or a week ago. It was asked for by the title, which the player fetches only when a panel wants it - so at the moment it was asked there usually was not one, and the line stayed empty until something else had loaded it. It is asked for by the key now.
The CC menu is narrower again, with the timing row tightened by the same amount so nothing wraps.

The CC menu is the width of its widest row and no wider, between a floor that keeps the timing row on one line and a ceiling that keeps a long file name from stretching it across the screen. "always" is never wrapped or cut.

The grey square around a subtitle in that list is gone: it was the press highlight, painted over the whole box because nothing had clipped it to the rounded ends. The row is clipped now and wears a white ring when the remote is on it.
The verify tick is a round button ringed white when the remote is on it, like every other button. The grey square behind it was the press highlight drawn over a box nothing had clipped.
The timing row sits on one line: a Material checkbox claims a 48dp touch target, taller than the pills beside it, which lifted "always" off the line.

A film paused for five minutes lets the television sleep again. Playing keeps the screen awake, which is right; keeping it awake around a still frame and a row of controls all night is how an OLED panel learns them.
The date on a release in What's new keeps its own line. With no weight of its own the title took the whole width of a phone held upright and left the date wrapping one character to a line.

Automatic timing runs when a film starts, which is the one moment it never did. It asked for the title first and the player fetches a title only when a panel wants one - so at the start of a playing there was none, and the run returned without a word. Pressing the button worked because opening the menu had fetched it. It goes by the key now, as everything else in the player does.

A new episode is noticed. The folder watch looked two levels down - the programmes, and the names of the seasons inside them - so an episode dropped into an existing season changed nothing it was looking at: not the programme's folder, not the list of seasons. Each season folder's own timestamp is watched now, which is the thing that actually moves. Until this, a new episode waited for the daily scan.

A subtitle track lifted out of a film draws again. ffmpeg writes WebVTT without the hour below an hour - "00:13.513" - and the app's reader insisted on it, so an embedded track came back as no cues at all and nothing appeared. Files beside the film were unaffected: those are converted from SubRip, which always carries the hour.

The Aa menu says grey is kinder to an OLED than white, with "Info" beside it: how bright each colour is against white - white 100%, yellow 80% with a third as much blue, green 66%, grey 64%, cyan 57% - why the blue matters, and the two other things that help. Shorter than it was, and it fits without scrolling.

A film whose only subtitle is inside it opens with that one chosen. The page took the one chosen last time, or a file beside the video, and stopped there - so a fresh download with nothing but its own English track opened with no subtitle at all, and nothing to say why.

The Aa panel fits on a television without scrolling. Four groups of choices, the gaps above them and a sample of the text came to a line more than the screen had: the sample is 46dp rather than 58, each group takes 5dp above it rather than 8, the OLED note is one line, and the dialog reserves 84dp for its own furniture rather than 130.

Sound cues no longer count as speech when a subtitle is measured. A track for the deaf writes "[jovial music]" and "(door slams)" exactly where nobody is talking, which is the opposite of the thing being looked for: on one episode every window came back under the line, two of them absurd - +79.7 s and -32.4 s. Ignoring those cues, the same windows read -0.1 to +0.8 and the subtitle was placed at +0.2.

The watch log records which build was watching again. Every other request names the app; the progress report - the one the log is written from - did not, so every line said nothing, which is exactly the line you want when somebody says a thing does not work on their phone.

A guest can vouch for a subtitle. Marking one verified is a fact about the file, and the person who has just watched it is the one who knows - but the tick was owner-only, so on a phone signed in with an invitation it answered 403 and appeared to do nothing. Removing or hiding a subtitle stays the owner's.
A refused tick says so instead of doing nothing quietly.

One window can no longer carry a whole film. A correction of a second or two from a single window is believed; anything past ten seconds has to be seconded - the candidate is applied to the subtitle and every window asked again, and a real offset makes several of them agree at nought while a lucky peak makes none. On one episode this turned a confident -104.5 s into no correction at all, which is the right answer: its first window read -2.1 s and the rest were noise.
When a large claim is refused, the quiet answer gets a chance: a window that was not sure enough alone but says the subtitle is nearly right, seconded the same way.

When five windows find nothing that stands up, it listens again in more places for less time at each - eleven of three minutes instead of five of four, capped by how long the thing runs. A film that could not be placed gets a second look before the answer is "could not place it", and the extra pass only happens when the first one failed.
Whole seconds in the CC menu, beside the tenths: a subtitle two seconds out is two presses rather than twenty.

A drift no single window can see is found by agreement between them. When nothing stands up on its own, the best few peaks from every window are taken - not just each window's favourite - and the line that most of them sit on is the answer. On one episode the windows read -35.8, +31.6, -3.2, -3.7 and +22.9, and four of them sit on a line from -1.8 s at the start to -4.5 s at twenty minutes, which is what the viewer had measured by eye.
A correction with a rate in it is called a drift rather than static.

The browser names the sync in force under the timing controls: "static +0.2s", "drift -1.8s -> -4.5s", "steps +1.2s, then +3.8s from 10:35", "by hand +1.0s", or none. A correction that is not a single number could not be read off the box beside the plus and minus, which showed nought over a subtitle the server had put right.
The watch log is newest first by when the viewing began, which is the time it prints - it was ordered by when each row was last touched, so a long viewing sat above a later short one.
Times are written 2026-08-26 22:41 rather than in the browser's own way, and Settings carries a Time row: 24-hour or 12-hour, kept per viewer.

The watch log says what kind of thing was watching - Google TV app, Android app, LG TV browser, Samsung TV browser, iPhone, iPad, Chromecast, Mac, Windows - beside the name the device calls itself by. Worked out from how it asks rather than from what it is called.

A title in the watch log opens what was watched: a film on its own page, an episode on its programme at the right season with that episode found. It was a line of text about something you then had to go and look for.
The browser and the app say the same five things about a subtitle's timing: "static +1.2s", "drift -1.8s -> -4.5s", "steps +1.2s, then +3.8s from 10:35", "by hand +1.0s", or "none".
A correction the film asked for is no longer called "by hand". The two are the same number in the same place, so the server now records which of them put it there, and says so when asked.
The line is written again when a measurement finishes rather than on a timer, so it no longer reads "none" over a correction that landed a moment later.
A drift is stored as a plan rather than as a plain number - stored as a number the rate was thrown away and the drift came straight back.

A rate that moves the last line of a film by less than a third of a second is called static, which is what it is: two windows measured a tenth of a second apart over twenty minutes will produce a rate, and dressing that up as a drift is precision nobody can see.
The subtitle timing says "Analysing the film" rather than "Listening to the film", in the browser and in the app. It is a measurement, not an ear.

The library's own P sits beside "Analysing" while a subtitle is being placed, in the browser and in the app - the same mark the top bar wears. In the browser it breathes gently, and holds still for anybody who has asked for less motion.

Reset, beside Sync to film in both clients: the subtitle goes back to what its own file says - the plan the server was applying and anything nudged on top of it, both gone. What the file says is always recoverable; a correction is not, which is why it is a button somebody presses.

The answer names its mode. "Subtitles: drift -1.8s -> -4.5s", "Subtitles: steps +1.2s, then +3.8s from 10:35", "Subtitles: static +0.9s" - a measurement that comes back as a rate means something different from one that comes back as a number, and the message used to hide that.

While a subtitle is being placed, the message over the picture carries the library's P in its own gold: on the television it is drawn by the app rather than handed to Android, which cannot colour a message; in the browser it leads the line in the toast.

title: Automatic subtitle sync
items: Subtitle auto-sync: ffmpeg decodes audio at 8 kHz mono, 100 ms frames, first 35 min; two signals (band energy 200-3000 Hz vs median, and band/total energy ratio); Pearson cross-correlation against cue on/off array; ±120 s search at 0.5 s, refined to 0.1 s.
Confidence = 1 − (best score ≥5 s from peak ÷ peak). Gate 0.35, minimum peak r 0.12. Below that: no offset applied, nothing written.
Measured: offsets of 0/1.4/2.7/3.5/7/8/12/45/110 s recovered exactly. Stereo film r=0.67, 7.1 UHD rip with an embedded track r=0.44, cartoon r=0.52, a subtitle from another film 0.00 (refused).
CC menu: "Sync to film" (one-off) and "always" checkbox (per viewer, server-side setting autoSync). Runs on playback start when no saved offset exists.
Offsets saved server-side per subtitle (key l<ratingKey>|<sub>), shared by all viewers and clients. Shift limit raised 30 s → 30 min.
Centre channel (pan=mono|c0=FC) used when layout is 5.1/7.1; falls back to downmix if silent. Halves runtime and doubles peak correlation on action films.
Per-film audio signal and extracted embedded tracks cached in memory (8 films): first sync 3-9 s, repeats ~0.3 s. Subtitle extraction from a UHD remux is ~80 s, once.
Applied client-side to cues already in hand: no restart, no re-fetch, picture untouched.
CC menu footer is one FlowRow including Close; was overlapping the confirm/dismiss slots and hiding Download.
Auto-sync failures are silent; only the explicit button reports.
Subtitle height "Bottom" no longer makes them vanish: a cue anchored at line 1.0 has its text clipped away at the view's edge, so the line is capped at 0.97.

A subtitle beside the film survives a restart. Sidecars are numbered -1, -2, so the "-1 means none" test threw the chosen subtitle away whenever the stream restarted - a change of soundtrack, of quality, or headphones connecting.

The player asks which screen it is on. It can start without the library screen ever running, and the subtitle look is kept per screen, so a television saving as a phone never read its own setting back.

Transcoding runs on AMD (AMF) and Intel Quick Sync as well as NVENC, and on VideoToolbox where that exists. The encoder is probed at startup with a one-second test encode - being listed in the build proves nothing - and the first that works is used, in that order, with x264 as the fallback.
The player's one trace line now says which subtitle is on, how many cues it holds, the correction applied, the height asked for, whether automatic timing is on and which screen it thinks it is.

Subtitle height is the cue's alone. The view was also being padded from the bottom, so measured on the television "Bottom" - which asks for 0.93 of the height - was drawn at 0.85: the padding had been applied from the default 0.08 before the real setting or a single cue had arrived.

A subtitle that drifts is straightened rather than shifted. Measured over the first half of the film and the last: when the two disagree by more than 0.6 s the correction is a rate as well as an offset, and the server serves the file already put right - one number cannot describe a drift. One episode measured +1.1 s at the start and +3.8 s at the end; it is now within a quarter of a second throughout.
When a drifting subtitle is straightened the player says so and fetches the corrected file, rather than reporting a correction of 0.0 and appearing to have done nothing.

A measured drift is rounded to a real framerate ratio when it plainly is one - 25 against 23.976 is 4.271%, 24 against 23.976 is 0.100% - since the exact figure is right for the whole film where a measurement is close for most of it. A rate that matches none of them is kept as measured: the episode that prompted this runs 0.400% slow, which is an edit difference rather than a framerate.

Drift is measured across the whole film. Two windows of twelve minutes, one at each end, rather than the first thirty-five minutes - a slope taken from the opening half hour and applied to a two-hour film is an extrapolation four times longer than the thing it was measured on. Both windows cost what one long listen cost.

The player says what the timing decided, every time: "auto +1.0s", "drift, straightened" or "could not place it", beside Timing in the CC menu and as a message on screen. It used to apply a correction of 0.0 for a straightened file and look as though the button had done nothing.

Subtitle height is counted in rows of text, one row per step: Bottom sits along the bottom, Just up is one subtitle above it, Raised two and High three. A fraction of the screen was clipped away entirely near the bottom and meant different amounts on different screens; a row follows the text size, which is what the setting means.
"Sync to film" closes the CC menu while it listens - the answer is about what is on screen, and the menu was covering it - and says so as it starts.
What the measurement decided is printed on the menu's heading line instead of among the buttons, where it pushed them along as it appeared and changed.

A straightened subtitle says what the correction comes to rather than naming the method: "runs slow against the film - corrected, -0.2s at the start and +4.5s at the end", and "drift -0.2s -> +4.5s" on the menu's heading.

title: Marks, subtitle timing, reports
items: Marks: marking a show or season now writes a mark on each episode, so a single episode can be removed. /marks returns all/some/none per key.

Watchlist and casual shelves return covers/part - which seasons and shows the marked episodes add up to - so posters and pages show the mark on the parent. Half-marked: hollow star, dimmed shuffle mark.
Both shelves grouped into season cards (ratingKey <item>-s<n>), with shelfCount when only part of a season is marked. Lone episodes and films unchanged.
Season card opens its show at that season instead of season 1.
Both shelves re-read on entry to every screen; app refetches watchlist/casual after any mark change (marksTouched counter in the cache key).
Per-episode watchlist and shuffle ticks in the browser, inheriting show/season state; show and season buttons set or clear all at once.
Subtitle timing: ±0.1 s per press in the CC menu, saved server-side per subtitle per episode. Browser shifts cues in place; app redraws its own cues - no restart either way.
Timing applies to embedded tracks as well as sidecars.
Subtitle timing and picked file kept while a title is part-watched or its subtitle is verified; swept daily otherwise.
Verification stays manual or earned by watching - moving a subtitle no longer marks it verified.
Per-viewer quality preference (height + Mbit) stored server-side, applied across browser, phone and TV; server ceilings still cap it.
Server ceilings settable from the app (LAN only), one box for in-house and remote.

Film page: qualities above the effective ceiling shown red and disabled with the reason; page opens on the best allowed rung; server rejects over-limit requests including direct play of files above the ceiling.
Same Mbit rungs everywhere: 20/12/8/5/4/2. Choosing 5 Mbps now asks the encoder for 5 Mbit.
Bitrate chip on film and episode pages in the app (e.g. 7.7 Mbit/s), as the browser has.
Runtime on the line under the title: "2024 · 1 h 50 min".
Next-episode delay setting: 0-5 s, browser and app, inside the Next episode box.
Reports: users can cancel their own requests (kept, marked withdrawn); owner can edit wording.
Reports tab hidden while Films or TV is open; lives on Home.
Top bar split into two rows on every screen; overflowing rows show an end arrow.
TV keyboard: å ä ö, punctuation row, and a shift key (once / lock / off), starting in caps.
Invite list and watch log record the client build; app names itself on every request.
Undated titles sort last in both directions for year and release.
Series cards sorted by release show last-aired date rather than first year.
Previous button restarts the episode; only within the first 10 s does it go back one.
Opening and closing a player no longer creates a Continue watching entry from the stop report alone.
Per-request identity in the library object: a guest's progress could appear in the owner's Continue watching.
Duplicate copies of one file (same size and duration) collapse into one version - one film was offered three times.
Genre selection cleared when switching between Films and TV unless the new tab has it.
Player shows one panel at a time; soundtrack and quality panels had no CSS rule and drew nowhere.
CC panel key drawn once, not twice.
Browser fault reporter installed at the top of app.js so a parse error still reports.
App: subtitles drawn once (Media3's own text track disabled), at the height the Aa setting asks (the view was padded as well as the cue).
App: film page fits a phone in landscape - poster and title shrink, facts row wraps, plot truncates; Aa and player buttons drawn as buttons.
App: Resume time re-read when returning from a film.
Version picker moved to its own row under the marks.
The old naming removed from all user-visible text; protocol paths and headers unchanged.
Update banner focuses the Update button on launch when one is waiting.
One subtitle at a time on TV: overlapping cues collapse to the most recent, max two lines.
Dual-language subtitle files (English cues followed by Chinese on the same timestamps) served as one language, chosen by the file's declared language; a few foreign lines are left alone.
Double episodes: two half-timed subtitle files joined into one, offset found from the black frames between parts and remembered.

Scanner: episode numbering checked against titles in the filename - a release that counts a double episode as two was one ahead for the rest of the season. 199 seasons checked, 1 renumbered; episodes move, so progress and marks stay with the file.

title: Quality limits, audio, media session
items: Player gear: picture size (original/1080p/720p) and Mbit, browser and app. Both settled at encode time, so a change restarts from the current position.
Choice persists across next episode, subtitle and soundtrack changes, and casual draws.
Settings → Quality: two server ceilings, one for the LAN and one for remote. Effective limit is the lower of viewer and server; the gear says which applies.
Media3's own settings button hidden - two gears said different things.
Player buttons sized against available width (32-48 dp), not fixed: eight buttons overflowed a phone in portrait and the gear was dropped.
Gear opens on first press (it was waiting on metadata another panel happened to fetch).
Phone: cast, CC and gear in the top-right corner sharing the info bar's line; TV keeps one row.
Aa dialog: two columns in landscape, tighter rows on short screens, Done on the title line.
Quality panel in two columns - Picture and Line.
Audio: unsupported soundtrack (Dolby on a box without a licence) detected and re-requested as AAC once, instead of silent playback.
Direct play picks the soundtrack matching the viewer's subtitle language rather than the first track.
Bluetooth headphones on a TV box get stereo AAC from the start.
Media session published: headphone and remote media keys pause and resume.
OffsetPlayer wrapper presents the film's own duration and seekability to the controls - a live encode's timeline has neither, which broke the progress bar and seeking whenever audio was transcoded.
Sidecar subtitles cut to the encode's start offset and re-fetched on seek; a live encode starts its clock at zero.
Audio focus requested on play and released on pause; a call now ducks the film. Keeps the Bluetooth link open while paused.
Playback pauses when headphones disconnect and resumes when they return.
One encode per device: previous encodes are stopped, and start timeouts raised - four concurrent encodes made casual episodes fail to start.
Update flow: download progress percentage, button locked while downloading, banner stays up during install, kept APK matched by version rather than size.
Compose focus-search crash on Google TV fixed (key dropped, focus cleared).
Full screen works in Safari on iPhone (webkitEnterFullscreen on the video element).

title: Casting, invites, portrait layout
items: Cast to a TV works: playlist reads reuse one ffmpeg session (each read used to start a new encode), VOD playlist written in full so the receiver has a duration, seeks restart the encoder at that point. Verified 373 segments, 1 s seeks.
Locked page for a browser with no invitation: what it is, plus a box taking the link or the 5-letter code, instead of a bare 403.
Invitation cookie lasts a year and renews on every visit.
Fix match closes with ✕, Escape or a click outside; watchlist and shuffle buttons match the Play button's height.
Film buttons wrap in portrait - Mark watched was off the edge of the screen.
Marking watched clears the resume point in both clients.

title: Subtitle matching by title
items: Subtitle search matched by episode title, not by number: OpenSubtitles numbered one series' season 3 an episode out from E29, so every fetch was an episode off.
Neighbouring episodes searched when numbering disagrees; candidates for other episodes marked and sorted below; automatic fetch takes the right episode or nothing.
Reports split into three tabs (new, errors, requests) in browser and app, each with its own compose box; guests see the same lists, addresses withheld, owner-only actions.
Now playing screen under Settings with totals: viewers, aggregate rate, data sent, transcodes, hours.
Watch log under Settings: who, what, when, how long, which device - backfilled from existing progress.
Player releases the video decoder when the device takes it back mid-film and returns as a transcode.
Player info line reads Mbit/s and cumulative data.
Casual play defaults to shuffle; stopping part-way resumes there without appearing in Continue watching. Rota mode removed.
Watchlist and Casual are separate tabs; Start over confirms and forgets half-watched episodes.
CC opens whether or not subtitles are on; Aa is appearance only.

title: Casual shelf
items: Casual shelf beside the watchlist: one control, two halves (yellow watchlist, green casual), independent of each other.
Casual play draws from the shelf; Turn takes one episode per programme in rotation, Shuffle takes anything; no repeats until the shelf is exhausted.
Each mode keeps its own position, counter and reset; the counter continues past shelf size (434/400 on the second pass).
Queue settled 10 deep so the next subtitle can be fetched during playback.
Casual watching does not touch watched state, Continue watching or series progress.
Marks work on show, season, episode and film, on every client.
Player next/previous: adjacent episodes, or the next and previous draw.
Changelog readable in the app under Settings.

title: Soundtracks, genres, fix match
items: All audio tracks indexed and selectable (second language, commentary, stereo beside 5.1), browser and app.
Genre filter and Released sort; Released is the default for films and TV.
Recently added TV grouped by season rather than one card per episode.
Fix match: re-identify a wrongly matched title - name, year, artwork, plot, episode list.
Continue watching shows one row per programme; posters can be ticked watched or forgotten.

title: Report handling
items: Reports can be resolved with cause and fix attached, visible to whoever reported it.
Resolved reports sink below open ones and stop counting as unread; clearing archives rather than deletes, and can be undone.
App reports its own faults with device and version.
Changelog page: what each version added.

title: Safari, TV browsers, guest settings
items: iOS home-screen install: own icon, standalone, pre-authenticated. Apple clients are served HLS, the only thing Safari accepts from this server.
LG and Samsung TV browsers served the same way.
App installable on a TV via a 5-character code in Downloader; the same code stands in for a token.
Guests get their own settings: subtitle defaults per screen, per-film overrides, fonts; reports read-only.
AC-3 in fragmented MP4 requires delay_moov - without it 237 files (7% of the library) returned a 984-byte header and no picture on TVs.

title: Subtitle download and verification
items: OpenSubtitles search and download inside the player; the next episode's subtitle is fetched five minutes before the current one ends.
Every downloaded variant kept and named for its release rather than overwritten.
Subtitles can be marked verified per episode per language, embedded tracks included; verified sorts first and survives an episode watched without subtitles.
Ranking prefers the release the video came from; PGS/VobSub are burned in.
CC chooses and downloads, Aa is appearance (size, face, colour, background, height) on every client, with a legend for text vs burned in.
Cues drawn by the browser's own layer - anything drawn over a hardware-overlaid video is invisible.

title: Invites and guests
items: Invitations: one link with a token, named, revocable, optionally expiring.
Guests reach the library, artwork, streams and the app download only - no config, no diagnostics, no other viewer's data.
The invite page exchanges the token for a session cookie.
Now playing: who is watching what, from where, direct or transcoded, at what rate.
Reports and requests from any viewer, visible to all.

title: Android app
items: One app for phone and Google TV: library, D-pad focus handling, Media3 player.
Direct play wherever the device can decode; the server's transcoder only where it cannot.
Casting from the app; in-app update from the server rather than a store.
Crash reporting with device and version.

title: Own library index
items: Own scanner: folder walk, ffprobe for real codecs, TMDB for artwork, plot and episode names.
Everything cached on disk; a rescan touches only what changed.
Films, shows, seasons, episodes, with progress per viewer.
No longer needs another server running.

title: NVENC transcoder
items: GPU transcoding: decode, scale and encode on the card with NVENC.
Measured 16x realtime for 4K → 1080p against 2.4x on the CPU.
Fragmented MP4 over one connection instead of segment files: one process, one response, no client-side library.
10-bit HEVC converted on the GPU (h264_nvenc cannot encode 10-bit); audio keeps its channel count.

title: First release
items: Browser client: browse films and TV, play in the page, cast to a television.
Direct play where the browser can manage it, a transcode where it cannot.
Continue watching with progress reported back.
Keyboard shortcuts for search and escape; sessions reaped when a tab closes.
